# TO THE MOST AUGUST PRINCE

## WILLIAM,

### KING of Great Britain, France, and 
### Ireland.

Had the demands of a grateful soul and a sense of duty not almost compelled me, I would not have dared to inscribe the sacred name of so great a Prince upon these studies of mine, whatever they may be. For to you, to whom we owe everything—our entire fortunes, our liberty, our life itself, and even that which is dearer than life, our Religion <note>This refers to the "Glorious Revolution" of 1688, where William III took the throne to protect Protestantism and English liberties</note>—it is too little to offer these small gifts of a slender wit or of literary leisure. Nor can we be equal to the task of celebrating your praises, we who are already unequal to the task of returning sufficient thanks.

<margin>Look! A comparison, not bad, or rather excellent, between two rulers <term>dynarchs; powerful lords</term> of the same age! Namely, both in the flower of their youth, both Arcadians <note>original: "Arcadas ambo"; a literary reference from Virgil's Eclogues meaning peers or equals in character</note>, both consumed by the same ambition—But you, conquered province, lament! <note>original: "At tu victria provincia ploras!"; a reference to the irony of a province "winning" a legal case but being financially ruined by it</note></margin>

Most Illustrious Prince, two virtues especially constitute a great-souled man: Fortitude <term>courage and strength of mind</term> and Clemency <term>mercy or leniency</term>. Not [only do we call] you Brave...

<summary>This is the opening of a formal dedication to King William III, expressing profound gratitude for his role in securing the religion and liberties of his subjects. The author humble-brags about his own literary work while positioning the King as a paragon of the classical virtues of fortitude and mercy.</summary>
<keywords>William III, dedication, Glorious Revolution, Protestantism, patronage, fortitude, clemency, Virgil, political loyalty</keywords>

# Dedicatory Letter.

We call you brave, but we also lament it: for you are reckless with a life upon which the safety of us all and the very lives of us all depend. Nor do we merely proclaim your Clemency <term>mercy or leniency</term>, which is known to the entire world; rather, we pray as humble suppliants that the Commonwealth <term>Respublica; the state</term> suffer no harm from the excessive indulgence of Caesar <note>original: "Cæsaris indulgentiâ"; here the author uses "Caesar" as a title of supreme imperial honor for King William</note>.

Let others seek after empty triumphs without the help of Mars <term>the god of war; military struggle</term>, or claim laurels without true Valor <term>Virtus; manliness and courage</term>. But for a great Leader or a brave Man who truly deserves honors, it is necessary that he count—if not his own wounds—at least his battles: those he waged, those in which he stood in the very midst, burning with zeal amidst swords and fires. And he who wishes to attain the praise of Clemency should not display to us or to our descendants the fires and ashes of cities and towns, nor the devastation of fields, as monuments to his mercy.

Furthermore, bad faith, broken treaties, and violated public oaths are unbecoming of a Great Man—those things which both divine law <term>jus divinum</term> and human law <term>jus humanum</term> have decreed to be binding and sacred among all nations, and which [the law] has willed to... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "volue-", likely for the word "voluerunt" or "voluere", meaning "willed" or "desired"</note>

<summary>This page of the dedication praises King William III’s genuine military valor and mercy, contrasting his authentic leadership with rulers who seek empty glory or leave destruction in their wake. It emphasizes that a true leader must uphold sacred treaties and laws.</summary>

These shall be your honors: there is no need to recount your lineage or your ancestors, however memorable they may be for their long succession and outstanding deeds. Yet your own Valor <term>Virtus; intrinsic merit and bravery</term> is enough for you; glory earned by one's own effort <note>original: "suo marte"; literally "by one's own Mars," a Roman idiom meaning by one's own military skill or strength</note> is sweeter than that inherited from forefathers. # PREFACE

->TO THE<-

# READER.

<margin>† and burden</margin>
In the history of the human race, the Republic of Letters <term>Res Literaria; refers to the collective world of scholarship, books, and the history of ideas</term> plays no small part. In the history of learning <note>original: "historiâ rei literariæ"</note>, however, nothing is more excellent or useful than to set forth the character <note>original: "ingenium"; the innate spirit or talent of a people</note> of each nation, its philosophical doctrines <term>placita philosophica; the established opinions or tenets of a school of thought</term>, and the progress it has made in the sciences. Other things that usually make up literary history—such as the lives of philosophers, their births, deaths, praises, travels, deeds good or bad, and more of this sort—these do indeed fill out <margin>and burden</margin> and adorn the subject matter. But they are of less importance when our goal is to investigate the seeds and progress of human knowledge, and the governance and divine plan <term>œconomiam; from the Greek word for 'household management,' here referring to God’s ordered administration of the world</term> of Providence in this regard. Therefore, in this work which is at hand, having set aside these trivialities or touched upon them only lightly, I shall treat the opinions <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "Veterum" indicates the next word is "of the Ancients."</note>

<summary>In this preface, Burnet argues that the true value of history lies not in the biographical details of famous men, but in tracking the growth of human knowledge and the divine order behind intellectual progress.</summary>

<keywords>Republic of Letters, literary history, philosophy, divine providence, methodology, human knowledge, history of ideas</keywords>

# Preface to the Reader.

Of the Ancients concerning the *Nature of Things* <note>original: "Rerum naturâ"</note> we inquire most of all. And this we do in praise and defense of Antiquity, so that we may show that our ancestors were not "mushrooms" <note>original: "fungos"; a common 17th-century metaphor for people who supposedly "sprung up" from the earth without heritage, culture, or intellectual history</note>, nor was wisdom born only with us.

From every age, as far back as one may trace the footsteps of our Fathers and recall the memory of times past, it is well-established that the human race possessed knowledge—not only of the Supreme Deity, but also of the natural world. They held knowledge of the Origin of things, their End <note>original: "Occasu"; literally their 'setting' or destruction</note>, and the intermediate changes (which three things encompass everything). This knowledge was not only true, but in some measure divine. Indeed, I believe these insights are to be traced back to the descendants of Noah <term>Noachidæ; the generations following the Great Flood who were believed to carry the wisdom of the antediluvian world</term> themselves, or perhaps even from the very origin of man, rather than from private discovery or scientific demonstration <term>demonstratione naturali; proof derived from observing the natural world</term>.

Furthermore, in other matters and chapters that constitute the second rank of philosophy—namely, speculations concerning the nature of the heavens, the celestial bodies, and the stars, both the Fixed stars and the Wandering stars <note>original: "Syderumque, tam Fixorum quàm Errantium"; "wandering stars" is the traditional term for planets</note>—it is clear from many examples that the Ancients did not judge these things poorly, nor did the matter and composition of these bodies entirely escape them. Moreover, regarding what is called the *System* of the World,

He suggests this wisdom was passed down from the time of Noah rather than being discovered through modern scientific methods.</summary>

# Preface to the Reader.

...or the form and order of the Universe. It is widely and rightly believed that **Pythagoras** did not discover this through his own genius alone, but rather found it among the <term>Secret Doctrines of the East <note>original: "ἀπόῤῥητα Orientalia"; referring to esoteric or hidden teachings from civilizations like the Egyptians or Persians that were not shared with the public</note></term>. Along with many other insights of no less value, he was the first to bring these ideas into Greece. 

Finally, as for the third class of philosophical systems—those concerning the "furniture" of this Earth, such as the Elements and the arrangements and qualities of terrestrial bodies—I admit the Ancients made little progress in exploring them. In this specific area, **modern philosophy** clearly outshines the learning of the old, and we do not begrudge it the praise it deserves. To put it briefly: Philosophy began with the greatest things and will proceed toward the smallest. Once the long race-course of literature, nature, and time has been run, wisdom will be brought to perfection alongside the end of the world, if God so wills.

I admit that what we still possess in a whole and undamaged state from "Barbaric" philosophy <note>original: "philosophiâ Barbaricâ"; in this context, "Barbaric" refers to non-Greek ancient cultures, such as the Hebrews, Egyptians, or Babylonians, rather than "uncivilized" people</note>, or even from the most ancient Greeks, is very little. Yet, just as we learn about and admire the *Architecture* of the Greeks from broken columns and weathered marbles, so too can we judge the remaining parts of an ancient philosopher’s work from a single large fragment. By following the laws of *symmetry*, and considering the whole structure...

# Preface to the Reader.

...remnant, we pass judgment. In any case, in unearthing these <term>Antiquities <note>original: "Archæologiis"; here referring to the study of ancient origins and doctrines rather than physical excavation</note></term> and the <term>dogmas of the ancients <note>original: "veterumque dogmatis"</note></term>, we have chiefly followed the **Classical and Greek writers**. Nor have we falsely attributed anything to anyone out of favoritism or spite. Instead, we have sometimes passed over errors which we suspect arose from the ignorance, carelessness, or even the ill-will of the narrators. We have considered it a worthwhile task to bring into the light and into public view especially that which is beautiful, useful, and worthy of memory.

Finally, in explaining ancient doctrine, we have discussed at length the *Fabulous mode of philosophizing* <note>original: "Fabuloso Philosophandi genere"; a style of teaching that uses myths, allegories, and stories rather than literal or scientific language</note>. This method prevailed through many centuries and among many nations. And although that kind of discourse has now become obsolete and has given way to a more rigorous doctrine, I thought it relevant to advise my readers of the figure of speech or the stylistic character that the ancients used so frequently. My goal is to dispel the darkness from their writings and protect them from unfair reproaches. For them, certainly, it was no matter of religious scruple to instruct the people through fables and <term>honest frauds <note>original: "honestas fraudes"; well-intentioned deceptions used by ancient teachers to convey moral truths to those unable to understand complex philosophy</note></term>—what we might call <term>lying out of duty <note>original: "officiosè mentiri"; a "noble lie" or a lie told for the benefit of the listener</note></term>. They believed their gods ruled the human race in a manner not unlike how we rule infants...

# Preface to the Reader.

<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 3, Chapter 4.</margin>
...lying stories to tell to children: adapting to the measure of their capacity and strength. They often hid the truth or disguised it with suitable colors so that they might better provide for the people's well-being. It is very well known that the ancients used these charms and ornate <term>Mythology <note>original: "Mythologiâ"</note></term>. They held it permissible for <term>lawgivers <note>original: "Legum latoribus"</note></term> and wise men to loosen the reins of truth for the sake of the public good and, as the occasion required, <note>original: "μετὰ τῶν πολλῶν συνασοφεῖν"; to play the fool along with the crowd—effectively, to speak down to the level of common understanding</note>. But I have always kept my hands off from interpreting their fables one by one—for nothing is more slippery than that task—mindful of the saying of <term>Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotelis"</note></term>: <note>original: "περὶ μὲν τῶν μυθικῶς σοφιζομένων, οὐκ ἄξιον μετὰ σπουδῆς σκοπεῖν"; those who philosophize by means of myths are not worth considering with serious effort</note>. But enough of this matter.

My intention was, after finishing the *Theory of the Earth* <note>original: "Telluris Theoriam"; Thomas Burnet’s most famous work, which attempted to reconcile the biblical account of the Flood and the Earth's formation with geological observation</note>, to which I have now added the final touch, to write a *Theory of the Visible World* <note>original: "Mundi Aspectabilis Theoriam"</note>. I did not intend this to be a universal theory—for I did not feel myself equal to such a vast province—but rather a *Sacred Theory* <note>original: "Theoriam Sacram"</note> for the use of students of <term>Theology <note>original: "Theologiæ"</note></term>. My goal was to explain the greatness and order of God's works and the laws by which they are governed, to the best of my ability. For it is in the interest of all learned men to know these things, and especially for theologians, so that they may be able to behold the Creator's wisdom and magnificence within created things, and celebrate Him with reason and understanding. Accordingly, it is necessary to know what...

# Preface to the Reader.

...what they are, and from what matter they consist—those greatest masses of the World, the <term>Stars <note>original: "Sydera"</note></term>: the hosts of Heaven, the Gods of the Nations. And what changes and transformations they undergo as the circle of time revolves. What difference there is between Stars—the Bright and the Dark, the Fixed and the <term>Wandering <note>original: "Errantes"; referring to the planets</note></term>: and what the origin of each may be, and to what extent each is inhabited, according to probable reasons. The contemplation of these things lifts and expands the soul, and fills it with the image of an immense world. From this, we fall into thoughts worthy of God, and we look down upon ourselves and our <term>Little Earth <note>original: "Terrellam"; a diminutive form of Terra, used here to emphasize the insignificance of our planet in the vastness of the cosmos</note></term> as if they were mere scraps or fragments of God’s Works, and consider them as nothing. 

Then, if one descends to lower things, it will be worthwhile to investigate from where the differences of Earthly Bodies arise, of what particles the <term>Elements <note>original: "Elementa"</note></term> consist, and how, from those particles, the power and properties of each emerge. And likewise regarding the rest of the Earth's apparatus, both animate and inanimate. Finally, we must ask in what both the distinction and the union of Body and Soul consist: and in what way external objects act upon our Body and our Soul. These and similar general and more weighty topics, which can serve as a kind of key—

# Preface to the Reader.

...are to be applied to the rest; if these matters were well understood by <term>Theologians <note>Scholars of religion and divinity.</note></term>, they would leave no room for <term>atheistic <note>original Greek: "ἀθέοις" (atheois)</note></term> pseudo-philosophers: whose evil cause is aided by our own ignorance in natural matters. I had once decided to treat these topics separately and as clearly as I could. Meanwhile, it is pleasing to have left some slight <term>monument <note>original: "monumentum"; here meaning a lasting written work or memorial of his thoughts.</note></term> of a life not spent in idleness: and, having completed a short period of <term>service <note>original: "militiâ"; the author uses the metaphor of military service to describe the hardships of his intellectual life.</note></term>, as it were, to rest henceforth from my labors.

# LISTING
## OF CHAPTERS.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER I.

*The reason and purpose of this work. To what extent it regards the <term>Theory of the Earth <note>original: "Telluris Theoriam"; a phrase likely referring to the geological and cosmological history of the world.</note></term>, and to what extent it regards <term>Philosophical History <note>The study of the origins and development of human thought and wisdom.</note></term>.*

## C H A P T E R  I.

### *The Reasoning and Purpose of this Work. To what extent it regards the Theory of the Earth, and to what extent Philosophical History.*

<margin>unsummoned? <note>original: "injussi 2?"; this marginal note appears to query the text's reference to "unbidden witnesses" below.</note></margin>
WHEN I first applied my mind to writing about the **EARTH** <note>original: "TELLURE"; the author refers to his previous major work, *Telluris Theoria Sacra* (The Sacred Theory of the Earth).</note>, my purpose was only this: that I should treat its Theory <term>physiologically <note>original: "physiologicè"; in this period, "physiology" referred to the general study of natural philosophy or physics (the "laws of nature"), rather than just biological systems.</note></term>, by the force of reason alone, and with nature as my guide; leaving entirely untouched either the **Sacred Scriptures**, or the **records of the nations** <note>original: "Gentium monumenta"; referring to ancient historical, mythological, and philosophical traditions of various cultures.</note>. But, as subject matter and arguments are wont to grow during the handling of a topic, so it happened to me in that Work: for while philosophizing, a new light arose, both from the **Sacred Books** as well as the writings of the ancients; which, like witnesses unbidden <note>original: "injusti"; in this context, it carries a legal sense of "unsummoned" or "not legally called," yet appearing to testify.</note> or uninvited, appeared of their own accord, the case having already begun.

Since indeed the first **foundations of Nature** and the **origins of things** are most worthy of repeated care and thought—both because of the dignity of the subject itself, and because they open an entrance for us to understand all other things in nature—I considered it worth the effort to write this commentary or appendix, as it were, to the **Theory of the Earth**, separately; and to embrace within it all those things which my "second thoughts" recalled to memory from the aforementioned records of both kinds <note>Referring to the "Sacred Books" and "writings of the ancients" mentioned above.</note>.

-># Philosophical Archaeologies: or,<-

a

<meta>catchword: historical <note>original Greek: "ἱστορικὸν"</note></meta>

There are, moreover, two parts in the aforementioned **Theory** <note>Referring to the author's previous work, *The Sacred Theory of the Earth*.</note>: the first deals with the past state of the World, and the second with its Future. The appearances and changes of the World that are still to come are primarily the **Conflagration** <note>original: "Conflagratio"; the prophesied destruction of the world by fire.</note> and the **Renewal** <note>original: "Renovatio"</note> that follows it—namely, the new Heavens and the new Earth. Regarding these matters, I have gathered so much evidence in the third and fourth books of that same *Theory*, drawn both from the **Holy Scriptures** and the **writings of the Nations**, that there seems to be no need for more or stronger proofs; especially since very few who bear the name of Christian bring these topics into doubt. However, the first part of the *Theory*, which treats the **Origins of things**, or the **Original World**, escapes the eyes and minds of many. To such people, those things demonstrated only **theoretically** <note>original Greek: "θεωρητικῶς"; by means of intellectual contemplation or abstract reasoning.</note> and from the study of causes seem thin and vanishing, like air or shadows. To assist them in some way, I show in the second book of this treatise that the **threefold** state of the natural World (which alone encompasses the entire Theory) is founded in the **Sacred Scriptures**, and is confirmed by the most ancient traditions of the wise men of old. This is done so that those who have a taste for truth in any form may not lack arguments of the specific kind they desire.

By the **Original World**, which I have just mentioned, I mean the **Antediluvian World** <note>The world as it existed before the Great Flood of Noah.</note>: following the example of Saint **Peter**, who calls it **the ancient world** <note>original Greek: "τὸν κόσμον ἀρχαῖον" (2 Peter 2:5).</note>, or the **Original World** as it is rendered in the **Vulgate** <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note>. Likewise, by **Archaeologies** <term>Archaeologies <note>original: "Archæologias"; here meaning "ancient histories" or "studies of antiquity" rather than the modern material science of archaeology.</note></term> I mean primarily those things that regard this **ancient world**. I do this in such a way, however, that I include under the same name the **Deluge** itself, and those things which relate to it or immediately follow it.

It is well known that the Ancients divided the past age of the World into three intervals: the **obscure** <note>original Greek: "ἄδηλον"; the "unknown" period of earliest antiquity.</note>, the **mythical** <note>original Greek: "μυθικὸν"; the period of legends and hero-tales.</note>,

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

Historical <note>original Greek: "ἱστορικόν"</note>: The **Obscure**, **Fabulous**, and **Historical** Ages. The **Obscure** age was that which preceded the **Flood** <note>original: "Diluvium"</note>, buried for the most part in darkness and oblivion. The **Fabulous** was that which immediately followed the **Flood** up until the **Olympiads** <note>The ancient Greek system of dating by four-year athletic festivals, traditionally beginning in 776 BCE, marking the start of reliable recorded history for the author.</note>; because among the ancients, there is no history of that interval except for what is uncertain and mythical. The **Third** age, however, beginning with the **Olympiads**, is subject to true history. Those things which look back to those two super-historical intervals can be called, appropriately enough, **archaeologies** <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαιολογίαι"; meaning "ancient accounts" or "discourses on antiquity."</note>; but more strictly and most properly, those things are so named which regard the first interval and the **Primeval World**.

But besides these most ancient matters, we have woven together a certain **Philosophical** history: not a universal one, but one pertaining to **Doctrines** <note>original: "Dogmata"; the core principles or tenets of ancient philosophical schools.</note>: and specifically those which regard the origins of things; noting, moreover, the character of each nation or sect, and their manner of philosophizing, whether common or secret, precise or mythical. These things occupy the first **Book**, and serve that purpose, among others, so that—having left behind the dregs and the more trivial and superfluous parts of ancient philosophy—we might retain what is clear and pure.

Indeed, just as those who undertake long **Voyages** sometimes enjoy the light of the **Sun** to direct their course, sometimes that of the **Moon**, and sometimes of the other **Stars**, as circumstances and the state of the **Heavens** allow; so when we must inquire into the most remote times and the memory of distant events, we cannot everywhere enjoy the same light, nor follow the same guides; but, according to the matters and the times, the strength of the light and the authority of the witnesses will vary. But having weighed all the factors of the case, let us allow ourselves to be inclined toward that side where the reasoning is clearer and more probable, if not altogether unavoidable.

### CHAPTER II.

# *An Overview of Ancient Philosophy among the Various Nations of the Earth: First, concerning the* Scythians, Celts, & Ethiopians.

Having explained the purpose and the primary reasoning behind this work, we must next ask what path should be taken to reach our goal. To leaf through every book by every author is neither possible nor useful; therefore, to cut away the unnecessary parts of a subject that is far too vast, I intend first to inquire into the origin and the seats of ancient Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientiæ"</note>, so that we may see in a brief and summary form within which records it is hidden and where it must be sought.

In this investigation, of whatever nature it may be, there will be no need to ascend to the times before the Flood <note>original: "ante-diluviana"</note> or the beginning of the world. For all knowledge of things that survived the Flood, and which could reach us from our ancestors, was once hidden in the heart of **Noah** alone; from him, it flowed to his sons, grandsons, and descendants, and along with their offspring, spread throughout the globe. Nor will it be necessary to follow the lineage and divisions of all these nations and peoples, since few among them were renowned for literature or Wisdom; it is sufficient for our purpose to divide the Ancient Nations, or arrange them in such an order, that we may encompass all those who were literate or famous for Wisdom.

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...the four quarters of the World; and this under the names of the **Scythians**, in the North; the **Celts**, in the West; the **Ethiopians**, toward the South; and the **Indians**—since no term is more expansive—for the remaining parts toward the East. These are the most common names used by the ancients; and since these peoples, who were not obscure in their culture, laws, and letters, surround and encompass our world in a circuit, we shall proceed through these headings to investigate the natural science <note>original: "Scientiam naturalem"</note> of the Barbarian Nations. However, because the ancients understood many different nations confusedly under the broad name of "Indians," once we arrive at that point, we must employ a new approach: treating those Eastern nations separately and in detail, for it is there that wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"</note> seems to have had its first seats. Likewise, the Greeks are to be divided into their various classes and schools. As for the Romans, however, we shall pass them by without mention, as they are notable for no particular kind of natural philosophy <note>original: "Physiologiæ," which in this context refers to the study of the physical world and the laws of nature</note>.

Among the nations mentioned, we will run through the first three with little effort, as they left no literary monuments of their own, nor has much been said by others—except very sparingly—regarding how they practiced philosophy. As for the **Scythian** nation, quite a few things are found among the Ancient writers concerning their antiquity and customs; but regarding their philosophy, or their dogmas about the nature of things, I find nothing anywhere. Nor is it sufficiently clear whether any specific tribe or group of men was dedicated to such studies among the Scythians, as is usually the case among other peoples. **Solon** <note>Solon (c. 638 – 558 BCE) was an Athenian statesman and lawmaker often counted among the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> is said to have admired **Anacharsis** the Scythian when he hosted him in Athens; but I believe this was because of the man’s natural disposition and sound mind, rather than for any knowledge of the sciences. Indeed, **Strabo** noted this in honor of that nation:

<margin>Book 7.</margin>
"For this reason, Anacharsis, Abaris, and certain others of their kind were held in high esteem among the Greeks; because they displayed a certain national character of easy-going nature, perfection, and justice." <note>original Greek: "Διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ὁ Ἀνάχαρσις, καὶ Ἄβαρις, καὶ τινὲς ἄλλοι παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησι τοιοῦτοι εὐδοκίμουν· ὅτι ἐθνικόν τινα χαρακτῆρα ἐπέφαινον εὐκολίας, καὶ τελεότητος, καὶ δικαιοσύνης."</note> And for that reason **Anacharsis**, **Abaris**, and others...

There has come to light in recent years a certain Northern Mythology, under the name of the ***Eddas*** <note>The Prose and Poetic Eddas, the primary sources for Norse mythology, which were being rediscovered by scholars in the 17th century</note>, which, besides not a few empty fables, seems to contain some things of a much higher origin. From the ***Scythians*** let us proceed to the ***Celts***, toward the West. It is well established that among these nations, there flourished from every age Philosophers, or an order of men, distinguished from the common folk and others by their name, their studies, and their way of life. They were called by everyone ***Druidae*** or ***Druids***; also ***Semnotheoi*** <note>A Greek term used by ancient historians to describe Celtic priests, literally "those who worship the gods"</note>; and they are usually distinguished by other names which are not relevant to our present purpose. These, like the ruins of ancient Temples, testify that something great once existed, though the remains themselves are of little account. <margin>Book 3, chapter 2</margin> These men [taught] the magnitude and form of the Earth and the World; the motions of the Heavens and the stars, says ***Mela*** <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer writing in the 1st century AD</note>, and what the Gods might intend...

It must be admitted that little remains among the ancient authors that is distinguished or unique regarding Ethiopian philosophy: there are few dogmas or famous doctrines. However, I more willingly attribute this to the "unfairness of time"—which easily allows difficult and remote things to slip away—than to a lack of material or the intellect of the people. They were certainly an ancient people, renowned for the praise of their integrity, their laws, the cultivation of their manners, their piety, and their commerce with the Gods. Furthermore, they possessed the most ancient use of letters; and with all these, they enjoyed leisure and long-lasting peace. If **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, author of the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note> is to be believed, they never experienced external rule, but remained in perpetual possession of their liberty and the bond of mutual concord. Finally, it is clear that they cultivated the knowledge of things and the study of wisdom, as evidenced by that family of Gymnosophist philosophers and by the colleges of Priests, which they always fostered in the manner of literate nations. # CHAPTER III.

## *A survey of the East Indians: specifically concerning the literature and philosophy of the Seres and Brahmins.*

So far we have traversed many lands without much profit: three regions of the world—the North, the West, and the South; and how few wise men have we encountered along the way? Now we have come to the Indians; by which name, taken in a broad sense, we shall embrace all of Asia and some neighboring areas. Here, moreover, the post-flood <note>original: *post-diluviani*; referring to the survivors of the Great Flood in the Biblical tradition, which 17th-century scholars believed was the starting point for modern civilizations.</note> people had their first seats, and in this nursery for the restoration of the human race, the origins of wisdom and literature must also be sought. Nor is it unknown or unacknowledged that the inhabitants of these regions were the very first to become famous for their learning and disciplines; for besides the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Arabs, Assyrians, and the more distant Indians, we read that they possessed no ordinary knowledge of human and divine matters before such disciplines were introduced into Greece; and from them, as if from springs, knowledge flowed through various streams and across different centuries to various other peoples. Come then, if you please, let us penetrate and travel through the remaining stretch of lands toward the East, so that we may see in brief by what right those nations—held to be the most cultured and wise—attained that reputation, what faith should be placed in it, or what monuments they have left behind.

And so that we may begin from more remote parts, it is right that we visit the ancient *Seres* <note>The "Seres" was the name used by Greeks and Romans for the people of northwestern China, famous for the silk trade.</note> in the far East, who today are called *Sinae* or *Sinenses* [the Chinese], a people notable for their letters and culture. Among the ancients, the history of these people is scarce; they were celebrated not so much for their scientific knowledge as for their longevity and the skill of manufacturing silk. The enemies of the Christian name—*Celsus*, *Porphyry*, *Julian*, and *Hierocles* <note>These were prominent Neo-Platonist philosophers and Roman officials who wrote polemics against early Christianity.</note>—who used to hold up famous and wise nations as examples to Christians (either to reproach them for the novelty of their theology or for the ignorance of their sect), did not include the *Seres* in this census. *Celsus* <margin>In Origen, book 7.</margin> mentions them indeed, but calls them "atheists" <note>original: *ἀθέους*</note> and associates them with wild and uncultivated nations, saying: "For neither the Scythians, nor the Nomads of Libya, nor the godless Seres, nor other nations most unholy and lawless [behave] thus." <note>original: *οὐδὲ γὰρ Σκύθαι τοῦτο, οὐδὲ Λιβύων οἱ Νομάδες, οὐδὲ Σῆρες οἱ ἄθεοι, οὐδ' ἄλλα ἔθνη τὰ δυσαγέστατα καὶ ἀνομώτατα.*</note> Nor is *Dionysius* <margin>Periegesis, verse 752.</margin> much different, speaking of "the barbarian nations of the Seres." <note>original: *καὶ ἔθνεα βάρβαρα Σηρῶν*</note> 

Yet I interpret both of these authors more mildly; Celsus calls them "Atheists" because they did not use temples, altars, or statues, nor that elaborate apparatus of superstition used by other nations. <margin>In Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, etc.</margin> It was by almost this same reasoning that the early Christians were called "Atheists" by the Pagans, because they took no pleasure in oracles, sacrifices, or images of the Gods. Dionysius, however, calls that nation "barbarian" either in the Greek manner <note>The Greeks often labeled any non-Greek speaker a "barbarian."</note> or because it was a "non-mixing nation," <note>original: *ἀπροσμιγὲς ἔθνος*</note> as <margin>On Cities.</margin> *Stephanus* says, and, like wild beasts, it fled from trade or social interaction with other nations.

In any case, it is argued from these points that the literature of the Seres—which has now become widespread in everyone’s speech—was very little known to the ancients. We owe our knowledge of this nation and region, previously impenetrable, primarily to merchants and Christian priests; and from their testimony and the monuments of the place itself, it is established that this empire has stood from the most ancient times, most flourishing in arts and literature. And this has been achieved without any [contact] with [other] nations...

If, however, the modern Chinese are compared with modern Europeans, I do not doubt that they are much inferior to our people, whether we look at the mathematical disciplines—both pure and applied—or at natural philosophy <term>Physiology: used here in the classical sense of *physiologia*, the study of the laws of nature and the physical world</term>. Since, however, whatever they possess they have born at home and cultivated by their own genius—not borrowed, nor repeated from other nations, as is usually said of the Greeks, Romans, and nearly all other Europeans—I believe this should be attributed to them as a singular merit; since, in wisdom as well as in status, they seem to be *Aborigines* <note>meaning original inhabitants who have occupied their land since the beginning of their history</note>.

Among their disciplines, they value the doctrine of Ethics most highly; its author was the most celebrated *Confucius*, the Socrates of the Chinese, whom he did not much precede in time <note>Early modern scholars often attempted to synchronize the lives of Confucius and Socrates to show a global era of philosophical awakening.</note>. They consider this liberal study so important, and so necessary to human life, that they choose all their magistrates from among philosophers alone; and they subject even the King himself, if he should degenerate, to their candid warnings. And so much for the *Seres*.

### Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

<margin>Book 15, p. 719.</margin>
It is clear from *Strabo* and others that the Brahmans, following established customs of exchange <note>original: *vendi instituta* - likely referring to the historical transmission or "trade" of knowledge between cultures</note>, cultivated **Natural Philosophy** <term>Physiology: here used in its classical sense, *physiologia*, meaning the study of nature and the physical world</term> and **Astronomy**. Nor is it surprising that their physical doctrine seemed foolish to many, since it was mostly wrapped in fables, or a fabulous shell. Thus, in the same place, *Megasthenes* says: *“Regarding nature, some of their views show a certain simplicity <note>original Greek: *εὐήθειαν* - this can mean either 'innocent simplicity' or 'foolishness'</note>; for they are better in deeds than in words, confirming most things through myths.”*

<margin>Strabo, Book 15, p. 713.</margin>
*Strabo* then adds some of their known dogmas, held in common with the Greeks: *“They agree with the Greeks on many points: for they also say that the world is created and perishable, and that it is spherical. The principles of all things are different, but the principle of the world-making <note>original Greek: *κοσμοποιίας* - cosmogony or the construction of the world</note> is Water.”* They held that the world was born and will perish; and that while there are other principles for the whole of the universe, for our created world, the principle is Water. For I think we must distinguish *“the universe”* <note>original: *τὸ σύμπαν*</note> from *“the making of the world.”* Furthermore, he adds concerning the soul: *“they also weave in myths, just as Plato does, concerning the immortality of the soul, the judgments in Hades, and other such things.”* You see what kind of things he calls fables. Finally, he hints that among them, according to the custom of the ancients, there were secret doctrines or *hidden things* <note>original: *ἀπόῤῥητα* - 'apórrheta,' or secret teachings reserved for the initiated</note>; from hearing these, they used to keep their wives away, lest they spread to the common people. *“The Brahmans do not share their philosophy with their wedded wives, so that they might not carry out any forbidden secrets to the uninitiated.”*

*Strabo* has preserved these things for us regarding the Brahmans from *Megasthenes*, *Nearchus*, *Onesicritus*, *Aristobulus of Cassandreia*, and others; from whom he says he took his Indian accounts. Nor do we find so much concerning Brahmanic natural philosophy elsewhere among all the ancient writers.

<margin>Stromata, Book 3.</margin>
To these, *Clement of Alexandria* adds **rebirth** <note>original: *παλιγγενεσίαν* - 'palingenesia' or regeneration</note>. *“They despise death,”* he says of these philosophers, *“and consider living as nothing, for they are convinced there is a rebirth.”* Nor do I understand this merely as **metempsychosis** <term>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of the soul into a new body after death</term>, but also as the [renewal] of the entire world...

Furthermore, King *Brachman*, according to *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>, wrote the laws and institutes of the *Brahmans*, and the constitution <note>original Greek: *πολιτείαν* (politeian)</note> of that nation in his own dialect. Moreover, *Nymphidorus*, specifically the one from *Amphipolis*, wrote the *Barbaric Institutes* <note>original Greek: *τὰ νόμιμα βαρβαρικὰ* (ta nomima barbarika). In this context, "Barbaric" refers to non-Greek or foreign customs</note>. In these writings, it is probable that he interspersed many details concerning the literature and disciplines of various nations. Finally, *Ctesias of Cnidus* wrote a singular book on Indian matters; however, in the *Excerpts of Ctesias* found in *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople who preserved summaries of lost ancient works</note>, I find nothing memorable regarding the philosophers or the philosophy of that nation.

This much regarding the Ancients. Modern authors, in their history of the contemporary *Brahmans*, add many other philosophical ideas, though these are mostly interwoven with fables. Nor does this seem foreign to their custom, for we have seen from *Strabo* <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> that this was a vice of the *Brahmans* in antiquity—that they were too delighted by mythological doctrine. Indeed, by this kind of doctrine—though it be impure and liable to many corruptions—the most ancient theology was handed down, both *Greek* and *Barbaric*. Whether this was done to suit the natural character of ancient men, especially those of the *East*, or so that they might make those things which were beautiful more difficult to attain and not discernable at first glance, remains a question. It is most certain that orders and tribes of philosophers still survive among the *Indians*, and that they use a sacred language <note>Burnet is likely referring here to Sanskrit, which was recognized by European scholars of this period as the liturgical and philosophical language of India, distinct from common speech</note>—that is, one not used by the common people—and a most ancient one, to preserve their philosophy. Thus, it is not incredible that the same philosophy, or a body of that same philosophy, has remained through so many centuries, even if it is variously distorted and encrusted, as it were, with new fables. Learned men who have spent a long time among the *Indians* have brought us some knowledge of this, and when the opportunity arises, we will perhaps present some specimens from their writings in the following book. But for the present, this is enough.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

...confused and interwoven. If, however, you wish to taste something of Chaldean Theology, as it is presented by its initiates, this is roughly how it stands regarding the orders of divine things. They distinguish things into those that are purely Intelligible, those both Intelligible and Intellectual, and those Intellectual only. <note>In the tradition of Neoplatonism, the "Intelligible" refers to the realm of pure ideas or forms, while "Intellectual" refers to the active faculty of the mind that perceives them.</note> In the first order is the supreme *Triad*: to the second they refer the *Iynges*, the *Connectors* (Synocheas), and the *Initiators* (Teletarchas): to the third, the lower Minds. Thus theorizes *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine scholar who preserved and commented on many ancient mystical texts.</note>. But at other times he substitutes another scale of things. Namely, the Triad of the *Implacables* (Amilicti), and the one *Membrane* (Hypezocos). These are the seven Sources, after which are the *Super-rulers*, then the *Unzoned*, then the *Zoned*; after them the *Angels, Demons, and Heroes*; and finally, the *Corporeal World*. <note>The "Unzoned" (Azoni) were celestial spirits free to roam the universe, while the "Zoned" (Zonei) were spirits bound to specific planetary spheres or "zones."</note> If you consult *Pletho* <note>Georgius Gemistus Pletho (c. 1355–1452), a Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced the Italian Renaissance.</note>, he arranged the furniture of his world a little differently; after the supreme Triad follows the intelligible *Iynx*: and after this the *Connector*, the *Empyrean*, the *Ethereal*, and the *Material* (Hyleus). After the *Connectors* are the *Initiators*: after these the *Source-Fathers*, who are also called the *authors of the World*. The first of these is called "Once Beyond," after this *Hecate*, then "Twice Beyond," after this the three *Implacables*, and lastly the one called the *Membrane*. It is wearisome to transcribe more. If these things please and profit you, Reader, rejoice and enjoy them. But let us return to the Oracles for a moment.

# CHAPTER V.

## Concerning the Persians and their Magi.

The wise men of the Persians were called *Magi*; a name indeed common to them and the wise men of other Eastern nations; for among the Arabs, Assyrians, Indians, and others, there were Magi; but those of the Persians were illustrious beyond the rest, occupied as much in the conduct of affairs as in the contemplation of nature. They were put in charge of instructing and educating the royal children. # CHAPTER V.
## On the Persians, and their Magi.

**T**he wise men of the Persians were called *Magi*; a name they certainly shared with the wise men of other Eastern nations; for among the Arabs, Assyrians, Indians, and others, there were Magi; but those of the Persians were more illustrious than the rest, being occupied as much with practical affairs as with the contemplation of nature. ...teachers, and especially Zoroaster, *the high priest of every divine mystery* <note>original: "omnis divini arcani antistitem"</note>. Therefore, it is clear enough that the Magi did not only look after sacred and civil affairs, but also investigated the principles and laws of nature.

The leader and chief <note>The author uses "coryphæus," a Greek term for a choir leader, to denote Zoroaster's preeminence.</note> of the Magi was Zoroaster, as many authors testify; but they agree very little on the history of this Zoroaster, or the various Zoroasters. Some establish one, others two, and others many. Since we seek the dogmas and doctrines of the ancient sages as the best and most desirable part of Philosophical history, we weigh their other conditions or circumstances less anxiously; but among the many things confusedly said by the ancients concerning the Zoroasters, it seems to be established, first, that there were at least two Zoroasters, both famous for the name of wisdom and magical doctrine. One was a Chaldean or Bactrian, whom many authors mention; the other was a Persian or Medo-Persian, about whom there is no doubt. Secondly, it seems to me established that the deeds, ages, dogmas, homelands, writings, and other matters of these two are often confused and mixed together by both the ancients and the moderns. This is something that usually happens in other cases of shared names <note>original: "Synonymis"</note>, whether regarding the Gods of the nations or illustrious men; the antiquity of time and the negligence of writers, through the similarity of things, bring about error and confusion. Leaving these matters aside, let us see in a few words what writings or fragments of writings Zoroaster left behind, or which now survive.

# Archaeological Philosophy: or,

...wearing a tiara <note>A high, often conical Persian headdress</note> wreathed especially with myrtle. He who offers the sacrifice, however, does not make vows for himself alone and in private, but prays for the good of all the Persians collectively; first indeed for the King; and among all the Persians, he who performs the sacred rites is himself included. When he has cut the flesh of the victim into small pieces and boiled it, he spreads out the softest possible grass, especially clover <note>original Latin: *trifolium*</note>. Having placed the meat upon this, a Magus standing by chants the **THEOGONY** <note>term: Theogony — from the Greek meaning "the birth of the gods." The author argues that for the Persians, this meant the creation of the natural world.</note>. This they regard as a sacred song or incantation. In this way, the Persians worshipped the Gods more purely and without pretense compared to other peoples. I am aware that some things are told differently concerning the Persians by Strabo <note>A Greek geographer of the 1st century BC</note>, but he refers either to their various sects or to different ages. It is most worthy of note that, while performing the rites, the Magi sang a Theogony. This could have been nothing other than a song about the origin of the World. For it had been said before which Gods the Persians had: namely the celestial bodies, the elements, and the parts and regions of the Universe. Therefore, the birth of the Persian Gods is the birth of these celestial and elemental bodies: that is, the birth of the Heavens, the Stars, and the Earth. This is the true ancient-barbarian Theogony. Indeed, the little Greeks <note>original: *Græculi* — a dismissive term for Greeks who were seen by later scholars as having corrupted purer ancient wisdom with myths</note>, who fashioned Gods of a human nature <note>original Greek: "ἀνθρωποφυεῖς"</note>, later converted this into the crude genealogy of their own Gods. ->### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.<-

...[Astronomical observati]ons, and four books, **On Nature** <note>original Greek: *peri physeōs*</note>: which I would gladly redeem at the expense of all the others. For, if there were any solid knowledge in that most famous Magus <note>Referring to Zoroaster</note>, its foundations would have to be laid in these books *On Nature*. However, we consider all these to be lost, if they ever existed; and whatever works are peddled among us under Zoroaster's name are either plainly apocryphal and pseudonymous <note>falsely attributed</note>, as noted by others, or they contain nothing extraordinary or beyond the common training of philosophers; so much so that, if they were genuine, they would diminish that man's fame and reputation in my eyes. From his genuine philosophy, Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher</note> has preserved one fragment for us, from Theopompus <margin>On Isis and Osiris</margin>; another by Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in *The Cave of the Nymphs*, from Eubulus. A third, though less mystical, is from Eusebius <note>An early Christian historian</note> <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1, Ch. 7</margin>, taken from a sacred Persian book which he claimed belonged to Zoroaster himself. And these few, along with some scattered opinions found mostly among Platonic authors, are the meager remains of the great Zoroaster.

Just as the origin and early times of the Persian Magi are uncertain, so there is no single and consistent opinion regarding their end and disappearance. When the Persian nobles wished to avenge the deceit and crime of the Empire being seized by the Magi, not content with the slaughter of Smerdis <note>A Magus who allegedly usurped the throne by posing as the brother of Cambyses II</note> and his associates, they raged against all Magi indiscriminately. They did so with such force that, as Herodotus reports <margin>Book 3</margin>, had they not been stopped by the arrival of night, they would have left not a single Magus alive. In memory of this event, they even established the **Magophonia** <note>original Greek: *Magophonia* — literally "The Slaughter of the Magi"</note>, a solemn Persian festival; on this day, it was forbidden for any of the Magi to appear in public. From this, it is easy to infer that the dignity of the Magi was diminished among the Persians, but their lineage was not extinguished; for Hostanes and Hystaspes <note>Famous figures associated with Persian wisdom and magic</note>, famous names, lived in a later age. It is well established that the Magi remained until the time of Alexand... <meta>catchword: ...er</meta>

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

<margin>Diogenes Laertius, in the preface.</margin>
...the times of Alexander <note>original: "Alexandri tempora"</note>; at which time some claim the Magi were destroyed along with the Persian Empire. Yet I do not entirely agree with them: for just as the Chaldeans did not immediately perish when the Empire was occupied by the Persians (since Ctesias mentions them in the time of Darius, when there was a matter regarding the visiting of his tomb), so too the Magi were not extinguished when the Greeks took control. Instead, they seem to have presided over their own sacred rites until the times of Heraclius <note>A Byzantine Emperor, r. 610–641 AD</note>, who <margin>Agathias, Book 2.</margin> destroyed the Persian *fire temples* <note>original Greek: *Pyreia*</note>, the groves, the sacred fire, and all the equipment of that cult. Shortly after this, the Muhammadan religion <note>original: "Mahometana"</note> succeeded it, in which the now-blinded Persians remain stuck, all ancient knowledge having been extinguished.

<margin>Pliny, Book 30, Ch. 1. Arnobius, Book 1.</margin>
So much for the Magi: Their doctrine and history would not be so difficult to explain if the primary writers on that subject had not already perished. Such writers included *Hermippus of Smyrna*, who, around the time of Ptolemy Euergetes, wrote *On the Magi*. There was also *Pallas*, who, as cited by Porphyry (*On Abstinence*, Books 2 and 4), most excellently collected and explained the *mysteries of Mithras* <note>Mithras was a Persian sun god whose mystery cult became popular across the Roman Empire</note>. *Eusebius* (Preparation for the Gospel, p. 42) cites the *Octateuch of Ostanes* <note>A legendary Magus; an 'Octateuch' is a work in eight volumes</note>. Additionally, *Eubulus*, an author of uncertain <margin>Book 2, Against Jovinianus; On Abstinence, Book 4.</margin> age, composed a history of *Mithras* and the *Magi* in many books, according to Jerome and Porphyry; and he distinguished their various ranks. Furthermore, *Theodore of Mopsuestia* composed three books *On Persian Magic* <note>original Greek: *peri tēs en Persidi magikēs*</note>. Finally, the authors whom <margin>Photius, Bibliotheca, Codex 81. In the preface and Pliny, as above.</margin> *Laertius* cites on this subject—namely *Hermodorus the Platonist*, the *Magicus* of Aristotle (or, according to Suidas, of *Antisthenes* or *Rhodon*), which treated Zoroaster—have all perished. So too has *Xanthus the Lydian*, who wrote the *Magica*, <margin>Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 3.</margin> and who seems, according to Laertius, to have traced the succession and lineage of the *Magi* from Zoroaster. In the same vein, Laertius also cites *Sotion* on successions, *Dinon* on Persian affairs, *Eudoxus*, and *Theopompus*...

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the Literary History of the Arabs and Phoenicians.

Let us move from the Persians to the *Arabs and Phoenicians*; both are famous for the renown of their ancient wisdom. *Job*, who was older than Moses himself, left behind an eternal monument of Arabian wisdom. He was a noble Arab, a *lover of God* <note>original Greek: φιλόθεος (philotheos)</note> and a *lover of truth* <note>original Greek: φιλαλήθης (philalēthēs)</note>, whose most upright heart was encased in "triple brass" <note>A classical metaphor, likely referencing Horace, signifying immense courage or an impenetrable defense against misfortune.</note> that no weapons of Satan could ever pierce.

He is an example of heroic virtue and unbroken fortitude. No adversities—neither physical ailments, nor the loss of his possessions, nor the wrath of heaven and the slaughter of his dearest children—could shake his steadfast mind. Not only did his enemies rage against him, but his friends also tormented him; and, what is most grievous to the noble and honest, they accused him of feigned piety, of secret crimes, and of offending the Divine.

He stood unmoved, like a rock; he would not blame God, whom he knew to be the Best and Greatest <note>original Latin: "Optimum Maximum," a title used to denote the highest deity</note>, nor would he accuse himself, conscious as he was of his own righteousness. This is a great and memorable example of how much power *natural religion* <term>Natural religion: A system of belief and morality based on human reason and the observation of the natural world, rather than on specific divine revelation or scripture.</term> can hold.

Those who wish for more information regarding this man's extraordinary piety and the sacred harmony of his life and character with nearly every precept of the Christian religion should consult *Eusebius, Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapters 5 and 6*, where he reviews all these matters in detail. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a landmark historian of the early Church; here he is cited to show that Job’s "natural" virtue mirrored later Christian teachings.</note> In the meantime, I shall not find it burdensome to add the eulogy for this most illustrious man which is found in the *Suda*:

<note>original Greek: Ἰὼβ ὁ μέγας ὄντως ἐκεῖνος... "Job, that truly great and noble champion of truth, who first opened that naked, great, and universal stadium; who threw down all opponents; who received blows and bruises even to his bones, and remained undefeated, though full of worms, and yet crowned as a victor. Not even death was able to lay him low and trample him into the dust; he still stands like an unswerving statue, or an indestructible anvil, throughout his whole life wrestling down and striking down the adversary. This man was the first to wrestle down the devil. He raised trophies of victory over that bitter enemy—not competing for the Nemean, Olympian, Isthmian, or Pythian prizes, nor any of those things Greek stories boast of—but competing for the sake of his children, his possessions, his cattle, his household, and his entire way of life. Even when he saw his house collapse and the very same rooms become the tombs and mass graves of the children he had fathered, he remained strong in soul. Those children, who in a single day and hour were feasting and eating together at the table, were laid low in a heap by that all-polluted one [the devil]. And yet, the rage and malice of the opponent were not satisfied even by these things, until he called the athlete himself out, naked, onto a dunghill. There, covering him in sores and filling him with worms, the devil made him a horrible and strange spectacle for all under the sun; for seven years the enemy gnawed at him with teeth and lashed the martyr's whole body with his tongue, until at last that all-polluted one brought defeat upon himself and inherited total shame."</note> <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia. This passage uses the metaphors of ancient Greek athletics—the "stadium" and "wrestling"—to describe Job's spiritual endurance as a "martyr" or witness.</note>

These extracts are somewhat long, but they are owed to the merits and the memory of such a great man.

Furthermore, it is clearly evident from his history that our Arabian [Job] was a man of **great learning and wide knowledge** <note>original Greek: πολυμαθῆ καὶ πολυΐστορα (polymathē kai polyistora), meaning "much-learned and well-versed in history"</note> and skilled in natural science. The *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note> says that this history contains **the natural philosophy of the whole creation** <note>original Greek: φυσιολογίαν ὅλης τῆς κτίσεως (physiologian holēs tēs ktiseōs)</note>. Certainly, both the dogmas and the precepts of the **Sons of Noah** <note>The 'Noachidarum' or Noachide Laws, a set of universal moral imperatives believed by ancient scholars to be binding on all humanity before the Law of Moses</note> are found in those commentaries <margin>Chapter 38.</margin>. And from the manner in which the **origin of the Earth** is celebrated by them, as well as its dissolution in the **Flood**—matters which are to be explained in the following pages—it is manifest that the first Arabian author of that writing was well-versed in the secret doctrine of both. I say the *first and Arabian author*; for whoever it was that arranged this work into its current form, unless we wish to consider the whole thing a fiction, he must necessarily have drawn the material of the work from Arabian records <note>original: 'adversariis,' referring to journals or public accounts</note> concerning the life of **Job**. Nor did the author conceal this, for he left many "Arabisms" in his work, which savor of the fountain and origin from whence they were drawn.

Let this be the first and most ancient monument of Arabian wisdom; for no nation, since the prophecies of **Enoch** <note>An ancient biblical figure; the author refers to the 'Book of Enoch,' which was largely lost to Western scholars at this time, though known by reputation</note> perished, can show a specimen of older or contemporary wisdom, since there is no doubt that the life of Job preceded the times of Moses. And thus, the use of letters and writing, as well as a knowledge of the stars, many points of natural history, and finally, the worship of the true God, prevailed in Arabia before **Moses** was born. And as for letters and learning, it will be worthy of belief that these flourished among the Arabians until the time of **Solomon**, if we believe that the **Queen of Sheba**, who came to see Solomon <margin>1 Kings 10.</margin>, was Arabian, as is gathered from many indications. Now, since she left her kingdom as if for a literary contest—namely, to test the wisdom of Solomon, to see if he lived up to his reputation and expectation—it can serve as an argument that the study of wisdom in that age, both in the royal court and in the schools

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...in the Arabian schools, to have flourished, and to be ambitious for praise and the glory of winning a debate. There is also another, if I am not mistaken, and more recent argument or example in the sacred scriptures concerning the wise men of Arabia: I mean the **Magi**, who came from the East to worship the infant Jesus. For I freely interpret these men as being from Arabia, since several of the Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians and writers who established orthodox doctrine</note> held the same view; and this very thing seems to me to be suggested by the Prophet in *Psalm* 72:10, since it is certain that that prophetic psalm ultimately refers to the Messiah. The gifts they brought were also the typical riches of Arabia; and "Magi from the East" <note>original Greek: μάγοι ἀπ’ ἀνατολῶν (magoi ap’ anatolōn)</note> seems to denote the same people as the "Children of the East" <note>original Hebrew: בני קדם (b'nei kedem)</note> in *Job* 1:3. Indeed, **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a towering Dutch jurist and scholar who wrote extensively on scriptural interpretation</note> notes and proves <margin>On Matthew 2.</margin> that Arabia was commonly called "the East" by the Jews. Finally, so that no doubt remains on this point, not only the wise men of the Persians were called Magi, but that name prevailed throughout almost the entire East, as can be seen in the works of **Lucian** and **Pliny**; <margin>Matthew 2. Pliny book 25, 2; book 30, chapter 1.</margin> and specifically, **Pliny** numbers **Hippocus** the Arabian among the Magi. Even **Balaam** <note>original: Balahamum</note>, whom the king of the Moabites consulted against the people of Israel (*Numbers* 22), whether you call him a Magus or a Prophet, likely belonged to this same order.

Among the Arabian peoples, the **Zabians** or *Zabaists* <note>Known in modern scholarship as Sabians, a group often associated in the Middle Ages with ancient star-worship and hermetic traditions</note> were noteworthy (the same people, it seems to me, as the Sabaeans or their priests), a very ancient nation, and religious in their worship and custom. The Jews say <margin>Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, part 3, chapter 29.</margin> that **Abraham** was originally educated in their faith and worship; but afterwards, in order to worship the one true God, he withdrew from them and attacked their dogmas. Furthermore, **Maimonides** <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher (1138–1204) who argued that many Mosaic laws were designed to steer the Israelites away from Zabian idolatry</note> maintains that **Moses**, in forming his laws, took the greatest account <margin>Ibid.</margin> of the customs and rites of the Zabians; and therefore he makes that nation older than his own Lawgiver, and worthy, along with the Egyptian nation, of being considered in his deliberations.

At the same time, they were animated by a study of philosophizing, as if revived; and when they had penetrated the West and Europe, they drank in a philosophy previously unknown and unheard of by the Arabs—namely, Greek and European philosophy. And therefore, I judge those philosophers to be poorly decorated with the title of "prime antiquity" among the Arabs; since they seem to have drawn the former idea from **Aristotle**, and the latter from other more recent writers. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origins of Things

...it often happens that they repeat the opinions of the ancients, one after another. Indeed, it is well established that since the time of **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahometis"</note>, Arabic wisdom has degenerated into fables and foulness. And had there not existed in the sacred scriptures <note>likely referring to the Book of Job, which many early modern scholars believed represented ancient Arabic/Edomite philosophy</note> certain specimens of a more excellent character among the Arabs, I would scarcely have included that nation in the rank of philosophers. For it is well known that for many centuries the Arabic genius has luxuriated, even to the point of disgust, in fictions and allegories. But enough about them for now.

<margin>The Phoenicians</margin>
Now we come to the *Phoenicians*; a very ancient people, situated on the lowest shore of the Mediterranean Sea; great numbers of whom **Joshua**, the Leader of the Israelites, expelled from their homeland. That this nation was among the first to be literate is beyond doubt; the very letters of the alphabet are said to be their invention; at the very least, they were the sources of letters for the Greeks, under the guidance of **Cadmus** <note>In Greek mythology, the Phoenician prince credited with bringing the alphabet to the Greeks</note>, before the Trojan War. They are also said to have invented numbers and **Arithmetic**; furthermore, **Astronomy** and the science of the stars; in addition, the **Nautical** art and new routes across the Ocean. Finally, they are even credited in some way with **Physiology** <term>Physiology: in this context, the study of the physical world or natural philosophy (from the Greek "physis", nature)</term> itself, if **Posidonius** <note>a Stoic philosopher and polymath</note> is to be believed, or the method of philosophizing through hypotheses. Indeed, lest anything be lacking from their praises, **Strabo** <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note> says they were rich in every kind of philosophy: <margin>Book 16</margin> *“A very great abundance of all other philosophy can be obtained from these cities.”* <note>original Greek: "πάσης τ' ἄλλης φιλοσοφίας εὐπορίαν πολὺ πλείστην λαβεῖν ἔστιν ἐκ τούτων τῶν πόλεων"</note> He is speaking, however, of the Phoenician cities.

What nation anywhere has contributed so much to the growth of the **Republic of Letters** <term>Republic of Letters: the long-distance community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th and 18th centuries</term>? Which one can claim for itself the glory of so many inventions, or has propagated them more widely through the sending out of colonies? Furthermore, **Thales** and **Zeno**, the leaders of two sects among the Greeks <note>Thales founded the Ionian school and Zeno of Citium founded Stoicism</note>, were Phoenicians, or descended from Phoenicians. Nor did **Pythagoras** travel to the Phoenicians any less than to the Chaldeans and Egyptians, so that he might learn the mathematical sciences. <margin>Porphyry in the *Life of Pythagoras*</margin> Finally, the teacher of Pythagoras, **Pherecydes**, in reading...

The words of **Strabo** are these: *If one must believe Posidonius, the doctrine concerning atoms is ancient, originating from a Sidonian man named Mochus who lived before the Trojan times.* <note>original Greek: "Εἰ δὲ δεῖ Ποσειδωνίῳ πιστεῦσαι, τὸ περὶ τῶν ἀτόμων δόγμα, παλαιόν ἐστιν ἀνδρὸς Σιδονίου Μόϰου πρὸ τῶν Τρωϊϰῶν χϱόνων γεγονότος."</note>
<margin>Against the Mathematicians, p. 367</margin> **Sextus** says much the same: *Democritus and Epicurus said that atoms were the elements of all things—unless this opinion should be considered more ancient, which, as the Stoic Posidonius said, was handed down from a certain Phoenician man named Mochus.* <note>original Greek: "Δημόϰϱιτός δε ϰαὶ Ἐπίϰουϱος ἀτόμους (ἔλεξαν εἶναι τὰ τῶν ὄντων στοιχεῖα) εἰ μή τι ἀρχαι- οτέραν ταύτην θετέον τὴν δόξαν, ἣ ὡς ἔλεγεν ὁ Στωϊϰὸς Ποσειδώνιος, ἀπὸ Μόϰου τινὸς ἀνδρὸς Φοινίϰος ϰατα- γομένην."</note> You see that the whole matter rests on the reliability of **Posidonius** alone, and both authors seem to doubt his word. Since, therefore, far more witnesses of more approved credibility affirm that **Leucippus** or **Democritus** introduced the **atomic hypothesis**—and among others **Cicero**, the disciple of this very Posidonius—I more readily agree with them. Especially since the same Cicero does not hesitate to label this philosopher as a fabricator of falsehoods:
<margin>On Fate</margin> *Posidonius—if I may say so with my teacher's permission—seems to invent certain things.* <note>original Latin: "Quædam etiam Posidonius, pace magistri dixerim, comminisci videtur."</note>

Furthermore, that method of philosophizing through **hypotheses** and **systems of principles** does not seem to me to suit the character of the most ancient times. Philosophers immediately adopted this method once atoms were introduced. These things are Greek in character, as is reasonable to believe, and belong to a later age. It seems to me that a "traditional philosophy" lasted beyond the Trojan times, which [proceeded] by reasoning and [searching for] causes...

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

it did not rely on an explanation of causes, but on a doctrine of a different kind and origin, primeval and handed down from the fathers <note>original Greek: πατροπαραδότῳ</note>. Finally, in the Phoenician philosophy of *Sanchoniathon*, no mention or memory of atoms or atomic dogma occurs; although the birth of things and the beginnings of the world are discussed eloquently, which would be the most appropriate place to treat such principles. Therefore, having weighed these matters, it is more believable that this was said by **Posidonius** either carelessly or out of envy; since in every age there are those who transfer the praise of inventors from a recent author to an older one. But let us proceed with our purpose.

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1</margin>
Regarding Phoenician theology or philosophy, nothing remains, as far as I know, except that excerpt from *Sanchoniathon* which **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> preserved, from the translation by **Philo of Byblos**. **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> also mentions the same Phoenician work and its Greek translator; Porphyry was a Tyrian, called *Malchus* in his native tongue. *Sanchoniathon* is said by **Porphyry** and **Eusebius** to have written before the Trojan times; **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous 17th-century scholar of biblical geography and Phoenician language</note>, a man most well-versed in Phoenician matters, agrees with them. As for the man's intellect, if **Philo** has depicted it correctly for us, it was most fit for the study of philosophy: he is called *multifarious in learning and industrious, desiring to know from everyone the things from the beginning, out of which all things were established.* <note>original Greek: πολυμαθὴς κὶ πολυπράγμων, κὶ τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ἀφ' ὧ τὰ πάντα συνέστη, παρὰ πάντων εἰδέναι ποθῶν</note>. *In many ways learned and curious, and especially desirous of learning from what beginnings or first principles all things were constituted.* <note>The author provides this Latin translation of the preceding Greek quote to ensure clarity for his readers.</note> This is the first and greatest duty of a philosopher: to inquire into the origins of things. And it is likewise clear from this fragment of the author that he primarily established a **Cosmogony** <term>Cosmogony: an account or theory regarding the birth and origin of the universe</term>, taking his beginning from the ancient **Chaos**. Then he established the primeval **Ilus** <term>Ilus: often interpreted as "mud" or "slime," representing the first stage of matter emerging from chaos</term> <note>original Greek: Ἰλὺν</note> as the immediate matter or nursery from which the first threads of things emerged; those, namely, which were brought forth upon the surface of the earth.

### Philosophical Archaeology: or,

<margin>Josephus, *Against Apion*, book 2.</margin> It was harshly said by *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius Molon, a Greek rhetorician known for his anti-Jewish sentiments.</note> that the *Jews* were the "most untalented of the Barbarians" <note>original: "ἀφυεστάτους εἶναι τῶν Βαρβάρων"</note>. And for this reason, he claimed they alone had contributed no invention to the benefit of human life. *Namely, that they are the most inept of the barbarians: and therefore they alone have produced no invention useful for life.* However, the ancient Schools and Academies among them were not so much formed and organized for "Encyclopedic" studies <note>The "circle of learning" or general liberal arts education.</note>, as is common today, but rather for religious instruction and for the purpose of imbibing prophetic gifts. For no nation throughout the world, no people, so abounded in Prophets and men touched by the celestial spirit <margin>See *Sepher Cosri* <note>The *Kuzari*, a famous 12th-century work by Judah Halevi defending Judaism.</note></margin> as the *Jews*: so much so that some divine power seemed to dwell in their very soil and climate. But besides those divine utterances and oracles, they claim to have preserved, from the times of *Moses*, or even from *Adam* himself, a certain secret doctrine called the <term>CABALA</term> <note>Kabbalah: a Jewish mystical and esoteric system of interpreting the scriptures.</note>, which unlocks the mysteries of both worlds—the natural and the invisible—and which surpasses both the ancient wisdom and the modern learning of all other nations.

Therefore, regarding Jewish literature, there remains only this to be asked: whether anything solid and sincere exists today, or ever existed, concerning this Cabalistic doctrine. I say, *"or ever existed"*; for although it is not permitted to doubt that *Moses* was a most wise man, well-versed in the secrets of nature and divine providence, it nevertheless seems uncertain how much of this secret knowledge he actually imparted to the *Israelites*. And it is certain that, however much there was, it has been corrupted in many ways since that time; and under the name of the *Cabala*, various figments of the imagination and trifling methods for extracting I-know-not-what mysteries are daily thrust upon their disciples by idle Rabbis <note>original: "malè feriatis Rabbinis," implying misguided or poorly occupied scholars.</note>.

# The Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things

...we must prune, first, that Literal, or Numerical, or Grammatical Kabbalah; which busies itself with building and weaving some sort of secret meanings out of the letters of the Alphabet, the Divine names, or words in the sacred scripture. But games and clever tricks of this kind fall far below the dignity of the Holy Spirit; whom we would have to suppose is not only aware of them, but also their author, if they were to be taken as true. Second, all magical and superstitious things must be cut away; which, born from the abuse of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>A Jewish mystical system of scriptural interpretation.</note>, are now too often mixed with it. Third, common notions expressed in uncommon words are not to be held as the true Kabbalah. This vice has crept into every kind of mystical literature: to propose common and publicly known things with great pomp under the mask of some *number, symbol, barbarous word, or figurative or fictitious term.* This is easy to see in some Pythagorean symbols, Egyptian hieroglyphs, the barbarisms of the <term>Hermeticists</term> <note>Followers of the mystical and alchemical traditions attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, and occasionally in the philosophical musings of the Kabbalists. Once all these things have been cast out, what remains of the Jewish Kabbalah is meager; let us now gradually examine its parts and form.

Therefore, for the sake of teaching, we distinguish the Kabbalah into *Nominal* and *Real*. The latter touches upon the things themselves more closely, albeit somewhat obscurely. The former, as was said, is entirely occupied with the mystical use of letters, names, and numbers: and so, from the characters of the Alphabet, the names of God, the letters, syllables, and words of the sacred text—and finally from numbers and numerical values—it carves out its mysteries. That *Nominal* Kabbalah is divided into three types: which are usually called <term>Gematria</term>, <gloss>גמטריא</gloss> <note>A method of interpreting biblical names and phrases based on the numerical value of Hebrew letters.</note>; <term>Notarikon</term>, <gloss>נוטריקון</gloss> <note>A method of creating acronyms from the first or last letters of words.</note>; and <term>Themura</term>, <gloss>תמורה</gloss> <note>A system of letter substitution or permutation.</note>. ### Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things.
