Yet it is primarily upon these two things that they are accustomed to practicing their trifling art.

Regarding the divine names, the Kabbalists have always maintained that mysteries or a singular power lie hidden within them. They primarily celebrate three names of God: the *Tetragrammaton* <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, the *Name of Twelve Letters*, <margin>יהוה <note>The Hebrew letters for the Tetragrammaton.</note></margin> and the *Name of Forty-Two Letters*.

As for the name *Tetragrammaton*, it is well known that the Jews have always universally attributed a certain holiness and veneration to it; for this reason, the name was not spoken by the common people, but only by the Priest, and only in the sanctuary during solemn occasions. It denotes, as they say, the very essence of God as He is in Himself, or in His state before the world, prior to all His external works. Therefore, as Maimonides says, it is called <margin>*Guide for the Perplexed*, part 1, ch. 16 <note>Modern editions of Maimonides' *Guide* discuss this in Chapter 61; the Latin "c. 16" may be a printer's transposition of "61".</note>. *Shem HaMephorash* <note>original: שׁם המפורשׁ</note></margin> the *Explicit Name*, because it teaches about the substance of the Creator clearly and without any ambiguity.

The other names of God, however, imply some divine virtue or excellence that relates to His external works. As for the other two names—of twelve or forty-two letters—there is no record of what they actually are. But the same Maimonides seems to have correctly noted that neither of them was a single word, but rather a sentence or a short phrase consisting of that many letters. # Philosophical Archaeology: or,

Having noted these points regarding the **Verbal Kabbalah**, it seems right to cut away this part from the rest of the body, like a useless and diseased limb. And let us bring the other Kabbalah—or rather that part of Kabbalah which we have called **Real**—to the examination of reason. In this Real Kabbalah, there are two primary and outstanding topics, as it seems to me: *The doctrine of the Sephiroth, and the doctrine of the Four Worlds, or Systems.* These two make up the whole of this mystic philosophy and are celebrated everywhere within it. Therefore, from these primary examples, we shall easily judge what should be decided regarding the remaining points of lesser note.

### The Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things.

Behold the ten Names or Voices, which they call <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>From the Hebrew for "enumerations" or "spheres"; they represent the ten attributes through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>, and which the Kabbalists <note>original: *Cabalistæ*</note> mention everywhere; but what notion, what sense lies beneath each one, is hardly clear. The common meaning of these words is well enough known: but in this context, they involve, or are believed to involve, I know not what great and sacrosanct mystery—as if all the treasures of wisdom, both divine and human, lay hidden away in these ten little boxes. Open your treasures, we beg you, Priest of the Kabbalah <note>original: *Mysta Cabalistice*</note>, so that we may see what is inside; for at first glance, they display nothing unique or exceptional. Do you wish these to be so many classes of things and highest genera, which they commonly call **Categories**? <note>Referring to Aristotle's ten "Categories," which were meant to classify all possible modes of being.</note> But that doctrine is too recent, nor can the orders and multitude of all known things be reduced to these ten headings. Do you wish for the *Platonic Triad*, or even the Christian Trinity, to be hidden here? But the number does not match, nor do the Jews accept that dogma. Finally, do you wish other divine natures, and more numerous ones, to be understood here? Or divine and human, simple and composite, superior and inferior? Only make the power of each Sephirah known clearly and distinctly, and you will find us ready to embrace the truth, from whatever source it flows.

Let us consult then, if you please, the expositors of these Tables, and even the Kabbalistic Lexicons; so that we may learn, first, what the *Sephiroth* mean in general and as a whole: then let us ask about each one: what its Name is, and what its notion and nature imply. By the Sephiroth in general, and their degrees, they seem to understand the *Emanations* <term>Emanations</term> <note>The philosophical concept that the universe flows out of a divine source, rather than being created from nothing.</note> of things from God, of whatever kind and in whatever way. I say *in whatever way*, for they present all these things indistinctly and confusedly; and not only the Sephiroth, but also the *World of Atziluth* <note>original: *Mundum Aziluthicum*; the "World of Emanation," the highest and most divine of the four worlds in Kabbalah.</note>, concerning

For unless there is agreement on these, it will be useless to dispute the remaining matters that depend on them. 

We, for our part, embrace the usual and everywhere-accepted reasons of things. We distinguish whatever falls within human conception first into the **Created** and **Uncreated**, the **Finite** and the **Infinite**. Furthermore, whatever is **Created** is either a **substance**, a **mode** of substance, or a **relation**. Substance, likewise, is divided into the **Corporeal** and the **Incorporeal**; and these, finally, are divided into their own orders and degrees. This is the common path, or rather the ladder of the human intellect, by which one ascends from the lowest things to the highest, and likewise descends from the highest to the lowest. Whatever we perceive is contained within these limits. Whenever, therefore, something must be defined and circumscribed, it is first reduced

Furthermore, since in every art or science there are certain words that are either entirely new or have a specific meaning different from daily use: lest they deceive a new reader, the learned in almost every discipline are accustomed to compose Lexicons or **Glossaries** <term>Glossarium</term>; there, the sense and purpose of less familiar terms are expressed through well-known and clear definitions. This same method should have been used by the **Kabbalistic Teachers** <term>Cabalisticis</term> <note>original: *Doctoribus Cabalisticis*; the Jewish mystics who transmitted the traditions of the Kabbalah.</note>, so that their meaning might be established. For in every science, just as one must agree upon first principles and the highest notions, so secondly one must agree upon the words, their use, and their accepted meanings. Therefore, as we have said, two things are lacking in **Kabbalistic philosophy** if we are to judge whether it has any value or not: first, a knowledge and consensus of principles, or a **Logical Scale** <term>Scala Logica</term> <note>A structured hierarchy of concepts, moving from the most general to the most specific.</note>, so to speak, of things and notions; then a **Glossary**, for the explanation of terms and words.

But to continue with our intended examination: Is it pleasing that we now follow the third **Sephirah** <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten divine emanations or attributes in Kabbalistic thought. so that in this part our investigation may proceed more favorably from the heart.

There are four Kabbalistic Worlds: *Aziluth* (אצילות), *Briah* (בריאה), *Jetzirah* (יצירה), and *Asiah* (עשייה). These are usually rendered as the **World of Emanation, Creation, Formation, and Manufacture** <note>original: *Mundus Emanationis, Creationis, Formationis, & Fabricæ*</note> or Action. At the summit of these, they place *En Soph* (The Infinite) or, as others call it, the **Ensophic World** <note>The realm of the pure, infinite divine essence before any manifestation.</note>: the first root of all others. But what are these new systems, you ask? What new worlds, unseen and unheard of before, do you bring us? We recognize an Uncreated or **Ideal World** <term>Mundum Idealem</term> <note>The world of perfect forms or ideas in the mind of God, a concept common in Platonic philosophy.</note>, and a created one: and this latter we are accustomed to divide into the Corporeal and the Intellectual. Beyond these, no other order of the universal reality falls within human thought or understanding. Nevertheless, let us hear what the Kabbalists philosophize regarding the nature, form, or structure of these worlds.

As for the **Aziluthic world** <note>The highest of the four worlds, associated with pure emanation and proximity to the Divine.</note>, the *Lexicon Zohar* <note>Likely a reference to the *Kabbala Denudata* by Christian Knorr von Rosenroth, which included a "Lexicon" of the Zohar.</note> explains, in its own way, both in general and in specific terms, what is to be understood by *Aziluth*; and lest we seem to deprive the reader of any light, we have decided to set down both definitions.

> *Aziluth* is the system of emanations. When a space was first emptied for the worlds, the surrounding Light of the Infinite and the Light sent into the vacuum did not contain themselves; instead, the Light of the Infinite flowed into that vacuum through a certain thin line or channel. That Light is the Emanative and Emitting principle; but the Light which is within the vacuum is the Emanating product. These two did not cling together except by means of the aforementioned line. Then *Aziluth* specifically, it says, denotes the first system of the four **Worlds** <term>Olamoth</term> <note>Hebrew: *Olamot*; the different planes of existence in Kabbalistic cosmology.</note>; which from then on is called Aziluthic. # Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

Behold the four worlds of the Kabbalists <note>These are Aziluth (Emanation), Briah (Creation), Jetzirah (Formation), and Asiah (Action/the physical world).</note>: the lower ones we recognize, but the higher ones, raised beyond every sharp sight of eyes or mind, are hidden in empty spaces and supermundane regions. Hidden, I say: for they are not revealed by their own light, nor by the borrowed light of commentators. Both the authors and the interpreters, deceived by the shadows of things, cover their errors with the paint <note>original: *fuco*, referring to cosmetic dye or a deceptive veneer</note> of new words. Whatever we ourselves understand clearly and distinctly, we gladly explain to others in an intelligible manner. But when we affect a mystical knowledge, we feign mysteries where there are none, or pretend that something great lies beneath sonorous and ambiguous words: we persuade the credulous that we indeed grasp it, but are unwilling to scatter such sacred things among the common folk. Therefore, those who seek hiding places and fear open speech are always suspected by me of silliness or imposture. Finally, to make an end, while reading writings of this kind—Kabbalistic, Theosophical, Hermetic, and every sort of pseudo-mystical <term>Pseudo-mystical</term> <note>Literally "false mysteries." The author is distinguishing between genuine philosophical inquiry and what he considers the deliberate obfuscation of these esoteric traditions.</note> work—the words of Christ often return to my mind (*John 3:19, 20, 21*):

> *Men loved darkness rather than light, because their works were evil. For everyone who does evil things hates the light: nor does he come to the light, lest his works should be rebuked. But he who performs the work of truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done according to God.*

I am not unaware that this saying regards the morals of men and their ways of living: but it fits no less the feigned pursuits of truth, and it reproves those shadelings <note>original: *tenebriones*, a derogatory term for those who operate in darkness or avoid the light of reason</note> who, by deceitful arts, flee the examination of clear reason.

### Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things.

So much for the Beard and the Little Beard. If, moreover, they are questioned about the nose, the skull, and the other parts, they respond in the same magnificent way—and in a manner no less foreign to all human understanding. *“We all occasionally act madly with reason”* <note>original: *Cum ratione quandoque insanimus omnes*; a variation on a Latin proverb suggesting that even logical systems can become irrational</note>: but it is a mental affliction common to Eastern peoples to act madly with *Allegories*, and peculiar to the Jews with their *Kabbalah* <term>Kabbalah: the Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition</term>. This much is certainly clear: either the things themselves, or the manner of proposing them, is ridiculous.

But what, you will ask, after weighing everything, is to be decided concerning the Kabbalah of the Hebrews? Does it possess no secret meaning, no hidden wisdom? And did it never have any in the past? ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

[...ity], they are suffocated. To speak plainly: Whatever truth and substance the Jewish Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah: The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</term> once possessed was, for many reasons, gradually diminished or corrupted. The Hebrew scholars, however, in order to retain for themselves the name of the ancient Kabbalah and the glory of some mystical science, patched up what had been lost with their own imaginary inventions. As time went on, with new commentators piling on one fiction after another, the whole tradition finally dissolved into confusion. Such is the medley that we call *Kabbalah* today.

We said above that the ancient Kabbalah set for itself the goal—so far as can be gathered through conjectures—of explaining to us the progression of all things from the First Cause, and the return of those same things back into the First Cause. For it must be noted that the Ancients believed that *nothing comes from nothing* <note>original: *ex nihilo nihil fieri*</note>; and that whatever substance exists has always existed in some way, and always will exist. For the doctrine of bringing things out of nothing and reducing them back into nothingness—a concept unknown to the Philosophers—seems to have been first introduced by Christian Theology, as can be seen among the Stoics, Platonists, and others. 

Nor are the Kabbalists of a different opinion, as it seems to me, since they explain the origin of things through *Emanations* <term>Emanation: the philosophical concept that all things "flow out" from a divine source, like light from a sun, rather than being created from nothing</term> from the first cause. Now, that which flows out from another already existed beforehand, though perhaps under a different appearance or form. They likewise speak of the drawing back of things into the first Being, their revolution, and their restoration to their primeval state. It is as if they had conceived of this idea: that the first Being, or the *Infinite* <note>original: *En soph* (from the Hebrew *Ein Sof*), referring to God as the "Endless" or "Infinite" before any manifestation</note>, contains all things within itself; and that the quantity of Being <note>original: *Entitatis*</note> in the universe is always the same, whether it is in a created or uncreated state. When it is in the uncreated or "pre-worldly" state, God is simply all things; but when the world is made, the degree or measure of Being is not actually increased, but rather God unfolds and evolves Himself through

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,
## [Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things]

...emanations and outpourings from the highest things to the lowest, by which the diverse forms and orders of created things are established. For this reason, they often speak of **Voids**, and of **Vessels** and **Containers** <term>Vessels/Containers: In Kabbalistic thought, these are the structures that 'hold' the divine light of emanation</term>, as if to receive these outpourings; and of flowing **Rays**; and of the channels through which they run down and are propagated. Finally, when God draws back these rays and absorbs them again, the external world perishes, and all things once more become God. *You send forth your spirit, they are created: you hide your face, they are troubled.* <note>original Latin: *Emittis spiritum, creantur: abscondis faciem, perturbantur.* This is a reference to Psalm 104:29-30.</note>

<margin>
The modern Brahmins <term>Brahmins: The priestly and scholarly caste of India; the author is comparing Eastern philosophy to Western mysticism</term> among the Indians teach the same thing.
</margin>

I have said, moreover, that the ancient sages taught nearly the same things concerning the origin and progression of things from God, and likewise concerning their return or resolution back into God. **Creation** and **Annihilation** in the modern sense are artificial words; for no single word occurs among the Hebrews, Greeks, or Latins that formerly possessed that specific meaning <note>The author argues that the concept of 'creation out of nothing' (ex nihilo) is a later theological development, not found in ancient linguistics</note>. Furthermore, as for the Philosophers, it is well known that the aforementioned doctrines prevailed in the School of the **Stoics**. For they say that all things, in their own way, participate in God, and specifically that our souls are *parts and fragments of God* <note>original Greek: *μόρια θεοῦ καὶ ἀποσπάσματα* (moria theou kai apospasmata)</note>. From this, Seneca says of the Soul: *Why, then, should you not believe that something divine exists in him who is a part of God?* <note>original Latin: *Quid est autem cur non existimes in eo divini aliquid existere, qui Dei pars est.*</note> And in Cicero it is said: *We have souls drawn and sampled from the nature of the Gods, and plucked from the divine mind.* <note>original Latin: *à naturâ Deorum haustos animos & delibatos habemus, & decerptos à divinâ mente.*</note> Nor do they less firmly establish that these souls must be poured back into God after certain

periods of time. *When the World is dissolved,* as Seneca says, *and the Gods are blended into one, Jupiter <note>Jupiter here represents the supreme Divine Intelligence or the 'World Soul'</note>, nature ceasing for a little while, rests within himself, surrendered to his own thoughts.* <note>original Latin: *Resoluto Mundo... & Diis in unum confusis, Jupiter, paulisper cessante naturâ, acquiescit sibi, cogitationibus suis traditus.*</note> They believed that the Universe alternates its states: existing now within Jupiter, now outside of Jupiter. # Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

<meta>signature: K</meta>

This hypothesis of the Stoics <term>Stoics: A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that the universe is a material organism governed by divine reason (Logos)</term> is easy to understand, but it is far too coarse; for they restrict all things to matter and material substances. By Jupiter himself, they understand nothing other than the simple **Ether** <term>Ether: In ancient science, the "fifth element" or the pure, fiery air of the upper heavens</term>, into which they believe the entire world will eventually be resolved. They believe that at a fixed time, the world will return again into the form and face of Nature—that is, into the various forms of bodies and orders of things which we call the World.

But beyond the power and scope of the material World, the Egyptians, Orphics, Pythagoreans, and Platonists acknowledge another realm. All of these, however, regarding the origin and end of things, have many points in common with **Kabbalistic** <term>Kabbalistic: Referring to Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), which describes the universe as a series of emanations from the Infinite (Ein Sof)</term> teachings. The Platonists suggest many times and in many ways that God is, in some way, all things; and that He produced the world through emanations or radiations of Himself.

The ancients of every school, as far as I can determine, believed that ***nothing is made from nothing*** <note>original Latin: *ex nihilo nihil fieri*</note>; nor can anything ever return to nothing. And they understand this principle not only *concerning generations* <note>original Latin: *de generationibus*</note> as they are usually called—that is, the transformation of one thing into another within a world that already exists—but also, to use the accepted terms, concerning **Creation** and **Annihilation**. It is as if, before the birth of the World, or after its final abolition, the essences of things were not utterly nothing. Instead, they believe these essences always have their own way of subsisting within the divine nature, although without any distinction between individuals.

Furthermore, they seem to have established a certain **Circuit**, to be completed through countless ages, between these two most diverse orders of the universe: namely, the **Created** and the **Uncreated** states.

Finally, they assert that this deified state of things will not be eternal, but, after immense ages, a new world will arise again; and these...

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...the shifts and alternations of fate will endure forever.

I have explained these things at length for this reason: that obscure matters become clearer when compared with things that are either similar or opposite. Nor is any philosophy or hypothesis known to me that comes closer to the **Kabbalistic** <term>Kabbalistic: Relating to Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that views the universe as a series of divine emanations</term> one than the theory already described. If perhaps some specific details which we added to complete this hypothesis do not appear in the writings of the aforementioned philosophers, at least the foundations and threads of them all are found there; and if they had wished to finish their tapestry and bring it to a conclusion, it would have to be woven with these threads. 

Then, as for the Kabbalah, perhaps even it does not fulfill every part of this hypothesis, since it is much more concerned with the origins of things than in explaining their ends and cycles. But what is missing or corrupted must be supplied and corrected according to the analogy of principles and in harmony with Kabbalistic elements, so that the entire work is consistent with itself and complete in all its parts. 

Finally, when I had reflected for some time whether there was anything in the wisdom of the ancients—whether Greek or **Foreign** <note>original Latin: *Barbarica*. In this context, it refers to non-Greek cultures such as the Egyptians or Chaldeans</note>—that had some kinship or similarity with the Jewish Kabbalah, I found nothing in either that seemed to reflect its character and appearance more than the aforementioned Hypothesis: concerning the origination of things from the **First Cause** <term>First Cause: A philosophical term for the ultimate origin of everything, usually identified as God</term> through outpourings and emanations, and the return of those same things into their origin once the circle is completed.

Geometry was invented by the Egyptians, according to the common opinion; and it was first employed in measuring and defining fields, the boundaries of which the rising Nile would confuse every year. But so that we do not attribute too much to any one people or age, I easily believe that this ancient Geometry of the Egyptians was not as skillful and profound, extending to all geometric magnitudes and subtle theories as modern geometry is; but rather, it stopped at what is called <term>geodesy</term> <note>the practical science of measuring and monitoring the earth’s surface and land plots</note> and other practical teachings which regarded the conveniences of life. Astronomy is also said by most to be an invention of the Egyptians; they practiced it earlier and more successfully than other nations, aided by a serene sky that was free of clouds and rain. However, I do not deny that this honor is attributed to others, and especially to the Babylonians; Herodotus implies that the Greeks learned the science of the stars from them, just as they learned geometry from the Egyptians. <note>original Greek: "δοκέει δέ μοι ἐντεῦθεν γεωμετρίη εὑρεθεῖσα... ἐς τὴν Ἑλλάδα ἐπανελθεῖν"</note> "It seems to me," he says, speaking of Egypt and the flooding of the Nile, "that geometry, having been discovered there, passed into Greece; for the Greeks learned from the Babylonians the <term>polos</term> <note>a bowl-shaped sundial used to track the sun's path</note>, the <term>gnomon</term> <note>the vertical rod of a sundial that casts the shadow</note>, and the twelve parts of the day."

<margin>Book 1.</margin>
Diodorus, however, claims that the Babylonians themselves, along with their arts, were descendants of the Egyptians; he argues that they established their orders of priests and their scientific studies after the Egyptian model. I will provide his own words: <note>original Greek: "Οἱ δὲ οὖν Αἰγύπτιοι φασὶ καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα..."</note> "The Egyptians say that after these events, many colonies were scattered from Egypt throughout the entire inhabited world. For they say that Belus—who is believed to be the son of Poseidon and Libya—led colonists to Babylon. Having established a seat by the Euphrates river, he appointed priests similar to those in Egypt who were exempt from taxes and free from all public service, whom the Babylonians call Chaldaeans. These men performed observations of the stars, imitating the priests, natural philosophers, and even the astrologers of the Egyptians."

Which the translator renders thus: *They say that many colonies were afterwards spread into the world from Egypt. Belus, son of Neptune and Libya, as it is believed, led a colony into Babylon; and having chosen a seat at the Euphrates, he instituted priests, according to the custom of the Egyptians, exempt from public expenses and burdens, whom the Babylonians call Chaldaeans. # Philosophical Archaeology: or,

...in Egypt, and they observe them following the example of Natural Philosophers <note>original: *Physicorum*</note> and Astrologers. Cicero seems rightly to have joined both peoples in this matter; the *Egyptians* and *Babylonians*, he says,
<margin>Book 1, *On Divination*</margin>
*dwelling in the level expanses of open plains, since nothing rose up from the earth that might hinder the contemplation of the heavens, they placed all their care in the knowledge of the stars.*

I place little value on those disputes regarding the primacy of letters among nations, or the first invention of the sciences; for nothing prevents the same things from being discovered by several people at once. It is of greater interest to us to know who increased and aided the sciences, how far they advanced them, and what monuments or doctrines they left to posterity, by whose help one might progress in cultivating those same fields. However, what we have said about *Barbaric Geometry* <note>Burnet uses "Barbaric" in the classical sense to refer to non-Greek, ancient civilizations</note>, I think almost the same must be said of their *Astronomy*: that it was not accurate or universal. The ancients "tasted" Astronomy, as *Plutarch* says of *Numa Pompilius*: "he also touched upon the study of the heavens, neither with precision, nor yet entirely without observation." <note>original Greek: ἥψατο δὲ καὶ τῆς περὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν πραγματείας, οὔτε ἀκριβῶς, οὔτε παντάπασιν ἀθεωρήτως</note> They observed certain phenomena of the heavens, but only those easier to observe: the rising and setting of the fixed stars, the periods and revolutions of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>; and, for the use of <term>Genethliacs</term> <note>the practice of casting birth charts or horoscopes</note>, in which they indulged excessively, they observed the parts of the Zodiac and the aspects of the Planets. Furthermore, they tracked the Equinoxes and solstices, and other things necessary for explaining the form of the year. And indeed, if I grasp the matter correctly, their Astronomy served solely, or chiefly, for the purposes of Agriculture, Genethliacs, and the Calendar. It is not established that the ancients penetrated or grasped the theories of the Planets—the most laborious part of that art. *Eudoxus* is said to have been the first to establish hypotheses of celestial motions; and *Ptolemy* the first to establish Tables of motions. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...I believe [these more complex methods] originated from the ingenuity of the Greeks; the ancients, or at least the most ancient among them, used less technical equipment in their studies.

You will perhaps say that both the *Babylonians* and *Egyptians* possessed celestial observations spanning many centuries. Quite right—but what kind of observations were they? Let them be produced and shown: we maintain that they were established based on manifest phenomena, like those we have already cited, or regarding *Eclipses* that had already occurred. I say "past" eclipses, for it is not established to me that any *Egyptian* or *Assyrian* astronomer ever announced a future *Solar Eclipse* by his own skill. For this reason, *Thales* is celebrated as the first to predict *Eclipses*, 
<margin>Diogenes Laertius; Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1; Pliny, book 2, ch. 12.</margin>
and as far as I know, no one among the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to non-Greek ancient civilizations like the Babylonians and Egyptians.</note> snatched this glory from him. Regarding the *Babylonians*, *Diodorus* testifies 
<margin>Book 2, page 117.</margin>
that they knew nothing precise regarding the calculations of *Solar Eclipses*: <note>original Greek: περὶ δὲ τῆς κατὰ τὸν ἥλιον ἐκλείψεως, ἀσθενεστάτας ἀποδείξεις φέροντες, οὐ τολμῶσι προλέγειν, οὐδ᾽ ἀκριβῶς ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς παραγράφειν τοὺς χρόνους</note> *bringing forward the weakest evidence concerning the eclipse of the sun, they do not dare to predict it, nor to accurately record the timing for it.* They dare neither to predict these things nor to define their timing.

Moreover, we have noted these points regarding "Barbaric" Astronomy not so much from history and certain witnesses, but because they follow logically from better-known facts, nor can they be refuted from any other source. I am not unaware that *Diodorus* hints once or twice that the *Egyptians* possessed an exact science of celestial things and 
<margin>Book 1, page 73 and page 46.</margin>
accurate observations; but I understand this only in comparison to other nations. Since, without geometry and telescopes, an accurate science of these matters could scarcely—or not at all—be obtained. ## Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...a journey to the East. And, so that we do not begrudge anyone their due, the Greeks must be credited for the form and arrangement of these sciences, and almost all the rest: however, in investigating their physical causes—which is the ultimate perfection—work is still ongoing. But having now left these matters behind, let us proceed to the Natural Philosophy <term>Physiology: used here in the classical sense of "Physiologia," meaning the study of nature or natural philosophy</term> of the Egyptians, toward which our discourse especially aims.

<margin>
Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 3, chapter 11.
</margin>
<margin>
Plato, *In the Timaeus*.
</margin>
<margin>
Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 5.
</margin>
The Ancients joined their Theology with Natural Philosophy; and when they discussed the origin and nature of things, they were also accustomed to treat the gods and their origin. Therefore, among them *Cosmogony* <note>original: Cosmogonia, the study of the origin of the universe</note>, *Theogony* <note>original: Theogonia, the study of the origins of the gods</note>, and *Theology* have almost the same value; and we now embrace all these under the name of Philosophy. What the Egyptians felt about the origin of things was explained to us by *Diodorus Siculus* in his first book; namely, they asserted that the sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay</note> was formed from a confused mass of elements, which the Greeks later called *Chaos*. And the *Theban* priests, as we learn from *Eusebius*, maintained that the first form of the Earth was *egg-shaped* <note>original: Oviformem</note>. Then, regarding the destruction of the sublunary world and the end of things, they established it to be twofold, by Water and Fire; which is related by an Egyptian Priest in the works of Plato. They were also among the first to teach the *restoration* <note>original Greek: ἀποκατάστασιν, or 'apocatastasis,' meaning the periodic renewal or return of the universe to its original state</note> and the Great Cycles of the World. Finally, regarding the heavens and the entire structure of things, I have no doubt that what we call the Pythagorean system of the world is the oldest of all and was brought from the East; however, while this was reserved for the Initiates <term>Mystae: those initiated into secret religious mysteries or hidden knowledge</term>, it is likely that another view became more widespread.

And truly, what the dogmas of the Egyptians were, and what they taught others, seems best known from their disciples, the Greek philosophers; who, as is well known, were accustomed to leave their homeland and seek out Egypt to obtain higher learning. Thus, for example, if Orpheus [received] his natural philosophy, as well as his sacred rites, from the Egyptians...

For that most ancient philosophy did not concern itself with conducting an examination of individual things; you will seek in vain among the Ancients for the source of the *Magnet’s* <note>original: Magnes</note> power, or the origin of the colors of the heavenly *Rainbow* <note>original: Iris</note>: what the matter of Fire is: what the particles of Water are like: or how great the force of compressed air is. Ancient wisdom was not occupied with those things, but was focused on WORLDLY Phenomena, as I might call them, which affected the whole of nature. *What is the Origin of things, what are their changes and cycles, and what is the final end?* If you ask these things of the ancients, you will receive an answer. On these, they say, Mercury <note>The Roman equivalent of Hermes</note> inscribed his doctrine in ancient times, and that the "second Mercury" expanded and clarified this same doctrine, encompassing it in many books. It is at least certain that both Greek philosophers and Egyptian historians drew many things from these columns. Regarding Plato, Proclus notes (citing Crantor) that the Egyptian priests affirmed he had borrowed the account of the ***Atlanteans*** <note>The story of the lost city of Atlantis from Plato’s *Timaeus*</note> from these columns, and that they were still surviving in the time of ***Proclus*** or ***Crantor***. *That these things were written on the pillars which are still preserved.* <note>original Greek: Ἐν σήλαις ταῖς ἔτι σωζομέναις ταῦτα γεγράφθαι.</note>

### Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...ancient pillars, which Plato and Pythagoras, having examined even before him, established their philosophy; <note>original: "παλαιὰς στήλας, ἃς Πλάτων ἤδη πρὸ ὁδεν κὶ Πυθαγόρας διαγνόντες, φιλοσοφίαν συνεστήσαντο" and "quas Plato & Pythagoras ante eum legentes, philosophiam inde constituerunt"</note>. Others also, such as the Phoenician ***Sanchoniathon***, used these same monuments: he is said to have drawn his philosophy and the record of historical events from the books of **Taaut** <note>The Phoenician name for Thoth, the god of wisdom</note> and from the temple inscriptions <note>original Greek: ἀναγραφαῖς</note>. 
<margin>Eusebius, *Chronicle*</margin> Finally, from the same source, ***Manetho***, the Egyptian writer and prophet, produced his sacred history—wherever that **Seriadic Land** was, in which he asserts these columns were placed.

<margin>Book 22</margin> ***Ammianus Marcellinus***, who had traveled through Egypt and was no indifferent observer of wonders, says that these **Pillars** <note>original: *Stelas*</note> were hidden away in certain caverns or subterranean vaults, which they called **Syringes** <note>original: Σύριγγας; referring to the narrow, pipe-like rock-cut galleries or tombs</note> in their own language; and this was not far from **Thebes**, or **Diospolis**. He adds, moreover, that they were stored here before the **Deluge**: so that, I suppose, they might be immune to the damage of the waters. ***Manetho*** likewise asserts that his own records were pre-diluvian; and ***Josephus*** says the same regarding his **Sethian** columns. From this one may not unreasonably suspect that these are the same columns—both these and those—under a different name; especially since there is not much difference between Josephus’s term **Suriadic** and Manetho’s **Seriadic**. It would indeed be a pleasure to look upon and read these pre-diluvian Archaeologies, or the literary monuments of another world; but since everything was turned upside down in the **Cataclysm** <note>The Great Flood</note>, I find it hard to believe that such inscriptions, of whatever kind they were, could have been preserved in that universal ruin or found intact afterward. Although, to tell the truth, if any way were to be tried, or any protection sought against the force and impact of so great a disaster, nothing could have been safer than what was carved deep into a solid and subterranean stone-quarry or mass of rock. ### The Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things

...wherever it stood, we shall not dispute the time or place.

Following the sacred inscriptions are the ***Sacred Books of the Egyptians***, which are somewhat more recent but no less famous. Most authors who have written on Egyptian matters mention these. ***Diodorus***, when speaking of the studies and duties of the Egyptian priests, says among other things that they stand by the rulers, *reading aloud from the actions recorded in the sacred books those that could be beneficial.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν ἐν ταῖς ἱεραῖς βίβλοις ἀναγεγραμμένων πράξεων, τὰς ὠφελῆσαι δυναμένας παραναγινώσκοντες</note> And from these Commentaries they report the names and a Catalog of Greek Philosophers (as we shall see below) who had been instructed in Egyptian wisdom: *The priests relate from the records found in the sacred books*, etc. <note>original Greek: οἱ δ' ἱερεῖς ἱστοροῦσιν ἐκ τῶν ἀναγραφῶν, τῶν ἐν ταῖς ἱεραῖς βίβλοις</note> <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 1, Ch. 9</margin> ***Philo of Byblos*** indicates that ***Sanchoniathon*** used these in composing his Phoenician work, when he says that he compared what he had written *with the secret writings of the Ammoneans* <note>Likely referring to the followers or temple of the god Amun</note> *found in the innermost shrines.* <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἀδύτων εὑρεθεῖσιν ἀποκρύφοις Ἀμμονέων γράμμασιν συγκειμένοις</note> <margin>Josephus, *Against Apion*, Book 1</margin> ***Manetho*** is also said *to have interpreted* his Egyptian history *from the sacred writings.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων μεθερμηνεύειν</note> For it was not only those things pertaining to the worship of the Gods or the laws of the empire that were written in these books, but historical matters of any great importance, miscellaneous subjects, and every kind of philosophy. Indeed, the task and care given to the priests was to record in these commentaries whatever was worthy of memory and for posterity; and to carefully preserve what they had received from their ancestors. <margin>In the *Timaeus*</margin> Thus, the **Priest of Sais** <note>original: *Flamen Saiticus*; though 'flamen' is a Roman term, it is used here to denote the high priest of the Egyptian city of Sais</note> related to ***Solon*** that *whatever was worthy of remembrance was written down in their temples.* <margin>Book 17</margin> And ***Strabo*** wonders why it was not recorded in these books what those among the ancients who had traveled through Ethiopia thought about the origin and flooding of the ***Nile***. *It is a wonder then how, from such opportunities, the account of the rains was not perfectly clear to those people, especially since the priests recorded such matters with great diligence into...* <note>original Greek: Θαυμαστὸν οὖν πῶς ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων ἀφορμῶν οὐ τελέως ἐναργὴς ἦν ἡ περὶ ὄμβρων ἱστορία τοῖς τότε καὶ ταῦτα τῶν ἱερέων φιλοπραγμονέστερον ἀναφερόντων εἰς</note>

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

<margin>Book 2 of Heliodorus’ *Ethiopian Story*</margin>
...the sacred letters, and setting aside those things which display an excellence of learning. <note>original Greek: τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, καὶ ἀποτιθεμένων ὅσα μάθεσιν περιττὴν ἔμφαινει</note> It is therefore strange why, with such great opportunities for investigation offered, the history of the rains of that age was not entirely known to men; especially since the priests recorded and stored in the **SACRED BOOKS** those things which possessed some more subtle knowledge. Heliodorus, however, seemingly better instructed in these matters, says that he replied to the Greeks—who were asking many questions about the sources and floods of the Nile—from his own knowledge and from those things which were prescribed in the Sacred Books: *whatever things concerning this river have been recorded in the sacred books, which only the prophetic priests are allowed both to know and to read.* <note>original Greek: ὅσα περὶ ποταμοῦ τούτου βίβλοις ἱεραῖς ἀναγεγραμμένα, μόνοις τοῖς προφητικοῖς καὶ γινώσκειν καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν ἔξεστι. In Egypt, "Prophets" were the highest rank of priests, the keepers of divine knowledge.</note>

These were the literary monuments of the Egyptians: the Inscriptions on the Pillars and the Sacred Books. In both kinds, some things were open and exposed to the public and foreigners, while others were reserved in the <term>inner shrines</term> <note>adytis: the most sacred, restricted areas of a temple</note> of the Temples. Heliodorus hinted at this above when he says, *whatever only the prophetic priests are allowed both to know and to read.* And Philo also refers to *those things found in the inner shrines* <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἀδύτων εὑρεθεῖσι</note>, which indeed were not known to all. From this Caesar, in Lucan, speaks thus to Achoreus, the Egyptian priest,

->*Whatever is inscribed*<-
->*in the ancient shrines, bring it forth.*<-

For there were two kinds of doctrine among the ancient peoples: the *popular* and the *secret* <note>original Greek: δημῶδες καὶ ἀπόρρητον</note>—the **common doctrine** and the **hidden doctrine**. This was not only because of the variety of the subject matter, but they often treated the same subject in two ways: the popular and the philosophical. The former was easily open to everyone through public monuments and common teachers; the latter, however, so that it would not become cheapened or corrupted by the hands of the people, was hidden and concealed in more than one way. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...[written] in an uncommon kind of characters; to be explained by fastidious priests, who were responsible for them, only after great preparation and prior training. Since these things are not entirely unworthy of being known, and seem to pertain to the knowledge of Egyptian literature, we shall further add a few points regarding their explanation, if you please.

There were two types, both of Learning and of Letters, among the Egyptians: *sacred* and *common*. This is testified by Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, and many others. Herodotus in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus’s *Histories*, named after the Muse of music</note> says of the Egyptians, "They use two kinds of writing," <note>original Greek: Διφασίοισι δὲ γράμμασι χρέωνται</note> "and some of them are called sacred, others common." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν ἱερὰ, τὰ δὲ δημοτικὰ καλέεται</note> Diodorus in his first book [writes], "The priests teach their sons two kinds of letters, those called sacred, and those whose study is more common." <note>original Greek: παιδεύουσι δὲ τοὺς υἱοὺς οἱ μὲν ἱερεῖς γράμματα διττὰ, τά τε ἱερὰ καλούμενα, καὶ τὰ κοινοτέραν ἔχοντα τὴν μάθησιν</note> He repeats this more distinctly below, asserting that the *sacred* ones are Egyptian and the *common* ones are Ethiopian; "For while the Egyptians have their own unique letters, those called common are learned by everyone indiscriminately; but those called sacred are known only to the priests among the Egyptians, who learn them in secret from their fathers; however, among the Ethiopians, everyone uses these forms." <note>original Greek: Ἰδίων γὰρ Αἰγυπτίοις ὄντων γραμμάτων, τὰ μὲν δημώδη προσαγορευόμενα πάντας μανθάνειν, τὰ δ᾽ ἱερὰ καλούμενα παρὰ μὲν τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις μόνους γινώσκειν τοὺς ἱερεῖς, παρὰ τῶν πατέρων ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις μανθάνοντας, παρὰ δὲ τοῖς Αἰθίοψιν ἅπαντας τούτοις χρῆσθαι τοῖς τύποις</note> *Since indeed the Egyptians have their own proper letters, called common, they are learned by all without distinction, but only the priests know those called sacred, handed down secretly by their parents; yet all the Ethiopians use these (Sacred) letters without discrimination.* From this, those priests are properly called <term>Sacred Scribes</term> <note>hierogrammateis: specialized priests who mastered the complex hieroglyphic script and served as keepers of the archives</note>.

<margin>On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, section 8, chapter 5.</margin>
A part, or mystical method, of the Hermetic Doctrine <note>Teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage synonymous with the Egyptian god Thoth</note> found in the <term>inner shrines</term> <note>adytis: the most holy, restricted chambers of a temple</note> of the Temple of Sais, is said to be "recorded in hieroglyphic letters," according to the testimony of Iamblichus. <note>original Greek: ἀναγεγραμμένη ἐν ἱερογλυφικοῖς γράμμασι</note> Nor was it inscribed only in Books, but also on the more notable columns, with these sacred letters; as in the Tomb of Isis and Osiris, which is said to be in Nysa in Arabia, Diodorus says there was "a pillar inscribed for each of the gods." <note>original Greek: στήλην ἑκατέρῳ τῶν θεῶν ἐπιγεγραμμένην</note>

...[written] in the sacred letters. <margin>Book 16.</margin> And the column of Sesostris <note>Sesostris was a legendary king of ancient Egypt, often identified with Ramesses II, who was said to have conquered many lands and left pillars behind.</note>, which was placed on the borders of Arabia and Ethiopia, indicated his crossing by these letters, according to Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian of the 1st century.</note>: "They say that there is a pillar of Sesostris the Egyptian there, signifying his passage in sacred letters." <note>original Greek: Φασὶν ἐνταῦθα στήλην εἶναι Σεσωστριδος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίου, μηνύουσαν ἱεροῖς γράμμασι τὴν διάβασιν αὐτοῦ.</note>

However, this custom of using two kinds of letters was not exclusive to the Egyptians, but shared with other Eastern peoples, particularly the Ethiopians and Babylonians. Democritus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his atomic theory and extensive travels.</note> seems to have written about the sacred letters of both, if we may judge from the titles of his books, <margin>According to Diogenes Laertius</margin> *On the sacred letters in Meroë* <note>An ancient capital of the Kingdom of Kush, in modern-day Sudan.</note> and *On the sacred letters in Babylon*. <note>original Greek: Περὶ τῶν ἐν Μερόῃ, & περὶ τῶν ἐν Βαβυλῶνι, ἱερῶν γραμμάτων</note> Lucian <note>A satirist and rhetorician.</note> <margin>On Long-Lived People</margin> mentions "interpreters of sacred words" <note>original Greek: Ἱερῶν λόγων ἑρμηνευτάς</note> among the Babylonians; and since Democritus is said to have taken moral discourses from a Babylonian column (as we noted above), I believe this refers to the same Babylon whose sacred script he wrote about, and in which that column was likely inscribed. Finally, the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of India.</note> of India use not only a different script but even a language different from the common tongue to preserve their philosophy. But let us proceed with our subject.

Beyond these mysterious letters, the priests were the nearly unyielding guardians of the sacred monuments; like dragons <note>A metaphor for the vigilant and protective nature of the priesthood over their hidden lore.</note>, they brooded over these treasures night and day. <margin>See Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 354.</margin> Whatever was written in the sacred books only reached the common people or foreigners through these interpreters. The Greek philosophers, who traveled to Egypt to acquire knowledge, complained of this difficulty, spending many years visiting and flattering the priests. <margin>Book 17, p. 806.</margin> Let us hear Strabo concerning the people of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun," a major religious and educational center in ancient Egypt.</note>, regarding Plato and Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician.</note>: "Eudoxus traveled here with Plato, and they stayed with the priests for thirteen years, as some have reported; for these priests were preeminent in the science of the heavens..." <note>original Greek: Συνεβη δὴ τῷ Πλάτωνι ὁ Εὔδοξος δεῦρο, καὶ συνδιέτριψαν τοῖς ἱερεῦσι ἐκεῖνοι ἐνταῦθα τρισκαίδεκα ἔτη, ὡς εἴρηταί τισι· περιττοὶ γὰρ ὄντες κατὰ τὴν ἐπιστήμην τῶν οὐρανίων</note>

These priests, however, because of their fear of the King, dared not offer any further excuse, but instead sought to deter him from his purpose by the magnitude of the labor and the hardships involved; and therefore they enjoined upon him, while he was yet a novice, things that were very harsh and entirely foreign to the religion of the Greeks. # Archaeologies of Philosophy: or,

<margin>
Commentary on Romans, ch. 3.
</margin>
...having entered the <term>Adyta<note>The innermost, most sacred part of a temple, inaccessible to the public and reserved for the priesthood.</note></term>, he would learn the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians. This was indeed required by the Egyptian priests, according to Origen, of all who were admitted to sacred or scientific studies. "Among the Egyptians," he says, "from whom almost all nations borrowed their sacred rites and ceremonies, no one studied Geometry or Astronomy, etc., unless they had undergone circumcision." There were, moreover, many types of trials and <term>hardships<note>original Greek: κακοπάθειαι (kakopatheiai); referring to the physical or mental ordeals initiates had to endure to prove their worth.</note></term>, as Porphyry calls them, with which they exercised those about to be initiated. I admit, however, that this was more or less the custom among other nations; the Druids of the Celts, the Essenes of the Jews, and the <term>Hierophants<note>Chief priests who interpreted sacred mysteries.</note></term> of the Greeks were unwilling to hand over their mysteries and secret discipline to the <term>uninitiated<note>original Greek: ἀμυήτοις (amyētois).</note></term>. Furthermore, they were sometimes bound by an oath to <term>keep these things in secret<note>original Greek: ἐν ἀποκρύφοις, ταῦτα ἔχειν (en apokryphois, tauta echein).</note></term>. <margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 1, p. 11.</margin> The same is correctly observed regarding the Persians, Syrians, and Indians. But besides the fact that many of these things are believed to be of Egyptian origin, passed on to other nations by imitation, if perhaps some were difficult in sacred matters, none proved themselves so difficult as the Egyptians in the study of the sciences.

Finally, to hide their doctrine, the Egyptians wrapped many things in hieroglyphic forms, symbols, enigmas, and fables. I say "hieroglyphic forms," for I think the **sacred letters** are to be distinguished entirely from **hieroglyphic forms**. Since so many and such great works were written in these sacred letters—the monuments of <term>Hermes<note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom tens of thousands of works on wisdom, religion, and nature were attributed.</note></term>, amounting to some tens of thousands of volumes; <margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, Section 8, ch. 1.</margin> all the **Sacred Books**, the **Sacred Columns**, and the inscriptions of the Temples—I can hardly bring myself to believe that arguments of so many and such diverse subjects (Physiological, Theological, Moral, Historical, and Political) could be expressed by various forms of animals, or members of the human body, or mechanical instruments. As for symbols and riddles, it is well known that it was the custom of ancient nations to convey the thoughts of the mind under these "coverings." This was done either to show off a certain sharpness and skill of wit, or to put forward in ambiguous and obscure ways a secret doctrine which they felt a religious scruple to describe clearly and openly. Regarding those games and contests of wit through enigmatic, symbolic, or hieroglyphic things or sayings, we have many examples among the leading men of the foreign nations. The King of **Scythia**, threatening war against **Darius**—who had crossed the <term>Ister<note>The ancient name for the Danube River.</note></term>—sent a symbol instead of a letter: <margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies*, Book 5.</margin> a mouse, a frog, a bird, a dart, and a plow. The interpreters of Darius explained this in various ways. Another King of Scythia sent these words to the people of Byzantium: <margin>Ibid.</margin> *Do not cause harm to my revenues, lest my horses drink your water.* He was hinting that unless they desisted, he would bring war upon them. 90 Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

The King of Ethiopia contended in this same manner, until **Bias** <note>Bias of Priene (6th century BCE) was one of the Seven Sages of Greece. Legend says he helped the King of Egypt win a bet against the King of Ethiopia by solving the riddle of how to "drink the sea dry."</note> explained to him by what means he might *drink the sea dry*. Furthermore, **Solomon** and the **King of the Tyrians** <note>King Hiram of Tyre, who according to Josephus, engaged in a riddle-solving contest with Solomon.</note> competed with riddles; as did **Samson** and the **Philistines** in sacred history. Among the Greeks, **Heraclitus** and his disciples delighted in obscure maxims; and the **Pythagoreans** in symbols. Here, however, the terms *enigma* and *enigmatic* are used broadly to mean obscure speech that covers the thing it designates, or the matter it treats, with wrappings and detours: whether it be in the form of a question, a command, or a simple statement. For this is what the Greeks call *speaking in riddles* <note>original Greek: αἰνίττεσθαι (ainíttesthai)</note>—to signify things known to oneself through obscure words; a practice that can encompass many modes of speaking. Finally, among the Hebrews, <term>mashal<note>מָשָׁל (mashal): a proverb, parable, or pithy saying.</note></term> and <term>chidah<note>חִידָה (chidah): a riddle or "dark saying" that requires interpretation.</note></term>—proverbs and riddles—seem to fulfill all the roles of the wise man. Whatever is said sententiously, skillfully, and gravely, is called a *mashal*; whatever is said mystically, as secret doctrine is usually handled, is called a *chidah*. In this sense we should understand the words of the Prophet in <margin>Psalms 49:3, 4; Baruch 3:23</margin> **Psalm 78:2-3** and the **Evangelist** in **Matthew 13:35**. For in sacred doctrine, just as in foreign teachings, there are mysteries or *secret things* <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητα (apórrēta)</note> which are brought forward obscurely; finally, in the end times, they are to be demonstrated openly and in public.

There were many ways of handing down Philosophy and Theology among the ancients, and they were mostly secret. They veiled the face of truth, as if shame forbade showing her naked to the common people. **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced much of medieval Christian and Islamic thought.</note> notes these methods in this way: <margin>Platonic Theology, Book 1, Ch. 4.</margin> <note>Burnet provides the original Greek from Proclus, followed by a Latin translation: "οἱ μὲν γὰρ δι' ἐνδείξεως περὶ τῶν θείων λέγοντες..." / "Qui enim per demonstrationem de rebus divinis tractant..."</note> *For those who treat divine matters through demonstration do so either symbolically and mythically, or through images and representations of things. But those who announce their thoughts openly do so either through scientific knowledge or through inspiration from the gods.*

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...nations; and among philosophers, all the best; and those who established sacred rites and ceremonies; even the Gods themselves in their Oracles made use of fables. Here, however, under the name of Fables, we should not understand those commonly so called—namely, little stories or narrations that are fictional in both matter and form, whether they are useful or merely pleasing. For "to invent fables out of nothing is not the Homeric way," says **Strabo**: <margin>Book 1, page 20.</margin> *To stitch a new monstrous tale onto nothing true is not Homeric* <note>original Greek: ἐκ μηδενὸς δ’ ἀληθὲς ἀνάπτειν καινὴν τερατολογίαν, οὐχ Ὁμηρικόν</note>. I would hardly dare to say that of Homer, but I will easily say: *It is not philosophical* <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι φιλοσοφικόν</note>.

For philosophical fables always have some foundation in reality; the threads are true, but false colors are overlaid. **Planciades Fulgentius** <note>A late antique Latin writer known for his allegorical interpretations of classical myths</note> correctly says of the <margin>Preface to the *Mythologies*.</margin> different kinds of fables: *Fables—a name which indicates a profession of falsehood—are written either for the sake of delight alone, or also for utility.*

Philosophers, rejecting those which only provide delight, divide the other species of fables in this manner: *Of those fables invented for the sake of utility, in some the material is fictional and the order of the narration itself is woven through lies, as in the fables of **Aesop**, which are famous for the elegance of their fiction. But in others, a truth of matter lies beneath, though this truth itself is brought forth through certain composed and fictional elements; and this is now called a "fabulous narration" rather than a "fable."* Such are the mystical traditions of **Hesiod** and **Orpheus** regarding the progeny or birth of the Gods.

Therefore, from this fruitful division we have described, the first species—which is conceived from falsehood and narrated through falsehood—is entirely alien to books of Philosophy. Only those are truly philosophical under whose <term>fabulous bark<gloss>an outer layer of mythological storytelling that conceals a deeper, often scientific or spiritual, meaning</gloss></term> a truth lies, and one that is not common. For the authors of mythological philosophy seem to have intended this: to preserve secret doctrine from being lost, while ensuring it was not exposed to the common crowd or to ordinary minds. ### Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

<margin>
*Chronicon*, p. 6, Greek.
"From the pillars located in the Seriad land, inscribed, he says, in the sacred dialect and hieroglyphic letters by Thoth, the first Hermes, and translated after the flood from the sacred dialect into the Greek tongue in hieroglyphic letters, and deposited in books by Agathodæmon, the second Hermes, father of Tat, in the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptian temples." <note>original Greek: 'Εκ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ση-ριαδικῇ γῇ κειμένων στηλῶν... ἐν τοῖς ἀδύτοις τῶν ἱερῶν Αἰ-γυπτίων.</note>

As far as I know, there are only two authors, or fragments of authors, available to us from whom these things can be gathered: *Manetho* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek</note> and *Philo of Byblos* <note>A Phoenician writer (1st–2nd century CE) who claimed to translate the works of the ancient priest Sanchuniathon</note>; and neither of them explains the matter clearly. *Manetho*, according to *Eusebius* and later *Syncellus*, says that the first *Mercury* <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hermes or Egyptian Thoth, the god of wisdom and writing</note> inscribed his teaching in a sacred dialect and in hieroglyphic letters on columns placed in the Land of Seriad <note>A legendary location, often debated by scholars, where the antediluvian (pre-Flood) wisdom was said to be preserved on pillars</note>. These, after the flood, were translated from the sacred language into the Greek tongue—likewise in hieroglyphic letters—and were committed to writing in the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptian temples by *Agathodæmon* <note>Literally "the Good Spirit," here identified as a second Hermes</note>, the second *Mercury* and father of *Tat*. But besides those rather difficult points regarding the pre-flood columns, the Land of Seriad (known to no one), and the use of hieroglyphic letters for the Greek language—besides these things, I say, *Manetho’s* account does not reach our specific goal. For he deals with translation into another language, not into a different style of writing; nor does he explain with what kind of style—simple or allegorical—those original *Mercurial* writings or *Seriadic* monuments were composed.

<margin>*Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 1, last chapter.*</margin>

*Philo of Byblos* comes closer to our subject. He says that the son of *Thabion* <note>An obscure figure, possibly a Phoenician priest</note> is said to be the first to have turned the Books of Mercury into allegories, and in that form this doctrine later descended to the Greeks; who, by their innate talent for decorating and amplifying things, made what was foreign into their own.

...on this matter, I remember none except ***Horapollo*** <note>original: *Orum Apollinem*. Accordingly, if you consider philosophy, the **wisdom of the Egyptians** is to be sought nowhere else than from their disciples, the **Greek Philosophers**. This is especially true of the most ancient among them: namely, the **Orphics**, the **Ionians**, the **Pythagoreans**, and the **Platonists**. We see the likeness of the fathers in their sons and grandsons; and from these students of the Egyptian discipline, it is possible to sketch or outline the image of that wisdom itself, however imperfectly.

Furthermore, another objection must be cleared away before we bring an end to this dissertation: namely, if the **wisdom of the Egyptians** was as great as we claim—if there was such vast knowledge of things divine and natural—how could it happen that this nation fell into **crass idolatry**, the most foul of all? I say "most foul" because they held as gods and worshipped not only the Sun, the Moon, and the Heavenly Bodies; and not only illustrious and beneficial men; but even beasts and tiny creatures—indeed, even vegetables themselves <note>This is a common trope in classical literature (e.g., Juvenal) mocking the Egyptians for supposedly worshipping leeks and onions.</note>. I respond that just as divine wisdom is unsearchable, so too is human folly. Therefore, matters that are certain and handed down with constant reliability should not be denied simply because they do not seem to agree with Reason, or because some things [oppose] others...

But truly, you will say, the Egyptians were most devoted not only to Idolatry, but also to <term>Natal Astrology</term> <note>original: "Genethliaca"; the practice of casting horoscopes based on the moment of birth</note> and Magic; the latter a wicked art, the former a most vain one. Even now, I say, when we ought not only to abhor all superstition more deeply, but when the nature of the Heavens has become known more clearly than light itself; namely, that the Planets are nothing other than so many opaque terrestrial masses, and the Fixed Stars so many fiery masses. Therefore, no theorem of <term>Judiciary Astrology</term> <note>original: "Astrologia Judiciaria"; the branch of astrology used to predict future events and human destiny</note>, as it is called, is founded in natural science, nor can it ever be so founded.

As for Magic, there are many kinds of it: strictly forbidden to us Christians, perhaps due to a change in the governance of the invisible world. But it is not so easily clear that every kind of commerce with <term>Genii</term> <note>original: "Geniis"; intermediary spirits or guardian souls that were believed to inhabit the air</note> is forbidden by the law of nature. However, if some have abused this commerce, whether to the harm of the human race or for the sake of pride and ostentation, that argues for the malice or vanity of the authors, but not for their ignorance. Finally, I easily agree with those who say that men were first taught both arts, the Astrological and the Magical, by evil Angels. For when I look upon the complex apparatus of both, they seem to me to be Inventions, or Deliriums, that are more than human. But enough of these things.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

Given that these things are so, and the ancient reputation of the Egyptians regarding literature and science remains secure, we must finally explain by what means it perished, and when exactly this ancient wisdom was gradually extinguished. How great is the instability of human affairs, and how remarkable are their cycles! Not only do empires change, but learning, customs, and religion migrate from one land to another; and since it is not permitted for all to enjoy these gifts at once, we enjoy them in turns. Human affairs are so arranged as if it were decreed that within the circuit of a predetermined time, individual lands and peoples would have their own turns, in both good things and bad. Knowledge began its course in the East, just like the Sun; moving toward the West, where we have long enjoyed its light. Who knows if, having left these seats, it is destined to progress further; or if, diffused everywhere, it will illuminate the entire globe with its rays at once. As for Egypt, it once flourished in every kind of learning, but is now overwhelmed by the most extreme barbarism. It held its literature and its sacred rites inviolate until the times of the Persians,

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

Since these things are so, and the ancient reputation of the Egyptians regarding learning <note>original: "literæ", referring here to the whole body of literature and science</note> and the sciences remains secure, we must now finally explain by what means it perished, and when at last this ancient wisdom was gradually extinguished. How great is the inconstancy of human affairs, and how wonderful the changes! Not only do Empires change, but learning, customs, and religion migrate from one land to another; and since it is not granted to everyone to enjoy these all at once, we enjoy them in turns. Human affairs are so arranged as if it were decreed that within a set circuit of time, individual lands and peoples would have their own turns, in both good things and bad. Like the Sun, learning began its course from the East; turning then toward the West, where we have now long enjoyed its light. Who knows if, after leaving these seats, it will progress further; or if, diffused everywhere, it will illuminate the whole world with its rays at the same time? As for Egypt, it once flourished in every kind of discipline, and is now overwhelmed by the uttermost barbarism. Until the times of the Persians, it held its learning and its sacred rites inviolate.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 17.</margin>

**The Persians.** "For the Egyptians, because the Persians had acted impiously toward the temples and ruled violently, gladly welcomed the Macedonians." <note>original: "Οι γ̅ Αἰγύπτιοι τῶν Περσῶν ἠσεβηκότων εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ κ̅ βιαίως ἀρχόντων, ἄσμενοι προσεδέξαντο τοὺς Μακεδόνας." This refers to the arrival of Alexander the Great in 332 BCE, who was seen as a liberator from Persian oppression.</note> But from this time, under Alexander’s successors <note>The Ptolemaic dynasty</note>, both the priesthood and the Egyptian wisdom seem to have gradually degenerated; nonetheless, in both intervals—under the Persians and under the Ptolemies—many Greek philosophers descended into Egypt; namely, as many as undertook that journey after Pythagoras (who was in Egypt at the same time as Cambyses). But after Egypt was subdued by the Romans, and the Library of Alexandria was burned, ancient literature <note>original: "Literatura Antiqua," referring to the collected body of written knowledge</note> perished along with it. Later, however, there was a distinguished School at Alexandria: not only of Greeks, but also of Jews, and then of Christians, until the Saracen times <note>The period of the Muslim conquests in the 7th century CE</note>. By them, and the later Turks, all Egypt—once the most flourishing seat of ancient wisdom—was finally reduced to barbarism.

Since it was the custom of the ancients to begin their histories or archaeologies with a certain **cosmogony** <note>A theory or story concerning the origin of the universe</note>, it is likely that Manetho did the same in this work. Furthermore, he wrote a separate *Egyptian Theology*, which, among the ancients, usually encompassed **physiology** <note>In the seventeenth century, "physiology" referred to natural philosophy or the study of the physical laws of nature, rather than just the functions of living bodies</note>. But let us hear Eusebius concerning the works of Manetho: <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 2, beginning.</margin> <note>The original text provides this quote in both Greek and Latin. It translates to: "Manetho the Egyptian translated the entire Egyptian history into the Greek tongue at great length, and specifically those things which relate to their theology, both in the sacred book which he wrote and in his other treatises."</note> Moreover, **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note> mentions the *Physiological Works* of Manetho; a work which, unless it was perhaps the beginning or a preface to his history, would most closely correspond to our purpose.

<margin>In the Preface to *On Abstinence*, Book 2, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 4, chapter 15.</margin> In addition to this, **Diogenes Laertius** cites Manetho’s *Epitome of Natural Philosophy*, and **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> cites his *On Antiquity and Piety*. Whether these were separate individual works, and whether they were all by the same Manetho of Sebennytus <note>A famous Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE</note>, I do not dispute, as it does not concern our immediate interest; however, it is clear they were of such a nature that they could have shed no little light on this subject.

**Sanchoniathon** <note>A Phoenician author believed to have lived before the Trojan War</note> wrote, according to Suidas, *On the Physiology of Hermes* and also an *Egyptian Theology*. **Asclepiades** also, according to the same author, being <margin>Under the word "Egyptian".</margin> highly practiced in those sacred matters, wrote *Hymns to the Gods of the Egyptians* and a *Commentary on the Agreement of All Religions*. He furthermore wrote a *History of the Egyptians*, containing the deeds of the **Ogygians** <note><term>Ogygian</term>: A term referring to the most ancient, primordial, or prehistoric times</note> dating back at least thirty thousand years. Thus he wrote. **Petosiris**, whom Juvenal mentions, and Pliny more than once, is said to have written *Astrological Works* and certain things about the Egyptian mysteries drawn from the Sacred Books.

To these names others could be added who wrote on Egyptian philosophy; but why should I linger over enumerating these authors one by one, since they have now perished, when many tens of thousands of books were lost in Egypt in a single stroke? I refer, of course, to the vast and most expertly furnished **Library of Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus expanded the Great Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE</note>. In this library were stored not only works of Egyptian literature but also, as it is reasonable to believe, all the surviving treasures of **Oriental** <note>In this 17th-century context, "Oriental" refers broadly to the ancient civilizations of the Near East, including Egypt, Chaldea, and Persia</note> learning.

## CHAPTER IX.

# On Greek Philosophy: and first on the Orphic.

<margin>Diogenes Laertius in his Preface.</margin>
Let these things suffice regarding *Barbaric Philosophy* <note>The author uses the term "Barbaric" in the classical sense to mean "non-Greek," referring to the ancient wisdom of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and others discussed in previous chapters</note>. Next follows the *Greek*, which was both later in time and derived from the former. This is admitted by nearly all the learned, and the facts speak for themselves. However, since some—either out of a love for the Greek nation or because they were less diligent investigators of antiquity—have called this into doubt, we must first provide proof of this fact. This will ensure that what we say later about this philosophy carries greater weight and clarity once its origin has been established.

<margin>Previous chapter.</margin>
We do not deny that many discoveries were made by the Greeks in the sciences, especially in **Mathematics**, which they cultivated brilliantly, as was mentioned above. In **Philosophical matters** as well, they made some observations and organized many things into a systematic form. In both respects, I would judge the Greek intellect to be far superior to that of the Romans. But just as they received the foundations of the mathematical disciplines from elsewhere, so too in Philosophy we assert that the Greeks received from the Barbarians <note>foreigners</note> not only the basics but also their greatest and most excellent doctrines. This is, or ought to be, the only point of contention. For regarding **Geometry**, **Astronomy**, and **Arithmetic**, we have the Greeks themselves as witnesses—or rather, confessing—that these sciences were first discovered and more or less cultivated by foreigners. This is attested by *Herodotus*, *Plato*,

Simplicius, Book 2 *On the Heavens*, page 123, quoting Porphyry: <note>original Greek: "ὑπ’ Ἀριστοτέλους..."</note> "...on the authority of Aristotle, whom one ought to follow and believe more than later writers, as they more accurately preserve the phenomena <note>astronomical observations</note>, since those earlier men neither perfectly preserved nor knew such phenomena; this was because the observations sent by Callisthenes from Babylon had not yet arrived in Greece—Aristotle having personally charged him with this task. Porphyry relates that these observations covered one thousand nine hundred and three years, and were preserved up to the times of Alexander the Macedonian." The same Simplicius had mentioned previously (Book 1 *On the Heavens*, p. 27) that the Egyptians possessed observations spanning two millennia, and the Babylonians even more: <note>original Greek: "καθότι ἐγὼ Αἰγυπτίους..."</note> "Just as I know that the Egyptians possess recorded observations of the stars for no fewer than two thousand years, and the Babylonians for even more."
</margin>

Aristotle, Diodorus, Strabo, Laertius, Achilles Tatius, and others agree on this point; hence, regarding those three disciplines <note>Geometry, Astronomy, and Arithmetic</note>, there was always a dispute for primacy among the three ancient nations: the Assyrians, the Egyptians, and the Phoenicians (to whom Lucian adds the Ethiopians regarding **Astronomy**). The Greeks did not even attempt to compete for the praise of discovery or original mastery. Therefore, Aristotle (*On the Heavens, Book 2, chapter 12*) supplements the Greeks' own deficiencies in observing the stars by drawing from the Egyptians and Babylonians. In the history of celestial knowledge, what record of observations, what watchtowers, or what astronomical instruments do the Greeks mention possessing in ancient times? In Babylon, in the **Temple of Jupiter Belus** <note>The Babylonian god Bel or Marduk</note> built by Queen Semiramis, there was an eightfold tower—or rather, eight towers built one upon the other—in which the astronomers used to contemplate the stars, as recorded by Diodorus. It was as if the **Giants** of old had piled mountains upon mountains to reach the heavens. Now, Semiramis flourished eight hundred years before the Trojan War, at a time when the Greeks did not yet possess the use of letters. Furthermore, after the capture of Babylon by Alexander, Callisthenes is said to have sent to Greece celestial observations spanning nineteen hundred and three years, which were preserved in the records of the Babylonians. If we calculate backward from the time of Alexander, these records rise far beyond the age of Semiramis; hence, it is highly probable that a great [part] of these observations were made by the **Chaldeans** <note>The priest-scientists of Babylon</note> in this very tower of Bel.

Finally, there is the famous, though immense, calculation of the Babylonians mentioned by Cicero in *On Divination, Book 1*; but since this surpasses all belief, it is not worth recording.
