Finally, as we descend closer to the Greeks and the era of the Greeks, Epigenes records seven hundred and twenty years of observations among the Babylonians; and those who recorded the least, Berosus and Critodemus, recorded four hundred and eighty years. <margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 7, chapter 56.</margin> These are the words of *Pliny: Epigenes teaches that among the Babylonians there were observations of the stars for 720 years inscribed on baked clay bricks <note>original Latin: "coctilibus laterculis," referring to cuneiform tablets</note>, being an author of the highest authority; those who say the least, Berosus and Critodemus, say 480 years.* <margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 7, chapter 3.</margin> If we take the age of Epigenes—who seems to have preceded Berosus and stayed among the Babylonians for the sake of his studies—to be around the time of Alexander the Great, the observations mentioned by him far exceed not only all those of the Greeks, but even those Babylonian records later collected by Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus of Nicaea (c. 190–120 BCE) was a Greek astronomer who utilized Babylonian data to develop his models</note>. And since Hipparchus and Ptolemy place the oldest of the Greek observations after the Babylonian ones—not only after the ancient ones we have reviewed, but even after the most recent and "lowest" ones, such as those from the era of Nabonassar <note>Nabonassar was a king of Babylon whose reign in 747 BCE became the starting point for astronomical calculations in the ancient world</note>—by that very fact they admit that the first authors and practitioners of this art were foreigners. Once the Greeks had received certain foundations and beginnings from them, they progressed further little by little, and explained more phenomena and the underlying reasons for those phenomena. For it has been correctly noted that the history of eclipses and other celestial observations came from the Barbarians <note>The term "Barbarians" here is used in the classical sense to mean non-Greeks, specifically the Babylonians and Egyptians</note>, while the causes, reasons, and calculations came from the Greeks.

But enough regarding Mathematical matters; since this is, as it were, to wander outside the main stakes of our inquiry. In the preceding sections, the argument was made for the Greeks against the Barbarians, just as here the argument was for the Barbarians against the Greeks. As the cause changed, we have fought in the camps of both; following the path of reason, rather than a partisan bias for one side.

Nor did he likely favor the rites and sacred ceremonies he observed; but since he was striving to entice <term>wild men</term> <note>original: *sylvestres*, referring to primitive people living in a state of nature, literally "men of the woods."</note> into society and to imbue them with some form of religion, it would have been foolish and useless to propose the pure worship of a pure <term>deity</term> <note>original: *numen*, a Latin term for divine power or a divinity.</note> to these—should I call them men, or merely living creatures? A pure doctrine of the deity and a pure form of worship do not touch the senses, nor do they stir the soul and the passions, for they are perceived by the mind and intellect alone. And since it would be difficult even for civilized and refined nations to adopt a religion of this kind, what progress could it have made among entirely barbarian men? The matter comes down to this: to put it briefly, Orpheus did not preach or institute the kind of deity or worship he *wanted*, but the kind he *could*.

Moses, however, did not struggle under such great difficulties. For besides the fact that he led a people who, though ignorant and dull, were nonetheless not unaccustomed to society and laws, he also possessed miracles and divine power. With these, he was able to strike terror into his people or bring them help from heaven. This power is the most effective of all for bending human minds and passions in any direction: when we are able to harm or help through divine means. But Orpheus, being destitute of this divine power, what weapons could he use to terrify the people, or what arts to draw them in? First, by **music**, in which he excelled, he called together and assembled these fierce men, disposing them to listen to his words. Then, once they were gathered and eager to hear, he fed them with fables and pleasant stories, into which he interspersed some truth. Afterward, when they began to marvel at and worship...

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...began their Orpheus, he dared to approach closer to the truth, to instruction, precepts, and the cultivation of morals, but always with some seasoning of **myths** <note>original: *fabularum*; stories used to convey moral or natural truths.</note>; "for the purpose of leading the people and commanding the masses," <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ δημαγωγεῖν καὶ στρατηγεῖν τὰ πλήθη</note> as **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian of the 1st century.</note> says concerning his own Homer. Then he began to mention the Gods and their lightning bolts, and urged that they be worshiped as the masters of all things; both so that they might turn away the evils to which mortal life is subject, and that they might send a joyful fortune from heaven to each person. Finally, he sang of the **Underworld** and the **Elysian Fields** <note>The mythological resting place for the virtuous.</note>, the abodes of the wicked and the blessed; so that when this life was extinguished, they might still have something to fear and something to hope for. In this way, and by these steps, he founded a kind of **Theology**, but one filled with myths; and he instituted a certain worship, but one quite superstitious. For Orpheus was no longer striving for the best things, but for the "least of the evils." And just as true religion is immeasurably superior to superstition, so superstition is as superior as possible to barbarism and the wildness of life and morals: Nor is there generally an ascent from this lowest step to the highest, except through that middle ground.

As for the myths, with which we do not deny that the Orphic doctrine was filled, their use has now faded away, and the naked truth is exposed to everyone; and it can scarcely be believed today how great the utility—or should I say necessity—of this kind of teaching once was. Uncultivated minds, accustomed only to the senses, like men recently led out of darkness or a prison, cannot bear the bright light of truth: But through myths, as if through a cloud, they delight to look. Neither toward the honor of morals and the discipline of life, nor toward religion and the worship of the Gods, does the unrefined and foolish common people allow themselves to be led directly, but they must be led through circuitous routes. Appropriately to this matter, and to prove Orpheus's institution, **Strabo**, speaking of the use of myths, says: "For it is not [possible to lead] a crowd..." <note>original Greek: Οὐ γὰρ ὄχλον τε. The sentence continues on the next page with the word "women."</note>

Indeed, the thunderbolt, the shield, the trident, the torches, the snakes, and the spears of the Gods tipped with the thyrsus are fables, as is the whole of ancient theology. For this reason, children begin to listen to and participate in stories more and more. The cause is that the myth is a kind of "new-telling," not describing things as they currently are, but other things besides these. Now, what is new is sweet, as is that which one did not know before; and this is precisely what makes one a lover of learning. When the marvelous and the monstrous are also present, it increases the pleasure, which is the very charm of learning. *And first...*

# Ancient Philosophy: or,

To begin with, it was not only poets who adopted these fables; much earlier, States and Lawgivers did the same. They did this for the sake of practical utility, considering the natural inclinations of man as a rational being. For man is by nature eager for knowledge, and a love of fables provides an entry point to that knowledge. It is from these that children first begin to listen and to enjoy conversation more and more. The reason for this is that a fable is a narration of new things—recounting not the usual and established order, but things different from them and fresh. Anything new and previously unknown is inherently pleasant, and this very quality makes people thirsty for knowledge. If wonders and portents are mixed into these fables, the pleasure increases; and pleasure, like a **love-potion**, generates a love for learning. Such was the opinion of the ancients regarding the use of fables. To this, if you like, add the sentiment of *Plutarch*: that philosophical truths are better absorbed when mixed with fables.

<margin>On Listening to the Poets</margin>
For it is clear to us that young people take more pleasure in, and are more obedient and manageable toward, those philosophical teachings that do not seem to be spoken in a strictly philosophical or serious manner. For they are seized by a certain divine inspiration and joy, not only when reading through Aesop’s fables and the plots of poets, but even when studying doctrines about the Soul that have been mixed with mythology. <note>The author provides both the original Greek from Plutarch's *De auditu poetis* and a Latin translation; both emphasize that "divine fury" or "inspiration" (enthousiasm) makes difficult philosophy palatable to the young.</note>

<margin>Roman Antiquities, Book 2, page 91.</margin>

Long after the age of Orpheus, the Evangelical Legislator <note>A reference to Jesus Christ, particularly his use of parables.</note> did not abstain from using pure and sacred parables. What we have already said should be understood as applying to Orpheus the Politician and Lawgiver. What he might have felt within himself, as a Philosopher, regarding divine matters—concerning God and nature—is a completely different question. It was once the custom for wise men to hold a double doctrine: the <term>popular</term> <note>original: "δημώδη" (demode) - intended for the general public.</note> and the <term>secret</term> <note>original: "ἀπόῤῥητον" (aporrhetan) - esoteric or restricted to initiates.</note>, or the *vulgar* and the *arcane*. They held one thing in their hearts and another for the people. We cannot doubt that Orpheus maintained this double method of teaching, since, despite what he preached or established in public, many points of a more recondite Theology and Philosophy are found within the Orphic doctrine. Furthermore, many testimonies and praises from the ancients regarding his skill and sharpness in the contemplation of things make us more certain of this.

I easily believe that nothing written by Orpheus himself survives today, as <margin>Book 1</margin> Origen noted long ago in his work *Against Celsus*. But those poems or other fragments praised by the ancients as *Orphic*—whether composed by Onomacritus, Cercops, or anyone else—are rightly judged to largely encompass the Orphic doctrine. Just as we do not doubt that the *Golden Verses* exhibit the theology and training of Pythagoras, even though nothing written by Pythagoras himself remains. In the same way, we retain the opinions and dogmas of Thales and other ancients whose writings have perished, as they were passed down by others.

### Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

We do not dwell much on what the poets relate concerning *Orpheus*; that he tamed wild beasts, that he drew forests and rocks after him, and other things of this kind. These stories testify that he excelled in the art of music, but, as for the rest, they are to be understood mythologically; just as *Horace* correctly explained. <note>In his "Art of Poetry," the Roman poet Horace argues that the myths of Orpheus taming lions actually represented him taming the savage hearts of primitive men through law and song.</note>

But what is handed down by the Philosophical Historians concerning *Orpheus* deserves the same credit as the rest of the accounts provided by those same authors. They relate that *Orpheus*, besides his admirable power in poetry and song and other successful inventions, established the foundations of civil life and Religion. Thus *Pausanias* writes in his *Description of Greece (Boeotia)*: <margin>p. 586.</margin> <note>original Greek: "πιστευομένῳ. ᾿Ορφεὺς εὑρεκέναι τελετὰς θεῶν, καὶ ἔργων ἀνοσίων καθαρμὺς, νόσων τὲ ἰάματα, καὶ τροπὰς μηνιμάτων θείων."</note>
> *Orpheus is believed to have discovered the initiations of the Gods, and the purifications for wicked deeds: likewise remedies for diseases, and ways to appease the wrath of the divine powers.*

<margin>p. 588.</margin> For this reason, he preferred his songs to those of *Homer*, because they savored more of religion. <note>original Greek: "Τιμῆς ἐκ τοῦ θείου, καὶ ἐς πλέον ἐκείνων ἔχουσι."</note> *They possess more honor from the divine, and have more of it than those others.* Certainly, *Orpheus* was the first to sow the seeds of religion among the *Greeks* and neighboring peoples, and he commanded sacred worship. This is attested by both the *Philosophers* and the *Greek Historians*: and some note that the memory of this very thing remains in the word <term>threskeia</term> <note>The Greek word for "religion" or "worship."</note>.

<margin>On the word "Threskeuein" <note>To practice religious ritual.</note></margin> Thus *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist.</note> says: <note>original Greek: "λέγεταὶ γὰρ ὡς ᾿Ορφεὺς Θρὰξ πρῶτος ἐτεχνολόγησε τὰ ῾Ελλήνων μυστήρια, καὶ τὸ τιμᾶν θεὸν, θρησκεύειν ἐκάλησεν· ὡς Θρᾳκίας οὔσης τῆς εὑρέσεως."</note>
> *For it is said that Orpheus the Thracian first systematically taught the mysteries of the Greeks, and called the honoring of God "threskeuein," as if the invention were Thracian in origin.*

Finally, he seems to have been the first in *Greece* to open the way to a future life, and the happiness therein for those who worship the Gods and virtue: since he promised <note>original Greek: "μετὰ τὴν τοῦ βίου τελευτὴν, εὐδαιμονίαν"</note> *happiness after the end of life* to those observing his precepts. This most sacred secret even that divine man, *Moses*, hardly dared to disclose to his *Hebrews*. <term>Orpheotelestae</term> <note>original Greek: "᾿Ορφεωτελεσταὶ" — Priests or initiators who performed Orphic rites believed to cleanse the soul and ensure happiness in the afterlife.</note>

### Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...to approach. And if you compare the excerpts of Orpheus that are found in the writings of the **Church Fathers** <note>The influential Christian bishops and theologians of the first few centuries AD, such as Clement of Alexandria or Eusebius.</note>, adding those that are read here and there, or in collections among foreign authors, you will rightly marvel at how many and how excellent are the chapters of **Natural Theology** <term>Natural Theology: the study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on supernatural revelation.</term> organized and established by that **Thracian** <note>Orpheus was traditionally said to be from Thrace, a region in the Balkans.</note>, from an antiquity almost as old as that of Moses. He recognized one supreme Deity—and as some will have it, a Triune one. 

Yet I am not unaware that many superstitious and some impure things are charged against Orpheus by the Fathers. I freely agree with them regarding the superstitions. Indeed, it could not have been otherwise in the age and among the people with whom he lived. In every discipline, one must begin with the basics; and just as humans progress from childhood to manhood, so they move from superstition toward a pure and healthy religion. 

<margin>
*Plato, On Laws, Book 6, p. 782.*
*Aristophanes, The Frogs, Act 4, Scene 1.*

But Orpheus did not sprinkle the altars of the Gods with human sacrifices—which was the custom of many nations—nor with the blood of animals, as Plato testifies. Aristophanes also seems to refer to this with these words: *For Orpheus showed us the rites and taught us to abstain from killing.* <note>original Greek: Ὀρφεὺς μὲν γὰρ τελετὰς δ’ ἡμῖν κατέδειξε, φόνων τ’ ἀπέχεσθαι</note> In sacred matters, he taught us to spare the slaughter of cattle. Furthermore, those who led an **Orphic life** <term>Orphic life: a lifestyle characterized by asceticism, purification rituals, and a vegetarian diet.</term> abstained from animal meat at the common table. 

<margin>
*Life of Pythagoras, Chapter 28.*
*Ibid.*
</margin>
According to Iamblichus, Pythagoras received from Orpheus a similar way of living, of worshipping the Gods, and his entire system of theology. Furthermore, Orpheus did not imagine the Gods in human form, *but as having a nature and form similar to the Universe itself.* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ τῷ παντὶ τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὴν μορφὴν ὁμοίαν ἔχοντας</note> This was a sign of a great mind, elevated above the common crowd. 

Finally, it is well known that both Orpheus and his follower, Pythagoras, made use of a double teaching: the **common** and the **philosophical**. Therefore, their more sacred dogmas and inner meanings are not to be measured by popular talk or public practices.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

I do not subscribe to the opinion that Chaos was coeval <note>original: "coæva" — existing at the same time as the beginning of all things.</note> with the Universe. Among the ancients, or the subsequent authors who reported the doctrines of the ancients to us, the **Universe** <note>The "Rerum universitas," referring to the entire cosmos.</note> is often confused with the **sublunary world** <term>Sublunary world: The region of the cosmos below the moon, traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</term>. Consequently, what pertains to one of these two separately is often said of either, or both, indiscriminately. From **Ether** <note>The "Aether," or "fifth element," believed by ancients to be the pure, fiery substance that makes up the heavens.</note> was made the celestial and primary fabric of things; from **Chaos** came the sublunary world—that is, our **Earth** and others like it—and this occurred after intervals of many ages. However, these matters, which ought to be treated separately because of both their material and their timing, have often been forced into one by unskilled authors. But let us proceed to the dual arrangement of the heavens: the **wandering** <note>The planets, from the Greek "planētēs," meaning wanderers.</note> and the **fixed**.

The ancients believed the **Fixed Stars** were composed of ether or fire. **Empedocles** <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 494–434 BC).</note>, a disciple of the Pythagorean **Telauges** who followed Orphic and Pythagorean principles, explained the manner in which the Fixed Stars are forged from ether. <margin>Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, 4.13.</margin> He does so in these words found in **Plutarch**: *Empedocles held that the stars are fiery; they are made from the fiery element which the ether, containing it within itself, squeezed out during the first separation.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐμπεδοκλῆς πύρινα τὰ ἄστρα ἐκ τοῦ πυρώδους, ὅπερ ὁ αἰθὴρ ἐν ἑαυτῷ περιέχων, ἐξέθλιψε κατὰ τὴν πρώτην διάκρισιν." Original Latin: "Igneas eſſe ſtellas voluit Empedocles; ex igne factas, quem in ſe continens æther, in primâ ſecretione eliſerit."</note> Specifically, the Fixed Stars are forged from those fiery particles which the celestial or ethereal matter, driven by a circular motion, presses down and thrusts toward the center of a sphere. And when a huge mass of this ether or fire has been collected in the center of any sphere, it remains there immobile, emitting rays in every direction, and takes on the power, form, and all the properties of a **Fixed Star**.

Furthermore, **Orpheus** established that any given star is a world suspended in the infinite ether. The **Pythagoreans** asserted the same. <margin>Ibid.</margin> *That each of the stars is a world; these doctrines are found in the Orphic writings, for they make a world out of each star.* <note>original Greek: "Ἕκαστον τῶν ἀστέρων κόσμον ὑπάρχειν· ταῦτα δὲ τὰ δόγματα ἐν τοῖς Ὀρφικοῖς φέρεται· κοσμοποιοῦσι γὰρ ἕκαστον τῶν ἀστέρων."</note> As reported by—

# The Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things
### Page 135

Did this doctrine have no author, no origin? Neither divine nor human? It was older than Pythagoras: for he followed and refined it, as the Pythagoreans themselves admit. Nor would there ever have been so many counterfeit writings under the name of Orpheus, unless there had once been a true Orpheus. For who would name a Centaur or a Chimera as the author of his work? By that, I mean an empty name or a fictitious thing. If the Sibyls <note>Prophetic women in the ancient world believed to possess divine knowledge</note> had never existed, nor Moses, nor Solomon, nor the Patriarchs, we would not have so many Apocryphal, Pseudonymous, and interpolated books with borrowed and false titles. ## Concerning the Greek Philosophers after Orpheus: and first, concerning the Ionians.

Let these things suffice regarding the most ancient philosophers of the Greeks, who were poets and mythologists <note>Those who communicated philosophical truths through myths and fables</note>. There follow the others, who wrote without fables, and for the most part without verse; and thus they alone are usually understood by most people under the name of *Philosophers*. Of this kind are *Thales* with his *Ionians*, *Pherecydes*, *Pythagoras*, *Xenophanes*, *Parmenides*, *Leucippus*, *Democritus*, *Empedocles*, *Plato*, and others; all the way to *Epicurus* and *Aristotle*, in whom philosophical antiquity ends—unless perhaps we find some of the ancient dogmas <note>Established beliefs or doctrines</note> among the *Stoics*. Many before Thales had discussed nature among the barbarian nations, and some among the Greeks—whom we have just now reviewed—but they wrote either mythologically, or they mixed their physiology <note>In the 17th-century context, "physiology" refers to the study of nature or physics, not just biological functions.</note> with Theology, as the ancients were accustomed to do; Thales, however, was the first to discuss nature in its pure and unadulterated state, without fables or theological commentaries. ### The Ancient Doctrine of the Origin of Things

Over this fluid matter, he set **Mind** as the leader and presiding authority. His opinion is well-known from the very beginning of the book he wrote: *All things were together in confusion, then Mind came and set them in order.* <note>original Greek: Πάντα χρήματα ἦν ὁμοῦ, εἶτα νοῦς ἐλθὼν αὐτὰ διεκόσμησε.</note> For this reason, he was called **Mind** (or *Nous*) by his contemporaries and by posterity. This title, in my judgment, is more honorable than those like *Africanus* or *Asiaticus* <note>These were honorary titles given to Roman generals, such as Scipio Africanus, for their conquests in those regions.</note>. Wherefore it was rightly said of him:

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 10, final chapter.</margin>

*This man was indeed the first to articulate the doctrine of principles; for he did not only declare the substance of all things, as those before him had done, but also the cause and author of motion itself.* <note>original Greek: οὗτος δὴ πρῶτος διήρθρωσε τὸν περὶ ἀρχῶν λόγον· οὐ γὰρ μόνον περὶ τῆς πάντων οὐσίας ἀπεφήνατο, ὡς οἱ πρὸ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τοῦ κινοῦντος αὐτὴν αἰτίου.</note> This insight—whether he received it from Linus <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology, often cited as a teacher of Hercules or a primal poet.</note>, as Laertius <margin>In the Proem [Introduction].</margin> claims, or from elsewhere—opens the way to a true **Cosmopoeia** <term>Cosmopoeia: The process of world-making or the creation of the universe.</term>; for without an efficient cause, matter is an inert and senseless thing.

But the manner and order in which this mass was arranged by the **creative word** <note>original Greek: ὁ λόγος δημιουργός (*ho logos demiourgos*)</note> was explained by Anaxagoras solely through the logic of gravity, in these words:

*Mind is the beginning of motion. Of bodies, those that are heavy occupy the lower place, such as the Earth; while those that are light occupy the upper place, such as Fire; whereas Water and Air occupy the middle.* <note>original Greek: Νοῦν μὲν ἀρχὴν κινήσεως. τῶν δὲ σωμάτων τὰ μὲν βαρέα, τὸν κάτω τόπον, ὡς τὴν γῆν· τὰ δὲ κοῦφα, τὸν ἄνω ἐπισχεῖν, ὡς τὸ πῦρ· ὕδωρ δὲ καὶ τὸν ἀέρα, τὸν μέσον.</note>

This is indeed correct; behold the four elements arranged according to their native places. But where shall we dwell? In what part or region of this world shall we and the living creatures reside? The Earth is the nucleus of this elementary globe, and yet it is entirely covered by the waters: by what method will you make it dry land? By what causes, or machines, or instruments? At this point, the Greek philosophers always "ran aground" <note>original Latin: *hæsit aqua*, a Latin idiom meaning to be at a loss or to reach a stalemate, literally "the water stopped." # Archaeologies of Philosophy: or,

...how they were able to extricate themselves; namely, to so arrange the elements, especially water, that the habitable Earth might remain. Moses here summoned a **God from a machine** <note>original: *Theum apo mēchanēs* (Θεὸν ἀπὸ μηχανῆς); a reference to the theatrical device "deus ex machina," where a deity is lowered onto the stage to resolve an impossible situation.</note> to scatter the waters; and rightly so, since he had to deal with the common people. But if we do not desert the camps of reason and philosophy, by what force or art shall we shake off this mass of waters? Neither Aristotle, nor Epicurus, nor any of the Greeks can untie this knot. They tried, indeed, by excavating the internal earth, or by imagining I know not what lagoons; but they did so without evidence and **unphilosophically** <note>original Greek: ἀφιλοσόφως.</note>. 

Indeed, Anaxagoras himself seems to have attempted the same thing, and with no more fitness: for it follows in Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, an ancient biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note>, *that because the earth was flat, the sea settled under it, the moisture being evaporated by the sun.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι διὰ τὸ τὴν γῆν πλατεῖαν οὖσαν, τὴν θάλασσαν ὑποστῆναι, διατμισθέντων ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τῶν ὑγρῶν.</note> What this means—*because the earth was flat*—is not easily apparent. Aldobrandinus <note>Thomas Aldobrandinus, a 16th-century translator and editor of Diogenes Laërtius.</note> rendered the sentence thus: *for so in the earth, which is wide, the sea subsides, the moisture being thinned by the sun.* But what does the width of the Earth contribute to the subsidence of the sea? If he had said that it was deep, or that it was hollow, he would have indicated some kind of cause. Therefore, I easily suspect there is an error in the word **flat** <note>original Greek: πλατείας (*plateias*).</note>, and it should be read as **deep** <note>original Greek: βαθείας (*batheias*).</note>: *that because the earth was deep, the sea settled under it.* 

I embrace this conjecture the more willingly because Anaxagoras’s disciple, Archelaus, seems to understand the matter in this way; for he says, *The sea consists of water filtered through the earth into the hollows.* <note>original Greek: Τὴν δὲ θάλασσαν ἐν τοῖς κοίλοις διὰ τῆς γῆς ἠθημένην συνεστάναι.</note> <margin>Aristotle, *Meteorology*, Book 2, chapter 7; Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 6, chapter 9.</margin> Nor can it be gathered that Anaxagoras felt otherwise from Aristotle and Seneca. But this is in passing.

Suppose that Anaxagoras wanted the sea or the Ocean to have settled in the depths and caverns of the earth. But what excavated the earth? Or that terrestrial nucleus, protected by so many layers and coverings of water, air, and fire? ...[subs-]ide <note>Continuing from the previous page: the heavier parts of the primordial fluid began to sink toward the center.</note> toward the middle, surrounded by all the other elements, who does not see that this central body would be whole and undivided, thick, full inside and out, and uniform? As we have shown more extensively elsewhere. Therefore, those who look for caverns, mountains, and the other inequalities of today's earth in this **subaqueous** and—so to speak—**uterine** Earth <note>The author uses "uterine" to describe the Earth in its developmental, "embryonic" state, encased in fluid like a womb.</note> search in vain. And all the Greeks fell into this error, and always labored over this part of the **Cosmogony** <note>original Latin: *Cosmopoeiæ*; the study or theory of the world’s creation.</note>; while, with awkward and futile intent, they desired to drain the waters into some unknown cavities, when the waters were not to be drained away, but rather covered over by a new world-orb, or vault; which is the unique mystery of the **cosmogony** <note>original Greek: *tēs kosmopoiïas* (τῆς κοσμοποιΐας).</note>. Silenus says that Anaxagoras stated the vault of heaven is made of stone, and is held together by the speed of its rotation so that it does not fall: but it will fall when the motion is slowed. This is a crude philosophy and unworthy of Anaxagoras, unless we suppose this to be a mutilated memory of the upper vault, surrounded by waters, and through the historian's ignorance and **lack of philosophy** <note>original Greek: *aphilosophian* (ἀφιλοσοφίαν); the author suggests the biographer Diogenes Laërtius did not understand the physics he was recording.</note>—which I believe is not infrequent in Laërtius—it was corrupted and transferred to the heavens. This is sufficiently proven in its proper place.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

The **primordial mud** <note>original Greek: ἰλὺς πρωτογενὴς (*ilys prōtogenēs*)</note> is mentioned by both the Egyptians and the Phoenicians in other words. And the words that follow—**that animals are born from the warmth of the earth, which sends up a mud similar to milk as a kind of nourishment** <note>original Greek: γεννᾶσθαι τὰ ζῶα ἐκ θερμῆς τῆς γῆς, καὶ ἰλὺν παραπλησίαν γάλακτι, οἷον τροφὴν, ἀνιείσης</note>—savor of Egyptian soil. Indeed, this entire **zoogony** <note>the theory of the origin of living things</note> corresponds well enough to the ancient "barbarian" philosophy; nor does it conflict with sacred truth, if we remember that Anaxagoras’s **Mind** <note>The *Nous*, or divine intellect</note> presided over and directed all these things.

To conclude these points regarding Archelaus, let us note here in passing an error in [Diogenes] Laërtius—as we did previously in the life of Anaxagoras—by which the meaning is clearly perverted. Archelaus derives all elements from moisture, doing so through thinning or thickening. Laërtius expresses this in these words: **"He says that the moisture, being melted by heat, insofar as it solidifies into a fiery nature, makes Earth; insofar as it flows around, it generates air."** <note>original Greek: Τηκόμενον, φησὶ, τὸ ὑγρὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ θερμοῦ, καθὸ μὲν εἰς τὸ πυρῶδες συνίσταται, ποιεῖν γῆν· Καθὸ δ’ περιρρεῖ, ἀέρα γεννᾶν.</note> Who does not see Archelaus's true meaning? Thickened moisture constitutes Earth; loosened and flowing moisture constitutes air. But Laërtius’s words, if rendered truly, sound like this: *He says that moisture, liquefied by heat, insofar as it grows together into a fiery nature, makes Earth, etc.* What kind of reasoning is this, I ask? Is there **concretion** <note>the process of becoming solid or dense</note> when water passes into fire, which is thinner? And would fire, once made, immediately constitute Earth? Therefore, instead of "fiery" <note>original Greek: πυρῶδες (*pyrodes*)</note> one must absolutely write **muddy** <note>original Greek: πηλῶδες (*pēlodes*); Burnet is correcting a likely typo in the historical manuscript where "fire" was written instead of "mud".</note>. In this way, all the points are clear and coherent.

<margin>
Aristotle, *Physics*, 
Book 8, Chapter 1.
</margin>
But to move forward: that one thing remains concerning the **MIND**, the ruler of all things and the principle of all motion; it remains, and shall remain forever, the glory and ornament of this philosophy. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...[In this physi]cs, first, that **Mind** <note>The *Nous*, or divine intellect</note> is the principle of all motion in matter; which of itself is inert and immobile. Second, that **Mind** is the author of all order in this motion; and therefore of the **arrangement** <note>original Greek: τ. διακοσμήσεως (*t. diakosmēseōs*)</note>, the beautiful and ornate composition of the world; which others, rashly, attributed either to fortuitous chance or to necessity. <margin>In the *Life of Pericles*.</margin> **"Over the whole of things first, he set as the beginning of the arrangement neither chance nor necessity, but Mind."** <note>original Greek: Τοῖς ὅλοις πρῶτον, οὐ τυχὴν οὐδ’ ἀνάγκην διακοσμήσεως ἀρχὴν, ἀλλὰ νοῦν ἐπέστησε.</note> So says **Plutarch** concerning **Anaxagoras**.

Therefore, in this argument, the Ionian philosophers distinguished themselves remarkably regarding the efficient and intellectual cause of the world; as for its material principle, they express it in various ways; but they all agree on this, that this prime matter consisted of minute particles, moved in various ways. **Thales** maintained this was fluid and called it **Water**; **Anaximenes** maintained it was volatile and named it **Air**; nor does it matter which they said, since they formed the remaining elements from one or the other. And some maintained these particles were similar, others dissimilar: and this in countless ways. These differences of opinion, which are recited variously by various authors, are of no importance: since in the course of philosophizing, once you have progressed a little, they return to the same point; different in name rather than in reality. Therefore, for the doctrine of this School regarding the origin of things, it will be sufficient to establish minute and mobile particles, first confused, and afterwards brought into order by the divine mind.

Furthermore, **Anaxagoras** arranged this fluid matter into **vortices** <note>circular or swirling motions of particles</note>, or he established that it was so arranged by the moving mind. <margin>P. 99.</margin> **Plato** teaches us this in the **Phaedo**, where **Socrates**, ignorant of and disdainful toward physical causes, ignorantly scoffs at the philosophical genius of **Anaxagoras**: and among other things, mentions with mockery the vortex placed by him around the Earth. This doctrine...

**Clement of Alexandria** mentions the views of **Anaxagoras** more explicitly, and with almost the same spirit, in these words: "For Anaxagoras was the first to set **Mind** <note>original Greek: τὸν νοῦν (*ton noun*)</note> over things; but even he did not preserve the dignity of the **efficient cause** <note>The 'maker' or active force in a system</note>, describing certain mindless **vortices** <note>original Greek: δίνας (*dinas*); whirling motions of matter</note>, along with the inactivity and folly of Mind." <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ καὶ Ἀναξαγόρας πρῶτος ἐπέστησε τὸν νοῦν τοῖς πράγμασιν· ἀλλ' οὐδὲ οὗτος ἐτήρησε τὴν ἀξίαν τὴν ποιητικὴν, δίνας τινὰς ἀνοήτους ἀναζωγραφῶν, σὺν τῇ τοῦ νοῦ ἀπραξίᾳ τε καὶ ἀνοίᾳ.</note> *For Anaxagoras was the first to add Mind to things: but neither did he preserve the dignity of the efficient cause, describing I know not what mindless Vortices, along with a cessation of the mind from acting, and as it were, a mindlessness.* He plays upon the words **Mind**, **Mindless**, and **Mindlessness** <note>original Greek: νοῦς (*nous*), ἀνόητος (*anoētos*), ἀνοίᾳ (*anoia*)</note>. Moreover, he attributes it as a fault to Anaxagoras that in the founding of the world, once the matter of things was arranged into vortices, he allowed the mind he had introduced to remain idle. Truly, this often happens <margin>See Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, p. 435.</margin> to the best of men—those similar to **Socrates** and **Clement**—that out of a love for divine causes, they neglect and look down upon lower and material causes. These, however, have their place, and should not be passed over in silence in an orderly explanation of things.

Finally, regarding the heavens and the celestial bodies, it is remarkable how much the **Ionians** <note>Philosophers from the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, known as the first "scientists"</note> progressed in their knowledge. They seem to have discovered that the <margin>Aristotle, *Meteorology*, 1.3. Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, 2.13. Diogenes Laertius.</margin> celestial regions consist of **ether**; that the **Planets** are opaque bodies, and the **Fixed Stars** are fiery, which is the pinnacle of celestial physics. Thus **Anaximander**: *"The moon is false-shining, and is illuminated by the sun."* <note>original Greek: Τὴν τε σελήνην ψευδοφαῆ, καὶ ἀπὸ ἡλίου φωτίζεσθαι.</note> And the same is said of **Anaximenes** <margin>* In his *Astronomy*.</margin> in the writings of **Theon**. **Anaxagoras** goes even further, asserting that *"The moon has dwellings, and even hills and ravines."* <note>original Greek: Τὴν σελήνην οἰκήσεις ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ λόφους καὶ φάραγγας.</note> *That the Moon is inhabited, and that there are also hills and valleys upon it.* For this reason, **Plato** in the *Apology of Socrates* addresses **Meletus** <note>The prosecutor of Socrates</note> thus: "Since he says the sun is a stone, and the moon is earth, do you think you are accusing Anaxagoras?" <margin>In the *Life of Nicias*, p. 538.</margin> Rightly, therefore, **Plutarch** says: *"For Anaxagoras was the first to set down in writing the clearest and most daring account of all concerning the moon's illumination and shadow."* <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ πρῶτος σαφέστατόν γε πάντων καὶ θαῤῥαλεώτατον περὶ σελήνης καταυγασμῶν καὶ σκιᾶς λόγον εἰς γραφὴν καταθέμενος Ἀναξαγόρας.</note> <margin>Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book 2, Ch. 28.</margin> Finally, he says the same in general regarding **Thales**: *"Thales and those..."*

Regarding the Fixed Stars and the Sun, the saying of **Anaxagoras** is well known—which almost cost him his life among the Athenians—that the Sun is a **red-hot mass** <note>original Greek: μύδρον διάπυρον (*mydron diapyron*); Anaxagoras was famously prosecuted for impiety for suggesting the sun was a physical object rather than a god</note>, an ignited and glowing mass; which indeed seems to indicate a burning matter, but one that is thick and solid. **Anaximander**, however, asserted that the sun is **purest fire** <note>original Greek: καθαρώτατον πῦρ (*katharōtaton pyr*)</note>, a liquid and most pure fire. Having observed these things, if what they established concerning the Moon were extended to the other Planets, and what they said of the Sun to the other Fixed Stars; and if we recall for ourselves the time in which these philosophers lived—the most ancient of the Greeks—we shall rejoice that the true **physiology of the heavens** <note>The physical laws and structure of the universe; what we now call cosmology</note>, which we have seen restored in recent centuries, was not unknown to the ancient sages. I will add finally, in praise of Anaxagoras, that not only the general doctrine of the heavens, but also the form of the old and the new moons, and the distinctions of their motions, were known to him—whether through an intuition of causes or through ancient tradition—as we have noted before.

</margin>

Since these things are so, you may ask, how could these Ionian philosophers have been ignorant of the motion of the Earth and the true system of the world? Nor does it seem to me that they were ignorant of it. For those who establish that the heavens are fluid, and that individual spheres are carried around in the manner of **vortices**, cannot prevent the bodies involved in these vortices from being turned along with them. And specifically regarding the Earth, **Anaxagoras** placed a vortex of this kind around it, **a vortex surrounding the earth** <note>original Greek: δίνην περιεχειν τῇ γῇ (*dinēn periechein tē gē*)</note>, as it is said in Plato. Therefore, the Earth could not help but rotate about its own axis. Then, as for the annual motion, **Anaximander** said (as reported by **Theon of Smyrna**), **that the earth is suspended on high, and moves around the center of the cosmos.** <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἔστιν ἡ γῆ μετέωρος, καὶ κινεῖται περὶ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου μέσον (*hoti estin hē gē meteōros, kai kineitai peri ta tou kosmou meson*)</note> That the Earth hangs in the heights, and is moved around the [center] of the world...

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

*...middle.* This is most easily understood regarding its motion around the Sun. These ideas indeed fit together aptly, both among themselves and with the opinion of **Pythagoras**, who held this **Thales** as the primary guide of his studies. But in collecting and interpreting the dogmas of the ancients, there will always be certain doubts and uncertainties.

So much for the Ionian philosophers; whose doctrine concerning the heavens and the universe of things you will perhaps marvel at for approaching so closely to today’s views. Or, you might accuse me of **philarchaism** <note>original Greek: φιλαρχαϊσμοῦ (*philarchaiismou*); an excessive love or preference for ancient things</note>, as if out of affection and zeal toward the ancients, I had too highly adorned their philosophy. I confess that I have, as much as I could, both in this and in other dissertations, favored the ancients: and from the many opinions which are circulated under their names, I have always chosen the one I deemed the best and closest to the truth above the rest. And this seems to be only fair: for since most of their works have been lost or corrupted by the vast length of time, if anything noble remains—like something rescued from a shipwreck—we ought to embrace it and be grateful. 

Furthermore, it must be noted that the **Pagan philosophers** <term>Philosophos Gentiles</term> often hid their true teachings for fear of the common people. This was especially true when dealing with celestial matters, lest, by speaking with too much liberty, they should seem to have offended the majesty of the Gods. Wherefore, since it was dangerous to speak too freely before the public about the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars, they took care that these subjects were discussed only sparingly, privately, and among friends. They did this so that their more secret thoughts would not creep out into the world to the ruin of themselves and their followers. 

**Plutarch** noted this best in the passage cited above <margin>In his *Life of Nicias*.</margin>, and confirmed it with examples. Let us hear, if you please, his own words. When he had said that **Anaxagoras** was the first to set forth in writing the doctrine of the illumination and shadowing of the Moon, he adds these words: **"nor was the account popular, but was still a secret, circulating among only a few, and proceeding with a certain caution or in confidence; for they did not endure..."** <note>original Greek: οὐδ᾽ ὁ λόγος ἔνδοξος ἦν, ἀλλ᾽ ἀπόρρητος ἔτι καὶ δι᾽ ὀλίγων, καὶ μετ᾽ εὐλαβείας τινὸς ἢ πίστεως βαδίζων· οὐ γὰρ ἠνεί- (*oud' ho logos endoxos ēn, all' aporrhētos eti kai di' oligōn, kai met' eulabeias tinos ē pisteōs badizōn; ou gar ēnei-*). The sentence concludes on the next page with the catchword "tolerating [natural philosophers]".</note>

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...they [the public] did not tolerate the so-called natural philosophers and "sky-talkers" <note>original Greek: μετεωρολέχας (*meteōrolechas*); a derogatory term for those who studied the heavens</note> at that time, as they reduced the divine to irrational causes, unseeing powers, and inevitable occurrences. *That doctrine was not celebrated or famous, but concealed and secret; it was handled with caution, or under a pledge of silence, among a few. For they [the public] would hardly tolerate the **Physicists** <term>Physicos</term>—those who philosophized about celestial matters—because they seemed to bind the divine power to irrational causes, blind forces, and involuntary effects.*

*Next, he [Plutarch] provides examples of this popular hatred toward Philosophers in these words:* "In fact, **Protagoras** went into exile, and **Pericles** only with great effort managed to free **Anaxagoras** after he had been thrown into chains. Even **Socrates**, although he had nothing in common with those specific studies, was nonetheless put to death under the name of Philosophy. But finally, the shining glory of **Plato**—owing as much to the man’s virtuous life as to the fact that he subordinated physical necessity to divine and more powerful causes—wiped away this slander and opened the path to these disciplines for everyone." <note>This passage is quoted from Plutarch's *Life of Nicias*, chapter 23</note>

The ancient common folk could not endure physical causes for heavenly things; nor can the common crowd of today—the learned as well as the unlearned—endure the idea of the **Sun’s stillness** and the **Earth’s motion**. In every age, as you see, truth breeds hatred; and it is an inconvenient thing to philosophize freely. Not without reason, therefore, did the ancient sages keep a **Secret Doctrine** <term>Doctrina arcana</term> to themselves: not only because it was beyond the grasp of the common people, but also because it went against their emotions and character. # Philosophical Archaeology: or,

...is not only through the injuries of time, but also through the fear and strategy of the writers, mutilated in a great part of itself: specifically in that more excellent part, the secret and less common part. And if there is anything true and right "among the surviving works" <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς σωζομένοις (*en tois sōzomenois*)</note>, if there is anything beautiful or exceptional in these remains, it will be fair to believe that it is the genuine offspring of the first *Author*: not birthed by the *Historian* or commentator, but preserved by them. But if anything should be otherwise, and foreign to reason, it is not ascribed to the original author with the same justification: since error and corruption can arise from many causes and in a thousand ways. Nor is it likely that he who played the role of the *Historian* discovered a more accurate doctrine concerning the nature of things than the *Philosophers* themselves. # CHAPTER XI.

## Concerning Pythagoras and the Pythagorean Sect.

Next follows **Pythagoras**, and the **Italian Philosophy** established by him in the sixth or seventh century before the birth of Christ. Since this philosopher either left behind no writings at all (as many believe) or nothing that survived for long, almost no scientific doctrines <note>original Latin: *dogmata physica*</note> of this Sect have reached our times. Pythagoras was preeminent among the traveling Greeks; none of them spent more time or underwent more labor and hardship in investigating the ancient wisdom among foreign nations. He undertook his journey to the **Egyptians** at the persuasion and advice of **Thales**, who predicted that he would turn out to be a truly great man if he studied under those teachers. Let us hear what **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 CE) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a significant biography of Pythagoras.</note> says on this matter:

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

<margin>Laertius on Pythagoras.</margin>
They say he was initiated into the sacred rites of both the Greeks and the foreigners. <note>original Latin: *Barbarorum*. In this context, "barbarian" refers to any non-Greek people, particularly the Egyptians and Persians from whom Pythagoras sought wisdom.</note> These, and many things of this kind, can be read in the works of *Laertius*, *Iamblichus*, *Porphyry*, and others. For many various stories are told about *Pythagoras*—scarcely more are told about any other philosopher. But of those things which one might most desire to know, very few are preserved. I mean his physical dogmas and the Pythagorean "physiology." <note>The term "physiology" here refers to the study of nature and the physical world, rather than the modern biological sense.</note> Pythagoras’s birth, homeland, travels, return, way of life, and even his method of teaching, the classes of his disciples, his discipline, and his institutes; finally, not a few deeds which he performed—wondrous things that are hard to believe—these and similar things are narrated at length. But of that supreme science for which he was once famous, and for which he is celebrated even now, they show us few specimens; at least in the realm of natural science.

One thing, I admit, they have retained: the foundation of natural science, the *Pythagorean System*, regarding the moving Earth and the Sun fixed in the center of our heavens. Furthermore, they held that the Moon is an <term>Antichthon</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίχθονα, meaning "Counter-Earth"</note>, or an Earth opposite to ours, and illuminated by the Sun. This doctrine, which we noted earlier in the Ionian school, shone forth more brightly later in the Pythagorean school; so that, regarding both the fixed stars and the wandering planets, both schools seem to have held the correct view.

<margin>Aristotle, *Meteorologica*, book 1, chapter 6.</margin>
Then, as for comets, we learn from *Aristotle* that both *Anaxagoras* and *Pythagoras* placed them outside our atmosphere, at the very least among the wandering stars. <note>That is, they recognized comets as celestial bodies rather than mere atmospheric disturbances.</note> Although otherwise, concerning the causes and nature of these phenomena, they perhaps erred.

<margin>Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book 2, chapter 13.</margin>
Finally, we previously stated based on *Plutarch* that the Pythagoreans established that the heavens are fluid and ethereal, and that they counted individual stars as so many worlds. And these things are roughly the extent of what we have regarding celestial matters.

As for the rest—the physiology of the Earth and the origin of the sublunary world—since *Pythagoras* was more inclined toward abstract and intellectual matters, he [adopted] the ancients' <term>cosmogo-</term> <note>The author likely refers to "cosmogony," the study of the origin of the universe.</note>

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

...[Pythagoras] seems to have turned the path into a certain <term>psychogonia</term> <note>original Greek: ψυχογονίαν, meaning "generation of the soul."</note>; at least if it is permitted to guess Pythagoras’s opinion from *Timaeus Locrus* and *Plato*. For those authors, when they are about to describe the origin of the world, occupy themselves mostly with explaining the composition of the **World Soul**; they do this through certain **Harmonic** ratios, composed of *indivisible* and *divisible* form, and of the **Same** and the **Other** <note>These are metaphysical terms from Plato's *Timaeus* used to describe the primary ingredients of reality.</note>: for so they love to speak. And regarding the structure of the corporeal world, they strive to arrange and adapt the boundaries, locations, and intervals of the elements based on certain congruencies of geometric bodies. These are <term>subtle trifles</term> <note>original Greek: Λεπτολογήματα (*Leptologemata*). The author views these complex mathematical abstractions as hair-splitting arguments that do not help explain the physical world.</note> which contribute nothing to natural science, nor are they founded upon it. However, it should be noted that these Pythagoreans assume a certain Chaos, or matter moved in a disordered way; and they place a Mind over it, so that it might be properly brought into a worldly order and form.

<margin>Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book 2, ch. 4.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book 1, ch. 11.</margin>
There is another Pythagorean writing by *Ocellus Lucanus*, who treated the universe and the origins of things much differently. For he established that the world is eternal, both in its form and its matter—and no less the human race. Therefore, unless we say that this man was a "Pseudo-Pythagorean," or that this little work is <term>falsely attributed</term> <note>original Greek: ψευδεπίγραφον (*pseudepigraphon*).</note>, then the Pythagorean doctrine concerning the origins of things is either non-existent or unsound. Moreover, you will find nothing in that writing of Ocellus which tastes of the Pythagorean spirit. Plato, a follower of the Pythagoreans, went in a different direction; finally, Plutarch testifies to something else: *Pythagoras and Plato say the world was generated by God: and, as far as its nature is concerned, it is corruptible.* <note>original Greek: Πυθαγόραν καὶ Πλάτωνα γενητὸν ὑπὸ θεοῦ τὸν κόσμον, καὶ φθαρτὸν μὲν ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει.</note> This is confirmed by Aristotle, when, about to relate the opinions of the ancients on the origin of the world, he says: *All indeed assert it to have been generated: some say it is eternal, others say it is corruptible.* <note>original Greek: Γενόμενον μὲν οὖν ἅπαντές εἶναί φασιν· οἱ μὲν ἀΐδιον, οἱ δὲ φθαρτόν.</note>

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...others, however, held that it would be perpetual, while some thought it would perish. Notwithstanding these disagreements, it must be admitted that both the Pythagoreans and the Platonists, as well as other ancient thinkers, leaned toward the opinion that: *The substance of things is eternal, while their forms and modes are fluid and unstable.*

However that may be, we do not deny that in these matters—and many others—the Pythagorean doctrine was passed down to or received by later generations in an uncertain and obscure way. I judge that this arose from several causes. First, there was no single "doctrine" of Pythagoras: one was *vulgar* <note>original: *vulgaris*, meaning the common or public version intended for a general audience.</note>, another was *arcane* <note>original: *arcana*, the secret or "hidden" teachings reserved for the inner circle.</note>, and yet another, as some say, was a *middle* path. Furthermore, there were various classes of disciples; the teachers trained each class according to their capacity and talent, not only in different subjects but even dealing with the same subject or argument in completely different ways.

For example, when the form and system of the world were to be treated, they instructed the lower classes in the common system, with the **Earth** placed at the center of the universe. Others, however, they instructed in the true and secret system, with the **Sun** placed in the center of the universe, or in the very heart of this great sphere. Likewise, if numbers were the subject, they taught the common use to some and the mystical use to others. And so it went for the rest of their studies: depending on whether their intention was to instruct <term>catechumens</term> <note>original: *Catechumenos*. While usually a Christian term for those being prepared for baptism, the author uses it here to describe philosophical beginners or "novices."</note>, so to speak, or the <term>adepts</term> <note>original: *adeptos*, those who have been initiated into the highest levels of secret knowledge.</note>. Thus, it is no wonder that differing or even contrary opinions emerged from the same school under the name of Pythagoras. 

Furthermore, since Pythagoras proposed the greatest part of his philosophy symbolically and "under wrappings" <note>original: *sub involucris*, a common Latin metaphor for allegorical or veiled speech.</note>, and wished it to be known only to his own followers (regarding the rest of humanity as no better than beasts), the knowledge became vulnerable to being forgotten or destroyed in two ways: both because the subject matter was obscure and because it was entrusted to only a few guardians. Hence, what sometimes happens to hidden treasures happened here: because he hid it too well, it remained concealed and was lost to posterity. To these factors, finally, is added the fact that many of the more ancient authors (whom we shall mention below)...

<header>The Archeology of Philosophy: or,</header>

...we have found) those who had written concerning the affairs and dogmas of the Pythagoreans have perished from our knowledge, swept away by the ravages of time or the injury of men.

It is agreed, however, among all who have treated this subject in any way, that Pythagoras made the greatest use of *numbers*, or numerical symbols, in handing down his philosophy. The ancients before Pythagoras wrapped their Theology or Philosophy in fables: for which reason, for the most part, the true doctrine perished over the course of time, overwhelmed by the mass of fables. Pythagoras, having rejected fables, substituted numbers. Yet not with a more fortunate outcome. For those shadows of things gradually vanished and escaped our senses. For who has ever emerged wiser from the Pythagorean numbers? Or learned from them a truth previously unknown to him? Certainly, those interpretations of Pythagorean numbers which I have happened to inspect thus far, whether among the ancients or moderns, display common information such as would be easy to learn elsewhere: or thin subtleties concerning the principles of things, without foundation and without fruit.

Among these mysteries of numbers, the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>original: *Tetractys*. A triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows (1, 2, 3, and 4), which the Pythagoreans considered a sacred symbol of the universal order.</note> always stood out: a torment for the intellects of many centuries. Furthermore, the <term>Septenary</term> <note>The number seven.</note> is not without renown; but the <term>Denary</term> <note>The number ten.</note> is said to be the most noble and fully perfect: because it contains within itself every number of diverse power and perfection. So be it: but it contains nothing within itself besides numbers; not Heaven, nor Earth, nor other things, however different they may be from numbers. Indeed, "everything," say some; but others more modestly say that all things do not lie hidden in numbers as if in their causes, but as if in so many <term>memory-boxes</term> <note>original: *capsulis memorialibus*. These are mnemonic devices used to trigger the recollection of specific philosophical principles.</note>, which may be used to call back to mind the main points of things, or the Pythagorean doctrine contained under those headings:

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

Hence they attach various titles, epithets, meanings, and orders of things to individual numbers, just as the Kabbalists do with their *Sephiroth* <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>, so that they may divide the subject of their studies into specific topics and classes. But if we interpret the Pythagorean numbers in this way, they signify only by convention, and not by their own inherent power and nature. Pythagoras, however, calls his <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A triangular figure of ten points</note> the "fountain of eternal nature" <note>original: *παγὰν ἀενάου φύσεως*</note>, the very source of things; and, by the consensus of all the ancients, Pythagoras established numbers as the principles, roots, and origins of things, as will be discussed below.

As for the <term>septenary</term> <note>the number seven</note> number, it is famous, especially among the Hebrews and Christians; and this is primarily, if I guess correctly, by reason of the **Sabbath** on every seventh day, and the **Sabbath-rest** to be celebrated in the seventh millennium. From this, as if from a fountain, many other symbolic sevens seem to me to have flowed in the writings of both Testaments. I had forgotten the <term>Ternary</term> <note>the number three</note>, the Platonic number, commemorative of the "three hypostases" <note>original: *τῆς τριῶν ὑποστάσεων*; the three fundamental substances or persons in Platonic and later Christian theology</note>. For the claim some make, that it is meant to designate "beginning, middle, and end," is cold and commonplace. But when some number has gained dignity from a sacred cause, people usually accumulate other secondary additions and interpretations of lesser importance, by the multitude of which the primary character is often overwhelmed. Finally follows the <term>Quaternary</term> <note>the number four</note>, the Pythagorean number; for by them especially, if not uniquely, this number is revered and consecrated. They once held this in such high regard under the name of the *Tetractys* that they treated it as a sacred oath; and by it, and its author <note>likely referring to Pythagoras himself</note>, they pledged their most holy faith to one another.

Among the ancients, I have consulted **Philo**, **Plutarch**, **Hierocles**, **Theon of Smyrna**, **Proclus**, **Nicomachus**, **Sextus Empiricus**, **Suidas**, **Martianus Capella**, **Macrobius**, and others: who either explained this subject with great effort or touched upon it in passing. Not a few among the moderns have also labored on this same argument; if I were to relate their conjectures individually, I would do too much. That theory which explains the Pythagorean Tetractys by the Jewish **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often transliterated as Yahweh or Jehovah</note> seems to excel. Yet this way of philosophizing lacks both foundation and order; for *Numbers* follow *Things* and the division of things. <page-num>159</page-num>
# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

They <note>Referring to numbers</note> could not bestow thought upon souls or minds, since they themselves lack both. It is manifest that numbers can generate nothing except numbers; they have no power or efficacy beyond that. They can indeed represent, in their own way, the degrees and kinds of things, but they cannot effect them; nor can they take the place of matter in the production of things. Come now, my Pythagorean friend: if you deny this, let us try for a moment. Make for me from your numbers—not a God, or a mind, as you are wont to boast—but some little body: a stone, for example, or if you prefer, mud. Gird yourself for the task. Which numbers do you have best suited for this purpose? Even or odd? Male or female? <note>In Pythagorean theory, odd numbers were considered limited and male, while even numbers were unlimited and female</note> According to your wit, take whichever you wish. But they are all sterile, believe me, and equally unfit for generating a stone. What if, changing your plan, you apply plane or solid numbers, or perhaps squares? <note>These are geometric classifications of numbers; for example, 4 is a "square" number, while "solid" numbers represent three-dimensional volumes</note> You will achieve nothing from this except certain imaginary figures; and from Nothing—whether square or cubic, plane or solid—nothing comes. Finally, if you join *units* together: if you take the *binary, ternary, quaternary*, and the rest, with their marvelous virtues—add, subtract, divide, compose; turn them in every direction, bring forth all their powers—they are still numbers, and nothing besides. Nothing stony emerges, much less anything human or divine. We have said these things in jest, but the matter comes down to this: *numbers bring forth nothing but numbers*; and they always produce things like themselves, in a way that is, as they say, *univocal* <note>original: "univoco"; a philosophical term meaning a cause that produces an effect of the same nature as itself</note>. Therefore, when Pythagoras composed all things from numbers, he could not have meant **Efficient** causes <note>The "maker" or source of change</note>, nor **Material** causes <note>The physical substance</note> (if I may say so without offending others), but in some way **Exemplary** causes <note>The ideal patterns or blueprints; the author argues Pythagoras used numbers as models rather than actual building blocks</note>; certain images of things arising from their own causes. For just as numbers proceed from unity, or the **monad** <note>original: "monade"; the fundamental "One" in Pythagorean thought, representing the source of all numbers and reality</note>, the simplest root of all, into

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...become more and more complex: and they take on new properties in that progression. Thus, the classes of created things recede step by step from God, the simplest Being, and retain characteristics that are in some way analogous to their numbers. It is certainly certain that the <note>original: μυστικωτάτους</note> most mystical of philosophers and theologians have labored greatly over this argument—namely, how to explain the origin and emanation of things from the First Being, and their progression through various orders from the highest to the lowest, if not by explicit reasoning, then at least through symbols and similarities.

<margin>Dissertation 29.</margin>
<margin>In Laërtius.</margin>
Yet we must not hide the fact that the Pythagorean and Platonic spirit suffered from this flaw: they resolved *physical* matters into *mathematical* ratios, numbers, and proportions; just as Aristotle later did with *logical* ratios. Both erred through excessive subtlety, attempting to catch <note>original: Divam Naturam</note> Divine Nature in the thin threads of a spider’s web, though she only allows herself to be bound by chains of iron or adamant—that is, by rigid reason and faithful observation. It is plain that these philosophers were more suited to, and more accustomed to, abstract contemplations rather than natural ones. Nor did the Pythagorean school have, as it seems to me, any stable <term>Physiology<note>In this context, "physiology" refers to the general study of nature or natural science, rather than the modern biological study of body functions.</note></term> common to the whole sect; instead, each man philosophized about the elements according to his own pleasure and in his own way. 

But if we recall to this class *Pherecydes*, the teacher of *Pythagoras*, and *Empedocles*, the semi-Pythagorean, we shall find among them the tracks of ancient natural science and the origins of things. *Pherecydes* wrote a *Theogony* <note>An account of the birth and origins of the gods</note> in the ancient and mythological style, as is clear from *Suidas* and *Maximus Tyrius*. And *Theopompus* says of him that <note>original: πρῶτον περὶ φύσεως καὶ θεῶν Ἕλλησι γράψαι</note> "he was the first to write for the Greeks concerning nature and the gods," a feat which many others attribute to *Thales*. Perhaps he was merely the first to write a *Theogony* in prose; the beginning of which writing *Laërtius* has preserved for us: "Zeus indeed..." <note>original: Ζεὺς μὲν</note>

As for Empedocles, we have called him a semi-Pythagorean: for although he was a student of Pythagoras, he imitated the <term>Physiology<note>In the 17th century, "physiology" referred to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world as a whole.</note></term> of the Ionians, who possessed a genius better suited to natural science. Let these things be said regarding the Pythagoreans, and briefly so, due to the lack of <term>physiologic<note>In this historical context, "physiology" refers to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world and its laws, rather than biological systems.</note></term> material in that sect, and also because of the lack of authors who have dealt with Pythagorean matters. As for **Pythagoras** himself, the debate still hangs as to whether he wrote anything at all. [Aristotle wrote on] the Pythagorean system and the Pythagoreans, according to the testimony of Diogenes Laërtius in his biography of the man; where he mentions one work *Concerning the Pythagoreans* <note>original: περὶ τῶν Πυθαγορείων</note>, and another *Against the Pythagoreans* <note>original: πρὸς τοὺς Πυθαγορείους</note>. Aristotle, however, was hardly fair toward the ancient philosophers: he usually reported their opinions and dogmas with the intent to burden them with envy and to refute them. Furthermore, Laërtius, in his histories of the philosophers, cites many others who treated Pythagorean matters: *Aristoxenus*, *Heraclides*, *Neanthes*, and *Hermippus*. *Syrianus* cites *Iamblichus’s* collection of Pythagorean Teachings. In addition to these, *Didymus* wrote on Pythagorean philosophy, as reported by *Clement of Alexandria*; and *Eudorus*, according to *Simplicius*. Likewise, *Moderatus of Gades* commented on the life and decrees of Pythagoras, as *Stephanus* testifies under the entry *Gadeira*, as does *Porphyry* in the works of *Eusebius*, and *Jerome* in his writing against *Ruffinus*. Finally, the Pythagorean symbols <note>These "symbols" were short, cryptic moral maxims used by the school.</note> were explained by *Alexander Polyhistor*, *Androcidus*, and others. I have reviewed these authors for this reason: so that you might wonder less why Pythagorean philosophy is so little known to us, since so many writers have perished from whose monuments it ought to have been drawn. Indeed, many more authors of the lower ranks <note>literally "of the minor benches," referring to less influential scholars</note> are now missing, upon whom I did not think it worth the effort to dwell. Let these things suffice regarding Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans.

# CHAPTER XII.

## On the Eleatic School: and on the Stoics.

**W**e have surveyed the Orphic, Ionic, and Pythagorean philosophies—the greatest lights of their times. Next follows the *Eleatic School*, established by *Xenophanes of Colophon* <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 570–475 BCE) who founded the Eleatic school in Italy; he is famous for his early critique of religious anthropomorphism</note>, during the era of the philosophers *Anaximander* and *Archelaus*; later, however, it received its name from his *Eleatic* disciples <note>Followers from the town of Elea, such as Parmenides and Zeno</note>. It appears to be composed of philosophers who differed among themselves in origin, customs, and doctrines: a *miscellaneous school*. Therefore, it cannot be presented under a single concept or a uniform sequence of principles. Consequently, it will suffice to indicate what one or another of those who were more prominent determined regarding the nature of things. Concerning the heavens and celestial bodies in the decrees of *Xenophanes*, I find only this worth noting: that he maintained the worlds were innumerable, and that there are infinite suns and moons <note>original: ἐξ ἀπείρων ἡλίων εἶναι καὶ σελήνας</note> in the immense sky, and infinite moons, not unlike our own. And he claims our moon is inhabited just like the Earth; for thus *Cicero* testifies (*Academic Questions*, book 4): he says *Xenophanes* claims people live *on the moon*, and that it is an *Earth of many cities and mountains*. These things are indeed not poorly said, but he maintained that these worlds were eternal and unchanging <note>original: καὶ ἀπαραλλάκτους</note>, and therefore without a beginning. Since he fell into this error, what he determined regarding the rest of nature matters little for our current purpose.

<meta>catchword: Part</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the Eleatic school of philosophy, focusing on its founder Xenophanes of Colophon and his remarkably modern belief in an infinite universe with multiple inhabited worlds and moons.</summary>
<keywords>Eleatic School, Xenophanes of Colophon, cosmology, plurality of worlds, inhabited moon, Cicero, eternal universe</keywords>

<page-num>166</page-num>
<header>Philosophical Archaeology: or,</header>

**Parmenides** <note>A Greek philosopher from Elea (c. 515 BCE) known for his poem "On Nature" which argues that reality is one and unchanging</note>, however, admitted a beginning or origin of things, and held that it arose from fire and earth as the primary elements. **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> adds that he believed *the origin of humans first came from the sun* <note>original: γένεσίν τε ἀνθρώπων, ἐξ ἡλίου πρῶτον γενέσθαι</note>; at least, that is how the text is commonly read. But what can this mean: *Humans are born from the Sun, as if from their own matter or element?* One should certainly read it as *from the slime* <note>original: ἐξ ἰλύος</note> instead of *from the sun* <note>original: ἐξ ἡλίου</note>, just as the Basel edition has it and as it is noted in the margin of the Roman edition. It is clear that **Aldobrandinus** <note>A 16th-century translator of Diogenes Laertius</note> read it no differently, since he translated the words this way: *and that the origin of humans first emerged from the mud.* This was indeed a common opinion among the ancients, and especially among the **Ionics** <note>Philosophers from the Ionian coast, like Thales and Anaximander, who sought natural explanations for the world</note>, from whom some say Parmenides heard the teachings of **Anaximander** and **Archelaus**. It seems to me that Parmenides held the exact same principles and views as Archelaus regarding the origin of things, both in their number and their nature—namely, *the cold* <note>original: τὸ ψυχρὸν</note> and *the heat* <note>original: τὸ θερμὸν</note>. This is easily seen by comparing the words of both. For Laertius says of Archelaus: *he said there were two causes of generation, heat and cold; and that living things were born from the slime* <note>original: ἔλεγε δὲ δύο αἰτίας εἶναι γενέσεως, θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρόν· καὶ τὰ ζῶα ἀπὸ τῆς ἰλύος γεννηθῆναι</note>, etc. Then regarding Parmenides: *that there are two elements, fire and earth; and that the origin of humans first came from the slime; and that these elements themselves consist of heat and cold, from which all things are composed* <note>original: δύο τε εἶναι στοιχεῖα πῦρ καὶ γῆν· γένεσίν τε ἀνθρώπων ἐξ ἰλύος πρῶτον γενέσθαι· αὐτὴν δὲ ὑπάρχειν τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρὸν, ἐξ ὧν τὰ πάντα συνιστάναι</note>. Finally, since many authors besides Laertius—such as **Aristotle**, **Plutarch**, **Sextus Empiricus**, and others—have recorded Parmenides and his dogmas, they would not have passed over that idea of the "Solar origin" of humans if it had been his, for it would have been highly *paradoxical* <note>original: παράδοξον; meaning strange or contrary to common belief</note> and more memorable than all the rest.

<margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, book 1, chapter 2.</margin>
The **Eleatics**, therefore, deviated very little from the **Ionics** regarding the origin of things—at least, if they established any origin of things at all; for that is not certain concerning all of them. And since some of them removed motion from the nature of things <note>The Eleatics, especially Parmenides and Zeno, famously argued that change and motion were illusions</note>, Aristotle does not admit these into the rank of natural philosophers, and rightly so; for without motion there would be no *generation or corruption* <note>term: generation or corruption; Aristotelian terms for the process of things coming into being and passing away</note>.

He also notes that Aristotle excluded certain Eleatics from the category of natural philosophers because they denied the existence of motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Eleatic school’s view of the universe. The previous page discussed Parmenides' theories on the elements and the origin of humanity from "slime." Here, the author examines the consequences of the Eleatic denial of motion and transitions into a discussion of the Atomists, Leucippus and Democritus.</meta>

<page-num>167</page-num>
### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

Indeed, all things would be the same; there would be no diversity of bodies, no structure, no order, nor anything else that could be called the *World*. Thus, it may seem strange what **Parmenides** <note>A philosopher from Elea who famously argued that change is an illusion and reality is a single, unchanging "One"</note>, **Melissus** <note>A student of Parmenides who defended the idea that the universe is infinite and motionless</note>, and others intended when they wished to remove motion from nature, or to claim it was merely *apparent* and not *real*. This aligns with the Pythagorean and Platonic mindset, which held sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses</note>—or the forms of sensible things—to be like phantoms or like nothingness, because they were fleeting, decaying, and unstable. Therefore, they fled toward abstract and immutable reasonings—such as *numbers*, *proportions*, or *Ideas*—as the true principles of things.

**Leucippus** and **Democritus** <note>The founders of Atomism, who proposed that the universe is composed of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms moving through a void</note>, celebrated and distinguished men who introduced the hypothesis of *Atoms*, are usually grouped with this **Eleatic sect** <note>A school of philosophy based in Elea, Italy; while the author groups them here, the Atomists actually broke away from Eleatic thought by affirming the existence of the void and motion</note>. Although this hypothesis is, in my opinion, false and poorly founded, it nonetheless provided the opportunity for philosophizing more strictly and accurately. For these men do not seek the principles of bodies or the forces of action among *numbers*, *proportions*, *harmonies*, *ideas*, *qualities*, or elementary *forms*, as others have done. Instead, they approach the bodies themselves and examine their physical and mechanical conditions: motion, shape, the position of parts, thinness or magnitude, and the like. From these, they estimate the virtues of each, define their actions, and explain their effects—rightly and solidly so, it seems to me, up to this point. 

However, their claims that these tiny particles are indivisible, or possess an innate impulse, or have inclinations toward certain places, or finally, that they are separated by empty spaces—these and similar claims are not only asserted without proof <note>original: "gratis dicta," meaning statements made without evidence</note> but even contradict clear reason. Nevertheless, since they opened the way to a sounder method of discussing physical matters, and in this regard have served the **Republic of Letters** <note>The long-standing community of intellectuals and scholars across the world</note> well, let us not cheat them of their due praise.

<meta>catchword: He recognized [Agnovit]</meta>

<summary>The author critiques the Eleatic denial of physical motion as an absurdity that would make the world non-existent, while praising the Atomists (Leucippus and Democritus) for shifting philosophy toward a mechanical and physical examination of matter, even if their specific theories on indivisible atoms and the void are flawed.</summary>
