<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Atomist school, moving from the general principles mentioned on the previous page to the specific cosmological theories of Leucippus and the education of his successor, Democritus.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>Philosophical Antiquities: or,</header>

**Leucippus** acknowledged the motion of the Earth around its own axis; and in the first origin and formation of the Earth, when the fluid mass settled into a spherical body, he said this globe was surrounded by a certain membrane, containing everything else: and this was at first wet and slimy, but later hardened. This primitive membrane of Leucippus can easily be interpreted as the first crust of the Earth, which was then still soft and tender: which, like a membrane, surrounded the **Abyss** <note>The great deep of waters beneath the Earth's surface</note> and enclosed everything else; and this same crust, increased on the outside and dried out, gave way to the first habitable world—consistent with those things which we explained about the birth of the Earth in our *Theory* <note>The author refers to his own work, *The Sacred Theory of the Earth*, where he argues the early Earth was a smooth crust over a watery abyss</note>. However, when philosophical matters are recounted by men who are not very philosophical—as **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A 3rd-century biographer of philosophers whose accounts are often seen as anecdotal rather than rigorous</note> seems to me to have been—it is no wonder if some things are recounted in a mutilated or confused manner, and the actual opinion of the philosopher is often lost. Thus, what is reported by Laertius regarding this **Leucippean Cosmogony** <note>original: "Cosmogoniâ Leucippeâ"; Leucippus's account of how the universe was born</note> seems to me neither consistent nor coherent, unless we explain individual parts very loosely. Often, too, the sense is corrupted because of the errors with which this book abounds. Beyond this, it should only be noted about Leucippus that he recorded that the position of the Earth had been changed: which we learn from **Plutarch** <note>A Greek historian and philosopher</note> as well as Laertius. Nor would this be difficult for him to conceive, since he acknowledged the Earth to be hanging and rotated around its own axis.

**Democritus** studied under Leucippus and followed him in Physics. One may conjecture that this great man progressed greatly in the study of the sciences, both from his own books and from the travels he undertook to almost all nations famous for wisdom. For besides the fact that from childhood he is said to have been instructed and trained in the science of divine matters and in **stellar knowledge** <note>original: "cognitione syderali"; astronomy and the study of the stars</note> by certain **Magi** <note>Zoroastrian priests and scholars from Persia</note> whom **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece</note> had left at his father's house; he was afterwards involved with priests—

...[by the] divine [force], of the Mind or the Word <note>original: *logos*</note>, it could be moved, agitated, and led into all forms. These things were indeed most correctly held by the Stoics, and according to the ancient Ionian doctrine, to say nothing greater. But in explaining this matter, and in the building of the world, they distinguish between *Elements* and *Principles*; and they consider the latter to be uncreated and incorporeal. *They say that principles <note>Greek: archai</note> and elements <note>Greek: stoicheia</note> differ; for the former are unbegotten and indestructible, but the elements are destroyed during the great conflagration <note>Greek: ekpyrosis, the Stoic belief in the periodic destruction of the universe by fire</note>.* As *Laertius* says in his life of *Zeno*: *They say that Principles and Elements differ from each other; for the former have never arisen and will never perish, while the Elements will perish in the burning of the World.* Then he adds another difference, <margin>With the word "shapeless" <note>Greek: amorphos</note></margin> *Furthermore, the principles are incorporeal*—for so I read according to Suidas—*and shapeless, whereas the elements are shaped.*

What the Stoics understood by these "beginnings" <note>Greek: archai</note>, these *initiates* or *principles*, is not easy to define. Others besides the Stoics indeed distinguished *Elements* and *principles*, but only by reason of simplicity; Plutarch noted this against *Thales*, <margin>On the Opinions of the Philosophers, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin> as he could have added regarding the Platonists, Aristotelians, and also the Epicureans: *Those around Aristotle and Plato think that the principle and the elements differ. But Thales the Milesian considers the principle and elements to be the same. Yet they differ greatly from one another; for the elements are composite, but we say that the principles are neither composite nor resulting effects.* *The principles are neither composite, like the elements, nor completely formed effects.* But the Stoics wanted them to differ not in form or degree, but in their whole kind, since they called these *principles* incorporeal and immortal, as if they had understood them as *Numbers* or *proportions*, like the Pythagoreans; or *Ideas*, or seminal reasons <note>Greek: logoi spermatikoi; the Stoic concept of generative principles that "seed" the development of the universe</note>. For the Stoics did not believe any substance to be entirely incorporeal; which [we will] demonstrate-

# Archæologiæ Philosophicæ: or,

<margin>Justus Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology*, Book 2, chapter 45.</margin>...as Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a famous scholar who sought to revive Stoic philosophy.</note> has shown: But they used those terms "bodies" <note>Greek: somata</note> and "incorporeal" <note>Greek: asomaton</note> at times too indistinctly.

Therefore, if those Pythagorean or Platonic principles do not please us, and we interpret the aforementioned terms more loosely, it would not be improbable to say that the Stoics called "incorporeal" <note>Greek: asomaton</note> matter <note>Greek: hyle</note> itself—naked and simple, shapeless <note>Greek: amorphon</note> and without quality <note>Greek: apoion</note>—insofar as it is opposed to the elements and completed bodies; nor that they understood anything else by the "principles" <note>Greek: tas archas</note>. This certainly corresponds to those things which Diogenes Laertius later presents from Zeno and Chrysippus, where he distinguishes between matter <note>Greek: hylen</note> and body <note>Greek: soma</note>, and makes the former identical to substance <note>Greek: ousia</note> and the foundation of all things: *They say that the primary matter is the substance of all things that exist; and matter is that from which anything whatever is produced. It is called by two names: substance and matter. But according to them, body is substance that is finite and delimited.* <note>original: οὐσίαν δέ φασι τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων τὴν πρώτην ὕλην· ὕλη δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐξ ἧς ὁτιδηποτοῦν γίνεται· καλεῖται δὲ διχῶς, οὐσία τε καὶ ὕλη· σῶμα δ᾽ ἐστὶ κατ᾽ αὐτὰς ἡ οὐσία, καὶ πεπερασμένη.</note> *Body, according to them, is a defined and bounded substance:* such as prime matter is not, and for that reason it is called "incorporeal" <note>Greek: asomatos</note>.

Finally, I am not surprised that they called these principles <note>Greek: archas</note> and this matter <note>Greek: hylen</note> "unbegotten and indestructible" <note>Greek: agennetous kai aphthartous</note>. For it must be admitted that many of the ancients established that simple, formless, and unmoved Matter existed from eternity and would exist for eternity. But they say the World had a beginning and is corruptible; or, as others distinguish, they say the *unformed* world is eternal, but the *formed* world is not eternal in any respect. 

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 15, chapter 15.</margin>Thus Didymus, in the writings of Eusebius, distinguishes this twofold world and marks it with these words: *[The world is] that which is qualified by the whole of substance, and that which possesses such an arrangement and order; wherefore, according to the former definition, they say the world is eternal; but according to its arrangement, it is created and changeable.* <note>original: Τὸ ἐκ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας ποιὸν, καὶ τὸ τὴν διακόσμησιν τὴν τοιαύτην καὶ διάταξιν ἔχον, διὸ κατὰ μὲν τὴν προτέραν ἀπόδοσιν, ἀΐδιον τὸν κόσμον εἶναί φασι· κατὰ δὲ τὴν διακόσμησιν, γεννητὸν καὶ μεταβλητόν.</note> Where the word "qualified" <note>Greek: poion</note> appears, it seems it should be read as "without quality" <note>Greek: apoion</note>, for matter is "without quality," or a substance without quality which is eternal. The words are thus rendered: The World is either the *simple mass of all things, or [made] from all substance...*

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...a mass devoid of qualities, or that which already possesses such adornment and order; therefore, in the former sense, they call the world eternal; in the latter, born and changeable. From a Mind, of course, coming upon the eternal mass and instilling motion, that simple mass was led into the various forms of things. The <term>Ionics</term> <note>Early Greek philosophers from Ionia, such as Thales and Anaximander, who sought the first "principle" of nature.</note>, <term>Pythagoreans</term>, <term>Platonists</term>, and <term>Stoics</term> seem to me to have held this opinion; as did all others who did not establish something worse and more alien to reason, such as the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world formed by the random collision of atoms.</note> and <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for teaching while walking in the Lyceum.</note>. For the idea that matter, produced from nothing, first existed only when the Earth was founded—namely, a few millennia ago—seems to be a dogma completely unknown and inconceivable to the ancient peoples and philosophers.

But let us return to the Stoics.

Given these principles of things, whatever they may be, they suppose that fire was made first from bodies, and from fire the other Elements, just as from the elements all kinds of mixed bodies arise. <term>Diogenes Laertius</term> <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers; his work is a primary source for Stoic thought.</note> reported this from <term>Zeno</term> and <term>Chrysippus</term> and others as follows: *The world comes into being when the substance is turned from fire through air into moisture; then its thick part, having condensed, is completed as earth; but the subtle part is turned into air, and this, being further thinned, gives birth to fire; then by mixing from these, plants, animals, and the other kinds arise.* <note>original: "γίνεσθαι δὲ τὸν κόσμον, ὅταν ἐκ πυρὸς ἡ οὐσία τραπῇ δι᾿ ἀέρος εἰς ὑγρότητα, εἶτα τὸ παχυμερὲς αὐτοῦ συστὰν ἀποτελεσθῇ γῆ· τὸ δὲ λεπτομερὲς ἐξαερωθῇ, ϗ τοῦτ᾿ ἐπιπλέον λεπτυνθὲν πῦρ ἀπογεννήσῃ· εἶτα κατὰ μίξιν ἐκ τούτων, φυτά τε, ϗ ζῶα, ϗ τὰ ἄλλα γένη."</note> They begin from fire and return to the same. But since the Elements arrange themselves and take their places according to the order of weight, with some higher than others, Water should therefore occupy and surround the whole Earth, just as Air surrounds the water. How then did the Earth emerge and come out above the waters? How was the ground laid bare and yielded into a habitable globe? This is the labor, this is the task <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*: "Hic labor, hoc opus est," suggesting a great difficulty.</note>. Since Stoic Cosmology does not reach that far, we leave it behind in this part as imperfect, or not sufficiently explained by the authors who survive.

<header>Philosophical Archaeologies: or,</header>

<meta>catchword: furthermore</meta>

What the Stoics felt regarding the heavens, we have already stated in a scattered fashion in the preceding pages. <term>Diogenes Laertius</term> <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers whose work is a vital source for Stoic thought.</note> noted that, according to the opinion of <term>Zeno</term> <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note>, the Sun is a "pure fire" <note>original: "πῦρ εἰλικρινὲς"</note>; the Moon is "more earth-like" <note>original: "γεωδεστέραν"</note>; and the other stars are "fiery" <note>original: "πυρινά"</note>. Furthermore, it is said in the same place regarding the motions of the Stars, "that the fixed stars revolve with the whole heaven, while the wandering ones <gloss>the planets</gloss> move by their own individual motions" <note>original: "τὰ μὲν ἀπλανῆ συμπεριφέρεσθαι τῷ ὅλῳ οὐρανῷ, τὰ δὲ πλανώμενα κατ' ἰδίας κινεῖσθαι κινήσεις"</note>. That is, the non-wandering stars revolve together with the whole heaven, while the wandering ones are indeed moved by their own specific motions. These things are not entirely true, but they are closer to the truth than the views of the <term>Aristotelians</term> and <term>Ptolemaics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle and Ptolemy, who believed in a complex system of rigid celestial spheres with the Earth at the center.</note>. Finally, concerning the Fixed Stars, they rightly established this: Not all are on the same surface, but some are higher than others.

<margin>Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues*, chapter on the nature of stars, etc.</margin>

This is how I understand the words of <term>Stobaeus</term> <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors.</note>: "Xenocrates thinks the stars lie upon a single surface; but the other Stoics think some are before others in height and depth" <note>original: "Ξενοκράτης κατὰ μιᾶς ἐπιφανείας οἴεται κεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀστέρας· οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι Στωϊκοὶ πρὸ τῶν ἑτέρων ἑτέρους ἐν ὕψει καὶ βάθει."</note>.

Finally, regarding the Worldly periods and the <term>Fate</term> of the Stoics, these things are better known than they deserve to be explained with repeated talk. Concerning those periods, see, if you like, my *Theory of the Earth*, Book 4, Chapter 5. And as for Stoic fate, it is nothing other than the immobile and immutable order of all things. Or, to express the same thing in more words, it is the necessary alternation of the created and uncreated world: together with the order of all things in the created world, both intellectual and corporeal: through all ages, all revolutions, forms, and appearances, until a return is made to the state of the Uncreated World. This is, according to them, until all things are dissolved back into God. For they begin the world from their <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The Stoics often used the name of the king of the gods to represent the Divine Reason or the primal fire that animates the universe.</note>, and into the same, once the cycle of Time is completed, they pour all things back.

<margin>Discourse 1, page 7.</margin>

The saying of <term>Perictione</term> <note>A name attributed to a female Pythagorean philosopher, though the identity of the author remains a historical mystery.</note> seems not to wander from this opinion, spoken concerning perfected wisdom, as found in Stobaeus: "Whoever is able to resolve all kinds of things into one and the same principle, and again from this to compose and enumerate them..." <note>original: "ὅστις ὦν ἀναλῦσαι οἷος ἐντὶ πάντα γένη ὑπὸ μίαν καὶ τὰν αὐτὰν ἀρχὰν, καὶ πάλιν ἐκ ταύτας συνθῆναι καὶ ἀριθμήσασθαι,"</note>

<header>Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.</header>

->This man seems both the wisest and the truest; and moreover, to have discovered a fine vantage point, from which he will be able to look down upon God and all things in their sequence and order, as they have been assigned to Him.<- <note>original Greek: "οὗτος δοκεῖ καὶ σοφώτατος εἶναι... τὰ ἐκείνῳ κατακεχωρισμένα."</note> *Whoever, therefore, is able to resolve all classes of things to one and the same principle, and again from that principle to compose and enumerate individual things—this man appears both most wise and most possessed of the truth. Indeed, he has found a beautiful watchtower from which he will be able to contemplate both God and all other things, separated from Him in their series and order. But enough of these matters.* <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the preceding Greek passage, emphasizing that true wisdom lies in seeing the unity between the Creator and the structured diversity of the universe.</note>

The **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that the universe is governed by divine reason (Logos) and that virtue is the only good.</note> wrote a vast number of books, all of which have now perished. **Laertius** <note>Diogenes Laertius, the 3rd-century biographer of philosophers.</note> enumerates the volumes of **Zeno**, **Sphaerus**, and **Chrysippus**, and the "most excellent books" <note>original: "κάλλιστα βιβλία"</note> of **Cleanthes**, as he calls them. Among these were treatises titled: *On Zeno’s Physiology*; *On the Gods*; *On things coming into being*; and *Archaeology* <note>original: "Περὶ τῆς τοῦ Ζήνωνος φυσιολογίας· περὶ θεῶν· περὶ γιγνόντων· Ἀρχαιολογία." In this context, "Physiology" refers to the study of the physical nature of the universe, and "Archaeology" refers to the study of origins or ancient history.</note>. If these were still extant, there would be hope of extracting more certain and excellent knowledge regarding **Stoic physiology** and the **Origins of things**.

Furthermore, **Laertius** cites the books of **Posidonius**, **Archedemus**, **Boethus**, **Antipater**, **Apollodorus**, and other **Stoics**, whom it would be too tedious for me to list here. Instead of all these, I wish that at least **Apollonius of Tyre** were publicly available; he wrote a history of the Stoic sect before the birth of **Christ**, <margin>Book 16.</margin> as **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> testifies (in addition to **Laertius**) in a book titled *A Table of the Philosophers from Zeno and of their Books* <note>original: "πίναξ τῶν ἀπὸ Ζήνωνος φιλοσόφων καὶ τῶν βιβλίων"</note>. It is said that this manuscript lies hidden and unpublished in certain libraries. Since this sect was so numerous and prolific in its writing, lasted longer than the others, and was held in such high esteem among the Roman people, it is truly astonishing that all its **Greek** records concerning **Physics** have disappeared. So much for the **Stoics**.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *On the Platonists, Aristotelians, and Epicureans.*

The Platonists, Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, named for the *peripatos* or covered walkways in the Lyceum where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note>, and Epicureans remain; regarding whom I shall say only a few things in summary: since it is well enough known what each of these posits on almost any matter. We have said before that the Platonists and Pythagoreans practiced physiology <note>In this 17th-century context, "physiology" refers to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world, rather than the modern biological sense.</note> with little success; it is as if they were born under a different star, being better suited to contemplating the rational principles of things abstracted from matter than the physical things themselves and their corporal properties. We have a manifest example of this in Plato’s *Timaeus* <note>Plato's famous dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and the creation of the universe.</note> regarding the origin of the world, where he assigns geometric shapes to the individual elements, and composes and arranges them according to geometry. But let us look, if you please, at the manner in which he philosophizes.

First, he demonstrates the number and arrangement of the Elements in this way: Since it is necessary for the world to be visible and tangible, and nothing is visible without fire, and nothing tangible without Earth (a solid body), these two elements were necessary above all. But so that the world might hold together and be a single entity, it was necessary that these two extremes be joined through some proportional medium. Now, solids are joined together not by one, but always by two mediums. God, therefore, arranged air and water between Fire and Earth as proportions; and therefore, out of these four elements,

<summary>The author begins a critique of the major Greek schools, specifically arguing that Plato’s approach to physics was too abstract and mathematical to accurately describe the physical world.</summary>

->Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.<-

elements, arranged in this manner, the world was necessarily fused together.

Then, since solid bodies are resolved into planes, and planes again—according to *Plato*—into triangles, he therefore willed that these elements be composed of triangles. And according to the logic of the shape he attributed to each element, he argues they are woven from these or those triangles, in greater or fewer numbers. Thus he posits that *Fire* is of a pyramidal shape, on account of its penetration <note>The sharp points of a pyramid or tetrahedron were thought to explain fire's ability to "cut" or penetrate other substances.</note>, and composed of four triangles. *Earth* is of a cubic shape, on account of its solidity, and therefore born from six planes, each of which consists of four triangles. He makes *Air* an octahedron, produced from eight surfaces, each of which is divided into six scalenes <note>Scalene triangles, which have three unequal sides.</note>. Finally, he makes *Water* an icosahedron, built from twenty triangles, each likewise compacted from scalene ones. What sort of physiology, I ask you, is this? Who emerges more instructed in the nature of *Fire* or *Earth*, *Water* or *Air*, from this account of their origin or composition? And when he had constructed the Body of the World in this manner, he inserted and joined to it a mathematical *Soul*, fused together from numbers and proportions.

Many interpreters of *Plato*—*Chalcidius*, *Proclus*, and as many as have commented on the *Timaeus*—have explained this *Platonic Soul*. Furthermore, *Plutarch*, in a singular treatise, has discussed at length *On the procreation of the Soul according to Plato*. But having read all these, you will gain nothing; except perhaps that you will be more firmly convinced that all who have sweated in this arena have utterly wasted their effort. To me, that Platonic <term>Psychogonia<note>original Greek: Ψυχογονία; the "generation" or "birth" of the soul.</note></term> seems like nothing other than a play of wit: or a magical Palace constructed in the air, the foundation of which we seek in vain. To whoever is familiar with that dialogue of the *Timaeus*, it will be enough to set down, not my own, but a recent Philosopher's [opinion] on that...

<margin>Book 2, Chapter 5.</margin>
...we will elucidate. Meanwhile, let these things be said briefly concerning Plato.

As for the Platonic writers, not a few remain: **Plotinus**, the leader of the Platonists <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, who synthesized Plato’s ideas into a complex spiritual system.</note>, **Porphyry**, **Iamblichus**, **Proclus**, **Maximus of Tyre**, **Alcinous**, **Chalcidius**, **Apuleius**, and others. The works of **Crantor**, the most ancient interpreter of Plato, have perished; as have those of **Taurus**, **Amelius**, and **Numenius**, of whom you may find some fragments in **Eusebius**. Furthermore, there are **Olympiodorus** and **Syrianus**, who wrote on the *Alcibiades* and the *Republic*. But we do not linger to review or examine these men, since the works of Plato himself survive; nor do we follow the streams or rivulets when it is possible to go to the fountainhead. So much for Plato.

<margin>The Peripatetics and Epicureans</margin>
We have now come to the dregs of philosophy: namely, the Epicurean <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the world was formed by the random collision of atoms.</note> and Aristotelian schools. From the time of Plato until the beginning of the current century, that entire interval is held by me to be *unphilosophical* <note>original Greek: "ἀφιλόσοφον"</note>; for that middle age neither retained the ancient wisdom, nor discovered new wisdom: unless it be a certain wordy kind, talkative without any fruit. Philosophical antiquity ended with Plato. Those who followed him savor only of Greek trifling, and are of no account among the ancients. As for **Aristotle** and his school, on this subject in which we are engaged—namely, the origin of things—they possess nothing sane or solid. They maintain that the world is **Eternal**, as much in its form as in its matter. They claim not only that the framework of the heavens and the mass of the Earth have been everlasting, but that we poor little humans, and every small animal in its kind, male and female, have birthed and been birthed in an endless chain without any first-born or beginning. They claim, moreover, that trees, meadows, flowers, and fruits, and all the equipment of the Earth, have never *not* existed. This is a doctrine not only irreligious, but all but ridiculous. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things ###

...as though it were his own property, he wished to claim the praise for himself and take precedence over all the ancients. <margin>Book 1 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 10.</margin> For he says, speaking of the world: "All men, then, say that the world had a beginning; but some say that having had a beginning it is eternal, others that it is perishable." <note>original Greek: "γενόμενον μὲν οὖν ἅπαντες εἶναί φασιν, ἀλλὰ γενόμενον οἱ μὲν ἀΐδιον, οἱ δὲ φθαρτόν."</note> *All the ancients say that the world was created: but some say it was created as an immortal thing, others as a perishable thing.* He, however, so that he might stand out with a unique distinction, maintained that it was not even created at all.

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or, #

Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotele"</note> held that the Sun and the Earth have existed from eternity, and are therefore of the same age. I ask, then: in what form was the Earth co-eternal with the eternal Sun? Was it in its <term>Elementary form</term> <note>Burnet uses this to describe a theoretical state where the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—rest in pure, separate layers without mixing.</note> (for so I call that simple form, shown in the diagram <note>Referring to the illustration on the preceding page.</note>, in which the individual elements occupy their own regions) or was it in its present form, consisting of land and water and being habitable? If he says the former—that the Earth passed, by the action of the Sun or other causes, from its Elementary form into its present state—then he acknowledges a beginning for this <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The region below the moon, which ancient philosophers believed was the only place subject to change, decay, and "new" beginnings.</note>, and thereby destroys his own opinion. But if he says the latter, he utterly overthrows everything he taught regarding the nature, laws, and natural places of the elements: and thus he kills his own theory with his own hand. Aristotle seems to have felt himself entangled in these difficulties: 
<margin>Book 2, chapters 1 and 2.</margin> 
for in his *Meteorology*, <note>original: "Meteoris"</note> concerning the position of the Earth and Water, and the generation of the sea, he speaks of these matters. Yet he touches upon that material most lightly, and flees from it immediately, as if he had touched glowing coals. But enough of this matter.

These are my thoughts on the origin of things. Now, what did Aristotle think concerning the nature of things—and first, concerning the heavens? He wished the heavens to be made of <term>adamantine</term> <note>From "adamas" (diamond/hardest metal). Aristotle proposed the heavens were solid, crystalline spheres.</note>, and the Stars to be fixed in the paneled ceilings of the Orbs like golden nails. This is a fiction that better suits a Poet than a Philosopher. Then, he imagined all the Orbs to be chained together in turn, and the entire Universe, however great it may be, to be revolved every twenty-four hours by the force of a certain <term>Prime Mover</term>. <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere in the Aristotelian system that gave motion to all inner spheres.</note> And he claimed this circle is repeated every day, for ever and ever. To this, he added that the Planets are carried by contrary motions at the same time: moving toward the East as well as toward the West at once. Finally, he established that the matter of the heavens is entirely different from anything sublunary: not only in degree and quality, but in its whole kind, so that one can never be changed into the other, nor could it ever be changed.

If we descend below the Moon, we immediately stumble into <term>Elemental Fire</term>: a <term>Will-o'-the-Wisp</term> <note>original: "Ignem plus quàm Fatuum." Burnet is punning on "Ignis Fatuus" (foolish fire/false light) to mock the Aristotelian belief in a sphere of pure fire located between the air and the moon.</note>: since

...lacks both light and heat. Descending to the middle region of the air, we will find the Aristotelian *Milky Way* <note>original: "Galaxiam"</note> and *Comets*. For that good philosopher holds these to be meteors <note>In ancient science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including clouds, rainbows, and comets, which Aristotle believed occurred below the moon.</note>, having contemplated the phenomena of nature with the eyes of common folk. Finally, on the Earth itself, Aristotle did not even explain general principles: such as the movement of the tides, magnetic phenomena, and the powers and compositions of metals and minerals. And as for individual bodies, to explain their actions and virtues—having abandoned local motion and the true differences of matter and its parts—he introduced some kind of *substantial forms* <note>original: "Formas substantiales." These were abstract "essences" that Scholastic philosophers used to explain why a thing is what it is, which Burnet considers a non-explanation.</note> and *specific qualities* <term>Specific qualities</term> <note>Hidden properties used to explain effects (like a magnet's pull) without explaining the physical mechanism.</note>. These are empty words: they have no more value in natural things than those he had previously rejected, the *Numbers* and *Harmony* of the Pythagoreans <note>Pythagoras and his followers believed the universe was structured according to mathematical ratios and musical intervals.</note>. And just as bodies act upon each other through these "forms" and "qualities," so too do they act upon our senses—if the gods allow it—through *intentional species* <note>original: "species intentionales." In Aristotelian thought, these were invisible "images" or "likenesses" that traveled from an object to the eye or mind to facilitate perception.</note>; painted-over shelters for his own ignorance.

Since things are so, and such was the philosophy of Aristotle, we cannot sufficiently wonder at the stupor of the Christian world: which, for so many centuries, uniquely embraced this discipline. It raised it to the heavens with praise, and recommended it to be publicly taught and lectured upon in all schools and universities. Indeed, the Church sanctioned it with authority, and raged against those who disagreed with Aristotle or attempted a new philosophy, as if they were heretics and enemies of the Christian religion. From this came the slow progress of the sciences: and in all the centuries during which this philosophy prevailed, it produced no inventions and brought no comforts to human life. How many volumes of commentaries have been written, great and useless? How many brilliant minds, forced to bear this servile yoke, labored in vain in cultivating unfruitful soil. The Christian world became sterile, as if sprinkled with sand, wherever this philosophy was sown.

<meta>This page continues Thomas Burnet’s critique of Aristotle’s natural philosophy. Having previously argued that Aristotle’s theories were evasive or contradictory, Burnet now provides a summarized list of specific "errors" that defined Aristotelian physics and cosmology, which dominated Western thought for centuries before the Scientific Revolution.</meta>

Philosophical Archaeology: or,

### A brief overview of Aristotle's errors.

He asserted that the World is Eternal in both directions:
Uncreated and indestructible.
That the heavens are solid, and at the same time
are driven in opposite directions.
That the matter of the Heavens is divine, made of a **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Quintessentialem." Aristotle believed the heavens were composed of a fifth element, distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, water, air, fire), which was supposedly unchanging and perfect.</note>, and is immutable.
That the fixed stars are the denser parts of their own spheres: and that the Planets are luminous by their own nature.
That Light is not a physical body, nor any kind of motion of bodies.
That **Elemental Fire** exists beneath the concave curve of the Moon.
That the Milky Way is a meteor <note>original: "Meteorum." In ancient science, "meteors" included all atmospheric phenomena. Aristotle incorrectly believed the Milky Way and Comets were vapors in the upper atmosphere rather than distant celestial objects.</note>: and likewise Comets, which he believed were not raised beyond the middle region of the air.
That the Earth remains immobile at the center of the Universe.
That "up" and "down" are fundamental to nature, according to immutable principles.
That the forms of living things are **substantial** <note>original: "substantiales." These "substantial forms" were abstract essences used by Scholastic philosophers to explain the nature of things, which Burnet and other moderns criticized as being unscientific.</note>: And that the qualities or properties of bodies are entirely distinct from their modes.
That sensation occurs through **intentional species** <note>original: "species intentionales." An Aristotelian theory suggesting that objects transmit a non-physical "image" or "likeness" of themselves to the senses.</note>. That rarefaction and condensation occur through the increase and decrease of extension within matter.
That Divine Providence does not descend below the Moon.
That the soul is **entelechy** <note>original: "ἐντελέχειαν." A Greek term Aristotle used to describe the soul as the "actuality" or "functional realization" of a body; Burnet considers this term meaningless jargon.</note> (a barbaric and ambiguous term), and of doubtful immortality.

If you ask about the man's character, he seems spiteful and **small-souled** <note>original: "μιϰϱόψυχοϛ" (mikropsychos).</note>: mostly unfair toward the ancient philosophers: whom he ignores in great matters, and refutes in trifles. Farewell, O **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira, hence the nickname "the Stagirite."</note>, to me you will always be a *bad Astronomer, a worse Theologian, and the worst Natural Philosopher.*

<meta>This page continues Thomas Burnet’s critique of ancient philosophers. # Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

Next follows *Epicurus* with his herd <note>original: "cum suo grege." A dismissive reference to the followers of Epicureanism.</note>, a man of little learning, but of no ordinary genius: yet so devoted to the senses that he believed the supreme norm and index of truth must always be taken from them. Let him rejoice in his omniscient senses: in his Sun that is only a foot and a half wide <note>Epicurus famously argued, based on sensory evidence, that the sun was roughly the size it appeared to be in the sky.</note>: in his Earth, not suspended in space, but rooted downward into infinity: and in the Sun returning every night through the sides of the earth to the starting gates of the East. If such things are befitting of a philosopher, what then befits the common crowd and the unlearned? I do not envy them their science or their pleasures—both of which are merely of the senses. These are souls worthy of living and perishing along with their bodies.

Regarding this man's philosophy, I have nothing worth commemorating. Furthermore, since this work, such as it is, was instituted for the sake of purifying ancient Philosophy, it should be enough to select and preserve only the best things, while the rest are consigned to oblivion. Thus, while preserving the honor we owe to our ancestors, we may benefit as much as possible from their rightly spoken words and discoveries.

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

### On the origin of Barbaric Philosophy.

Some maintain that philosophy was discovered by those very nations through their own natural genius; others claim it was deduced from the Hebrews and derived by the other nations from them—specifically from Moses or Abraham, whom they consider the princes of all sciences. I find it difficult to agree with either of these opinions. As for the first, who can point out to me such sharpness of mind, such force of reason, or such skill and practice in debating among those ancient men? What investigations of nature, what observations, and what experiments did they pass down to posterity? Give me some examples and specimens among the Egyptians, the Chaldeans, the Brahmins, and the others, of this distinguished and inventive character, so that we might not rashly believe they acquired for themselves the knowledge of such great things by their own power and reasoning. They deliver their dogmas for the most part nakedly and simply, with no preceding discussion and fortified by no reasons; they are to be received by the mere nod and authority of the teacher. Or, if by chance they do offer reasons, they are vague and unstable, carrying more or less weight according to the reader’s whim and disposition.

The future **CONFLAGRATION** <note>original: "CONFLAGRATIO." The ancient belief, common to Stoics and many "barbaric" cultures, that the world would be destroyed by fire.</note> of the world is a very ancient dogma, brought from the "barbaric" <note>In the classical sense, "Barbaric" refers to non-Greek civilizations like the Egyptians or Persians, rather than implying they were "uncivilized."</note> nations to the Greeks. Yet we do not read of it being proven by either group, nor did they explain the causes or methods of such a terrifying decree. If they had reached the knowledge of this matter through arguments sought from the nature of things and through a rational style of speech (as they say), they would have used those same arguments to persuade or convince others whom they imbued with that same doctrine. But having received these ideas "nakedly" (without proof), they reported them "nakedly"—just as "ancestral traditions" <note>original: "πατϱοπαϱάδοτα" (patroparadota). Things handed down from one's fathers or ancestors.</note> are usually transferred. Furthermore, the most celebrated doctrine of the ancients concerning world periods, the cycles, and the renovations of things, rests upon no demonstrations, but on repeated and irrefragable <note>Inescapable or undeniable.</note> authority. And, to bring forward an example of another kind, the doctrine of *metempsy-*

->Archæological Philosophy: or,<-

reincarnation <note>original: χώσεως, part of the Greek term *metempsychosis*</note>, or regarding the **pre-existence & cycle of Souls**: a doctrine most ancient and universal, if ever there was one. It prevailed not only throughout the East everywhere, but also in the West, as among the <term>Druids</term> <note>Ancient Celtic priests and scholars</note> and the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their belief in the migration of souls</note>. This doctrine, I say, as if sent down from heaven—**without father, without mother, without genealogy** <note>original: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος. A biblical allusion to Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:3), here used to suggest the doctrine's origin is mysterious and untraceable</note>—has traveled across the entire world. Yet, we are still unable to prove, by physical reasoning, that souls pre-existed before bodies, or that they return to them repeatedly. Finally, not to add more examples, the **Cosmogonies** <note>original: κοσμογονίαι; accounts of the birth of the universe</note> of the Ancients, or their doctrine on the origin of the world from **Chaos**, though ancient and widely diffused, was never philosophically explained or proven through proper reasoning. Some explained the generation of things **mythically** <note>original: μυθικῶς</note>, under the names and genealogies of the Gods; others **ethically** <note>original: ἠθικῶς</note>, through *Love* and *Strife*; still others indeed **physically** <note>original: φυσικῶς</note>, through the principles of the Light and the Heavy, but in a way that was loose, vague, and incomplete. By such means, they were never able to complete the work and lead their Chaos from its starting point to the goal—from a confused mass into the form of a habitable world.

I shall not cite further examples. For those who are even moderately well-versed in the literature and readings of the ancients know well enough that it was not the custom of those primeval sages to establish *Theories*, nor to demonstrate their dogmas through Causes or Effects, as modern Philosophers are accustomed to do. The Philosophy of the first men was less laborious, as they were not yet equipped with such a great apparatus of things for conducting observations—whether in the heavens, or on the earth, or in the sea; or concerning the air, or water, or concerning those things which happen to other bodies by the force of fire. Just as the customs of men and human life were simpler in the first ages, so likewise was their knowledge simpler and content with little. **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A 2nd-century Christian theologian who studied the relationship between Greek philosophy and faith</note> rightly notes that the "ancient-barbaric" philosophy was easy and brief, consisting of questions and answers; it was not argumentative and contentious,

It seems clear enough from this that the philosophy of the Ancients was derivative or traditional; but from what origin, finally, do you ask? Some say from the Hebrews, and they attribute all ancient barbarian wisdom to Moses or Abraham. As for Moses, it is clear from the Holy Scriptures that he was later than the Egyptian wisdom, and a student rather than a teacher of that literate nation; for he is said to have been instructed and trained from his childhood in the wisdom of the Egyptians. These are the words of Saint Stephen: "Pharaoh's daughter took him up and nourished him for herself as a son. And Moses was learned or instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians." <note>Acts 7:21–22</note> This wisdom, therefore, was not first born with Moses; it preceded his birth and must be sought from a higher origin.

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or, #

Similarly, regarding *Arabic* wisdom, Job—a much-celebrated and very learned Arab <note>original Greek: πολυκλητὸς κὶ πολυμαθὴς (*polyklētos kai polymathēs*)</note>—in whose history many traces of ancient wisdom occur, is considered older than Moses. This is evident by many signs. First, because he nowhere mentions the deeds performed by Moses—whether in Egypt, at the Exodus, or in the desert—even though he frequently and at length celebrates the greatness of God. Nor did his friends mention these things when reflecting on the justice and power of God; yet there has been no history since the Flood <term>Diluvium</term> <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note> from which the glory of the supreme Deity, just and powerful, could have been more aptly illustrated than from that Egyptian history.

Second, although he was a pious man and a worshiper of the true Deity, he acted contrary to the Mosaic Law in the performing of sacrifices. He performed the office of priest himself, by a certain natural and primitive right by which the Father of the family was both King and Priest among his own people; following the example of Noah, Abraham, Jethro the Midianite, and others who performed sacred rites before the Law was given by Moses.

Third, from the measure of his age and life, he seems to be placed more or less in the third century after the Flood. For he lived over two hundred years. Furthermore, in the history of Job, everything breathes a certain extreme antiquity.

<margin>Chapter 31: 26, 27</margin>

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...philosophy. Although it has reached us—the late-born progeny of the <term>Noachides</term> <note>The descendants of Noah; in this context, all of humanity living after the Great Flood</note>—after several millennia, and though it is speckled with many stains or wrapped in filth, it is not entirely difficult to wash away these blemishes once the truth has been discovered and explored from other sources. I have often noticed, not without wonder, that in these gems of the Ancients—though they are discolored by age—vivid sparks still shine through. But let us return to Noah.

It is right to believe that the <term>Antediluvian Fathers</term> <note>The biblical patriarchs who lived before the Great Flood, such as Adam, Seth, and Methuselah, whom the author believes possessed great scientific and spiritual knowledge</note> were not blockheads, witless, or lacking in knowledge. Noah was the common heir to these men; he lived as a contemporary to many of them and shared in the learning of the others through easy tradition. Therefore, it is probable that whatever those long-lived Patriarchs understood was known to Noah for the most part, since for six hundred years he was able to benefit from their company and their studies. **HE**, therefore, in my judgment—as an *inhabitant of both worlds* <note>original: "utriusque mundi incola"; referring to Noah living in the world both before and after the Flood</note>—handed down the lamp of the sciences from them to us. Along with his own offspring and the earliest peoples, he spread throughout the world certain seeds of both natural and moral doctrine. 

But I freely admit that in later ages both types of doctrine withered greatly and were nearly choked by growing weeds. These cannot easily be restored from ancient monuments; instead, everything must be renewed from the principles of nature and clear reason themselves, and likewise amended and established through properly constructed Theories. Thus, as the end of things approaches, may the truth reborn shine forth more clearly as a prelude to the future renewal.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

Moreover, this treatise is twofold, as you see: and just as it was proposed in the preceding book to run through the individual literate nations and bring to light the Philosophy and Doctrines of each, both concerning the Macrocosm <note>The "Greater World" or the universe as a whole.</note> and the Sublunary <note>The "Lower World," specifically the Earth and its atmosphere below the moon.</note> world; concerning the Heavens as much as the Earths, and the origins of both; so in this second book we look uniquely at the Earth, and separately and more diligently seek what traces remain among the ancients of its own birth and primeval form. There remain, however—unless my opinion deceives me—no small remains: which we are about to prove in what follows by citing examples.

To one examining the doctrine of the ancients concerning the origin of the Earth, one must begin *from the first-born chaos* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πρωτογόνου χάεος"</note>, as if from the primary matter <term>materia prima; the fundamental, unformed substance from which the universe was created</term> or seedbed of this nature and sublunary world. Furthermore, the "Ancient Chaos" <note>original: "τὸ Ἀρχαῖον χάος"</note> was a widespread concept among the most ancient sages, both the Theologians and Poets, as well as the more recently named Physicists and Philosophers; and that doctrine flowed from the Barbarians to the Greeks, from the Greeks to the Romans, and to all nations everywhere. That our world has always and eternally existed under the same form and appearance which it enjoys today, no one openly asserted—excepting Aristotle and perhaps some pseudo-Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who may have deviated from his original teachings; Burnet suggests the idea of an eternal, unchanging Earth is a later error.</note>. But all that we call the Globe of the Earth and the habitable world was once a formless mass, murky and indistinct, called Chaos: as it were, a first draft of the world to come; all wise men have handed down this truth with one voice.

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...their opinion, *Diodorus Siculus* <margin>Historical Library, Book 1</margin> writes that *according to the original constitution of the universe, heaven and earth had one form, their natures being mixed together; but after this, when the bodies separated from one another, the world embraced the entire visible order within it.* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς τῶν ὅλων σύστασιν, μίαν ἔχειν ἰδέαν οὐρανόν τε καὶ γῆν, μεμιγμένην αὐτῶν τῇ φύσεως, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα διαστάντων τῶν σωμάτων ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων, τὸν μὲν κόσμον περιλαβεῖν ἅπασαν τὴν ὁρωμένην ἐν αὐτῷ σύνταξιν."</note> Nor does the "Sacred Word" <note>original Greek: "ἱερὸς λόγος"</note> attributed to *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many ancient mystical and philosophical works were attributed.</note> say otherwise; imitating Egyptian philosophy, it mentions both Chaos and the Abyss, and the birth of things from those first beginnings.

There is no need to mention the *Greeks* and *Latins*. *Orpheus*, *Hesiod*, *Menander*, *Aristophanes*, *Euripides*, and the writers of the *Epic Cycle* all sang of the ancient Chaos. Furthermore, among the Greek philosophers, the Ionics and the Platonists construct the framework of the world from a confused mass. Finally, the Stoics establish their cycles and renewals from Chaos to Chaos. I pass over the *Latins*—*Ennius*, *Varro*, *Ovid*, *Lucretius*, *Statius*, and others. In short, whoever maintains that this world was created, in whatever nation or sect, begins their <term>diakosmesis</term> <note>original Greek: "διακόσμησιν" — a term for the ordering or arrangement of the universe.</note> from a raw matter.

Therefore, it should be noted that those among the ancients who wrote *Cosmogonies* <note>Accounts of the origin of the cosmos.</note> always recognized Chaos and laid it as the foundation of their work. Finally, those who wrote *Theogonies* <note>Accounts of the origin and genealogy of the gods.</note> began their mythology from that same Chaos. ### Philosophical Archaeology: or,

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

If they worshipped the Elements—Fire, Water, and Earth—and held them as Gods, it follows that their *Theogony* <note>The genealogy or birth of the gods.</note> is their *Cosmogony* <note>The origin or birth of the universe.</note>; or rather, that the births of the Persian Gods are the births of the Elements and of Worldly Bodies. Indeed, this flaw or error frequently occurs among the ancients: they established "born" gods <note>original Latin: "nativos"</note>, to use *Cicero’s* term, and they assigned the same beginnings to the Gods and to the World. They did this either by fashioning deities out of their own matter, or at least by not considering them to be eternal and without a beginning.

However many led their Gods out of Chaos, they much more led our Earth out of that same source; they likewise celebrate its birth in their Theogonies. Since we find these Theogonies everywhere among the ancients, we may conclude that the doctrine of the *origin of things from Chaos* was received among the early peoples like a common proverb or an Oracle. It will not be irrelevant to note some Theogonies of the Ancients as witnesses to this fact.

<margin>Suidas, under the entry</margin>
We mentioned the Persian Theogony above. *Aristeas of Proconnesus* <note>A legendary Greek poet and miracle-worker.</note> is also said to have written a Theogony; he flourished in the time of *Cyrus* and composed a history of the *Arimaspi* and the *Hyperboreans* <note>Mythical peoples of the far north.</note>, which many have recalled. *Orpheus* wrote a Theogony, as *Cedrenus* reports from *Timothy*, an ancient author. That this *Theogony* amounted to the same thing as a *Cosmogony* is easily apparent from the *Orphic* remains or imitations that survive. Nor does the *Epic Cycle* <note>A collection of Ancient Greek epic poems related to the Trojan War.</note>, which we have mentioned more than once, do otherwise; it begins from the mixing of Heaven and Earth, and from there proceeds to the lineage of the Gods and the origin of the world. Having therefore established this foundation, we must next examine what changes the ancients believed occurred within this Chaos: what new forms appeared, through whose intervention it transitioned from a confused mass into a habitable World. For Worlds are not created in a single stroke, like statues cast from a mold. Rather, through long-lasting action and slow progress, nature gradually extricates and unfolds itself from that disordered state, striving toward order and beauty. Indeed, first out of that confusion and mixture of unlike parts, there arises a strife and struggle <note>original Latin: *lis & lucta*</note> throughout the entire mass. From that struggle and contention comes a breaking apart, and the separation and withdrawal of the conflicting elements from one another. By this means, the Mundane Chaos was divided into various spheres and smaller circles: much like the different floors or levels of a building <note>original Latin: *tabulata aut contignationes*</note> made of elementary bodies, stacked one upon another. Antiquity seems to have noted this; as Orpheus says:

-> *First, the honey-sweet hymn of ancient Chaos; how it changed its natures... and separated one thing from another.* <note>original Greek: πρῶτα μὲν ἀρχαίου χάεος μελήφατον ὕμνον· ὡς ἀπάμεψε φύσεις, — — — — — — τε διέκρινε τἄλλον ἀπ᾽ ἄλλου</note> <-

Truly, Orpheus sang in his *Chaology*—that is, in his explanation of the world's birth from Chaos—of the various changes, secretions, and diverse appearances that the mass underwent time and again, until it reached the form of a habitable globe. And this is the same as establishing a *Cosmogony* <note>An account of the origin of the universe</note>.

# C H A P T E R II.

## Concerning the Form of the Primordial Earth, and the Triple State of the World.

<margin>Book 1, chapters 4, & 5.</margin>
We have treated thus far the origin of the Earth from the first Chaos: and that after various motions and metamorphoses. Indeed, just as small creatures <note>original Latin: *animalcula* — in this context, referring to insects or larvae</note> are accustomed to pass from an egg or a worm into one kind of insect after another, until they have reached their final form: so, through various successive changes and fleeting forms, the habitable Earth is finally made from Chaos. But we must next ask, *What was the form and surface of this primordial Earth*, when it was first compacted out of Chaos? Was it the same as today's, or different? I answer, the Earth could not have been established from the beginning in the same form it has today: because of the mountains and crags, and the bed of the sea, and inequalities of this kind, which could not have arisen immediately from Chaos, or on the surface of a fluid mass. This is what we have abundantly shown in the *Theory* <note>Referring to the author's own famous work, *The Sacred Theory of the Earth*</note> itself. Consequently, it is necessary that the primordial Earth was of another form and appearance from that of today.

# Ancient Doctrine concerning the Origin of Things.

The hinge of the matter turns on this point, and whoever provides proof for this conclusion holds the winning case. By *proven*, however, I do not mean by physical reasons—for that has already been done in the place cited above <note>Referring again to his *Sacred Theory of the Earth*</note>—but we are doing something else now: namely, to show that the same thing was handed down by the ancient sages. We wish to show that there still exist—not so much in complete books as in fragments or excerpts of the ancients—no obscure traces of this same truth. And we do not undertake this new work because it is strictly necessary for the aforementioned Theory (which stands on its own physical merits), but rather to clear Divine Providence from every stain <note>Burnet wants to show that a "disorderly" Earth isn't a mistake by God, but a result of historical change</note>, and to meet the obstinacy of those who refuse to receive the truth unless it has been handed down and recommended to them by their ancestors.

Come then, let us approach the matter itself; let the conclusion to be proven be this: *That the world was once of a different form and position from the present one.* By *the World*, however, I do not mean the immense universe of all things; for we do not know its borders or its shape, nor the order of its remote parts. I mean our world: namely, the Earth and the visible Heavens. Therefore, our assertion comes back to this: *that the Earth was once of a different form from the present, and of a different position toward the heavens*; this we assert in the first place and in general terms. Wherein this difference specifically consisted will be explained more conveniently in the following pages, when the properties of that primeval Earth are to be weighed separately.

Meanwhile, to confirm this general distinction with authorities, it must be noted first that there is a triple state of the natural world—of Heaven and Earth—according to the Sacred Scriptures. Here we are clearly dealing with the triple state of the Creature or <term>the creation</term> <note>Greek: *tēs ktiseōs*. Burnet argues this term refers to the physical universe.</note>: the primeval state, not yet subjected to vanity; the state subjected to vanity; and finally the state of future redemption and liberation from vanity and corruption. Thus far, I believe, all interpreters agree. But we must inquire further: what is to be understood *by vanity*? And what *by the creation*, which is subjected to vanity and is to be liberated from it at the appointed time? I answer that by vanity is understood here mutability, inconstancy, and a decaying and fleeting nature that is easily prone to corruption—such as the nature we see today. And the Creature is said *to serve*, or to suffer servitude, because of the servile labors of both men and beasts of burden in this age, from which they will be unburdened in the age to come.

Between the world <note>original: "Orbis Terrarum"</note> of the modern and the primeval state, there are manifold and innumerable differences: which can nevertheless all be reduced to two main headings: namely, the **Form** and the **Situation** of each Earth. You see the state of the case. The adversaries deny that there will be any future destruction or change of the natural world. They are led to this belief because they have seen or heard of no inconsistency or change in Nature until now—not from the times of the most ancient Fathers, nor from the furthest memory of men, nor from the very beginning of things.

What does the **Apostle** reply to these men? He says that they "willingly forget" the primeval state of nature, or the ancient **Heaven & Earth**; which, having been established out of water and through water, for that very reason—or because of that specific constitution—perished in the flood of waters. But the **Heavens** and **Earth** of today, he says, being differently constituted, are destined to perish by fire. And in their place, new Heavens and a new Earth will eventually follow, in which the **Just** shall dwell, *verse 13*.

This is the core of the Apostolic response: it argues in several ways that the **world before the flood** <note>original: "Mundum antediluvianum"</note> was different from the world of today. **First**, unless you assume this difference, there is no force in his response; it would carry no weight against the argument of his adversaries. In fact, it would rather strengthen and confirm their position. For if the face of nature remained the same and unchanged both before and after the **Flood**, then it has indeed remained the same since the very beginning of things—which is exactly what the <term>scoffers</term> <note>original Greek: οἱ ἐμπαῖκται (*hoi empaiktai*), those who mock the idea of divine judgment</note> were contending. Therefore, under such an interpretation, the Apostle does not merely fail to refute them; he actually concedes the very point that needed to be disproven.

### Philosophical Archeology: or,

They pretended to be ignorant that the **Heavens and Earth** before the flood <note>original Latin: "ante-diluvianos"</note> were established differently than those of today; and that as they perished in the destruction of the **Flood**, "the heavens and the earth that are now" <note>original Greek: τοὺς νῦν οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν</note> succeeded them, possessing a different form and different qualities from the ancient ones. <margin>* "Through which" <note>original Greek: Δι’ ὧν</note>, according to the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>. "Through which things," says the **Apostle**, "the world that then was perished" <note>original Greek: ὁ τοτὲ κόσμος ἀπώλετο</note>. But for what reasons? Or by what causes did that world, having been inundated, perish? Was it not because of 그 specific constitution and position regarding the waters which he had noted in the preceding verse? If this is granted, you have a clear distinction between the two worlds and a conclusion properly drawn. If this is not granted, there is no force in the conclusion or the inference.

**Finally**, in *verse seven*, the **Heavens and Earth of today** are contrasted with those of the world before the flood: "the heavens and the earth which are now" <note>original Greek: οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ</note> against "the heavens and earth of old" <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἔκπαλαι οὐρανοῖς καὶ γῇ</note>; just as later (*verse 13*) the **new Heavens and Earth** are distinguished from those of today. But if the entire structure—both that before the flood and that after—had been exactly the same, there would be no room for this contrast, and no reason for a distinction. Indeed, instead of using a word of contrast, the **Apostle** should have said "the same heavens and the earth" <note>original Greek: οἱ αὐτοὶ οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ</note>, etc.—meaning the same Heavens and Earth which were previously submerged in water are now being **reserved** for fire.

<meta>catchword: reserved.</meta>

He highlights specific Greek phrasing to show that the "world of old" and the "world that is now" are two distinct physical states of the planet.</summary>

I have explained these things at length because I know well that this passage of *Saint Peter* is a stumbling block <note>original: "lapidem offendiculi"</note> to many. We, however, build our **Theory of the Earth** <note>original: "Theoriam Telluris"</note> chiefly upon this rock, at least regarding sacred authority; and we have always considered this an immovable foundation. Nor is the interpretation we have given of this passage entirely new or unique. For many commentators, compelled by the force of the words, confess that the **Apostle** is speaking here of the physical, natural world. And some have asserted—based on the authority of this Apostolic discourse—that the pre-flood <note>original: "ante-diluvianos"</note> Heavens and Earth perished (in terms of their form, I mean) and that the modern ones are different from them.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Concerning the nature, manner, and causes of Floods: and especially concerning the universal one.

There follows an inquiry into the Flood, which the Apostle <note>Saint Peter, whose second epistle is the primary subject of Burnet’s commentary.</note> mentions here, and by which he says the Ancient World perished. But what kind of Flood this was, from what causes it drew its origin, and by what means it overwhelmed the globe of the earth, is a difficult question, debated in every age. <margin>Book 1, chapters 2, 3.</margin> To untie this knot, we have established three things in the *Theory of the Earth*: first, we investigated the quantity of water required for a universal Flood that would cover and envelop the peaks of the highest mountains; and we discovered by clear calculation that it would exceed the mass and magnitude of at least eight Oceans. From these three main points, collected together, it is rightly proved: First, that the **Modern Earth** is not liable to a *Flood* <note>original: *Diluvio*</note>; nor, by reason of its form and position, is it capable of one. Second, that the **Antediluvian Earth** <note>The world before the Great Flood.</note> was of a different form and position from the modern one: otherwise, it would not have perished by that kind of fate. Finally, assuming that form and position, or that construction of the ancient Earth over the face of the *Abyss* <note>original: *Abyſſi*</note> which we gave previously: (which is conformable both to the sacred writers and to the laws of nature and the origin of things from *Chaos*:) a universal *Flood* would arise from its dissolution and its fall into the underlying *Abyss*. And it would be such a flood that it would correspond to every phenomenon and meet all objections. For this hypothesis would not suffer from a lack of water, nor would it be difficult to lead away and remove those same waters when the *Flood* ended; and whatever other inconveniences weigh down the common hypotheses, they have no place in this one, or exert no force.

*But you will say* perhaps, that a hypothesis of this kind concerning the dissolution <note>original: *diſſolutione*</note> of the Earth and the eruption of the *Abyss* indeed responds to all phenomena, both of the universal *Flood* and of the modern Earth, but that this dissolution is fictitious, or stated without proof. *I answer*, that a hypothesis which fits and agrees with every phenomenon of the subject matter is not considered fictitious or stated without proof; it fulfills its parts, performs its duty, and in those natural things which are not subjected to the eyes, there is no other method of philosophizing or investigating the truth than through *Hypotheses* of this kind. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

...the dissolution of the Earth and the breaking open of the Abyss in the Flood <note>original: *Diluvio*</note>, two things are furthermore to be observed: first, what sacred history has handed down concerning this matter. Second, what the natural history of Floods has produced regarding their manner and causes. If history records openings in the Earth, eruptions of water, and similar events in minor floods as characteristic and associated features, then in the greatest of all floods, there would be even more need for these weightier causes.

Regarding the first point, therefore, *Moses* records in the history of the Flood that the great Abyss, or <term>Tehom-Rabbah</term> <note>A Hebrew phrase meaning "the Great Deep," referring to the vast primordial waters.</note>, was broken apart at that time, which could not have happened without the rupture or dissolution of the Earth. Furthermore, he establishes this disruption as the primary cause of the Flood: thus the subterranean waters went out or erupted from this Abyss, which then inundated the whole world. Nor did the Earth merely gape open, but it also fell down into the underlying Abyss; this is sufficiently proven by the fact that otherwise the subterranean waters would not have been expelled from their resting places. Much less could they have raised themselves to the height of the highest mountains if no force or impulse had been exerted upon them. Finally, since the Flood of which *Moses* speaks was not local to this or that region, but spread through the whole world, it is clear from this that the ruin or dissolution of the Earth—by which the waters were moved and expelled—was universal. Every part of our hypothesis embraces and confirms that brief narrative of *Moses*.

Not dissimilar to this disruption of the *Tehom-Rabbah* is a passage in the History of *Job, chapter 38*, where the origins of the Ocean are celebrated, when it came forth from the womb of the Earth; for so I understand that womb from which the sea is said to have erupted, the barriers by which it was enclosed having been broken. These are the words, according to the Septuagint <note>The influential third-century BCE Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>: "I shut up the sea with gates, when it burst forth, proceeding as if from its mother's womb." <note>original Greek: ἔφραξα δὲ θάλασσαν πύλαις, ὅτε ἐμαίμασσεν, ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς αὐτῆς ἐκπορευομένη.</note>

In general, **Inundations** are accustomed to happen in three ways: either by the irruption of the sea into low lands, when barriers made by nature or by art are destroyed or overcome. Or by immoderate rains. Or finally by eruptions of subterranean waters. And it is worth noting here that, just as no overflow of the Ocean is possible because of its position (which is lower than the lands), so too can a <term>Universal Deluge <note>original: "Diluvium universale." Thus, no general inundation can be produced from it. As much water is restored by the rains as had previously departed in the form of vapors.

Finally, the third kind of Deluge, which arises from earthquakes and the eruptions of <term>subterranean waters <note>original: "aquarum subterranearum." Waters located in the Great Abyss beneath the Earth's crust.</note></term>, is the most severe. It is infamous for deadly disasters, whether you look at the nature of things or the human race. From this cause, islands are sometimes swallowed up, or great tracts of the continent submerged, mountains changed into abysses, and firm land into the sea. Lastly, the greatest changes and transformations, which we see arising on the face of today's world, or know to have arisen long ago, draw their origin from here. Nor do these floods rage any less against men and animals; cities with their inhabitants are destroyed by this, as are fields and forests with their wild beasts, and regions of the earth with all their infrastructure. These events are true <term>miniatures <note>original: "compendia." Literally "abridgments" or "summaries"; Burnet means that local floods caused by crustal collapse are smaller versions of the Great Deluge.</note></term> of that great and <term>universal Deluge <note>original: "œcumenici Diluvii." From the Greek *oikoumene*, the inhabited world.</note></term> by which the whole world of lands perished.

### CHAPTER V.

## *On the position of the primeval Earth in direct relation to the Sun, and the properties resulting from it; such as Perpetual Spring, or a perennial Equinox throughout the entire globe; a Rainless Sky without a Rainbow; and the Longevity of the first men.*

We have previously distinguished the **Primeval Earth** <term>Tellus Primigenia: Burnet’s term for the Earth in its original, perfect state before the Great Flood.</term> from the **Earth of Today** in two ways: by its **Form** and its **Position**. Moreover, that different **Position** was likewise twofold: either with respect to its own structure and placement upon the waters of the **Abyss** <note>original: *Abyssi*. In Burnet's theory, the "Abyss" refers to a massive subterranean ocean that was trapped beneath the smooth outer shell of the first Earth.</note>; or with respect to the **Sun** and the **Heavens**. We have already dealt with the former; it remains for us to discuss the latter—the celestial position. Since this is the primary issue in this inquiry—from which other differences and notable conditions flow—we must seek all the more diligently to see if, beyond natural reasons, the testimonies of the ancients exist to confirm that state of nature.

Regarding the **Golden Age** <note>original: *Aureo sæculo*. A mythical period of primordial peace and prosperity when humanity lived in harmony with nature.</note> and the **age of Saturn**, the ancients handed down many accounts plainly foreign to our own times and to nature as it is today. Because of an ignorance of their causes, as well as the fables mostly mixed in with them, these accounts rarely gained belief. But for those who have perceived upon what [foundation...] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "funda-", likely continuing "fundamento" (foundation) on the next page.</note>

This original state of things rests upon a foundation; and for those who understand from what causes the difference between that state and our modern one arises, it will not be difficult to distinguish the true from the fabulous, and the genuine from the spurious. Having set aside the errors, they will rejoice to embrace the remainder with a good heart and hold it in the highest esteem, as the most ancient monument of **natural history**.

In the second book of the *Theory*, we have sufficiently explained the **Primeval Earth** <term>Tellus Primæva: The original, perfect Earth before its crust broke to cause the Great Flood.</term> regarding its physical aspects. The principles of that theory need not be repeated here, but rather its conclusions. The one currently under consideration is this: *The orientation of the primeval Earth was upright*, assuming and always maintaining its axis in a line parallel to the axis of the **Ecliptic** <note>original: *Eclipticæ*. The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; Burnet argues the Earth originally had no axial tilt, meaning no seasons.</note>. From this, the motions of the heavens would all be uniform, and the course of the year would be simple and without differences in seasons. The question now is whether any vestiges remain of this form of the year, this motion of the heavens, and the subsequent change of the state of things into what we see today.

Let us begin with **Plato**, the ornament of his nation and his age. He mostly deals with divine matters, but he also presents—scattered throughout his works—several very ancient traditions concerning the natural world: its periods, **Catastrophes**, and great changes. These, I believe, he collected from priests while traveling in Egypt. He proposes these primarily in three dialogues: *Timaeus*, *The Statesman* <note>original: *Politico*</note>, and *Phaedo*. Here we must deal only with the latter two, and first with *The Statesman*, or *On Kingship*. There, under the guise of a **Fable** <note>original: *Fabulæ*. Burnet often uses "fable" to mean a mythological narrative that contains a hidden physical or historical truth.</note> about the **age or reign of Saturn**, he displays a dual order of the World—the primeval and the modern—and the conditions of each. Moreover, he says that this narrative of his was handed down from the most ancient times, and by our ancestors who lived closest to the first revolution of the world.

In this discourse, he distinguishes two ages of the world, as has been said, and two states of nature and human affairs: the first under **Saturn** <term>Saturnus: In ancient mythology, the ruler of the "Golden Age." This is the first chapter and the crux of the matter: that the state of the **sublunary world** <term>sublunary: Literally "under the moon"; a term used in older science to describe the Earthly realm, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the unchanging heavens.</term>—whether it be happy or unhappy—depends upon the motion of the heavens, whether it is regular or irregular. Furthermore, he mentions the spontaneous fertility of the Earth, the tameness of wild beasts, and a **Divine Rule** <term>Theocrasia: A government by God or divine beings directly, rather than by human laws or kings.</term> in the governance of the world. These are remarkable characteristics, which he seems to have taken from the prophet **Isaiah** (*chapter 65:17, etc.*). He repeats that Divine Rule quite often, from which he had introduced this entire discourse on the changes of things—planning especially to discuss the origin of government and its various kinds. He says that in the first state of things, God himself alone exercised command. But as the human race degenerated and the order of nature was perverted, God withdrew from the helm of the world and, as it were, abdicated his office. This left humans with the license to rule the world in their own way. These things are stated somewhat freely; yet they correctly indicate a **Divine Rule** <note>original: "Theocrasiam"</note>, both of the first age and of the future world when it is renewed. And thus the unbridled government of today's world—born and driven, as it were, by the impulse of an evil spirit—is silently rebuked by these words.

Finally, although Plato mentions neither a **Flood** <note>original: "Diluvii"</note> nor a **Great Conflagration** <note>original: "Conflagrationis"</note> in these revolutions and catastrophes of the world, he does mention a massive shaking of the Heaven and

Earth during this reversal of things; and from that shaking, all things were thrown into confusion, and every kind of animal was extinguished. This corresponds quite clearly, in our opinion, to the dissolution and slaughter that occurred during the Flood, affecting both the living and the inanimate world. # Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

These things from Plato’s *Politicus* concern the regular and uniform motion of the heavens, the position of the Earth, and the equality of the years in the first ages of the world. There follows in the *Phaedo* a similar passage that must be examined. Indeed, one should note as the first theorem in this matter—and the foundation of what Plato said in both the *Politicus* and the *Phaedo*—that **there are two world-orderings** <note>original Greek: "διττὰς εἶναι διακοσμήσεις"</note>, differing in form and position. He explained this difference in the *Politicus* chiefly in terms of the Heavens; but here in the *Phaedo*, he explains it in terms of the Earth. Under the name of a certain "pure Earth" placed in the ether, he lists many properties that do not fit today’s Earth at all, but fit our original Earth (or the new one to come) perfectly. These properties can be reduced to two main points: **Position** and **Form**. In both respects, they can be aptly applied to the original Earth, though they are incompatible with the modern one.

This is especially true for those matters regarding the form or position of the **Earth** <note>Latin: *Telluris*</note>. There are many other things found in other authors concerning this same argument; but Plato alone is worthy to take the stage and hold our full attention.
