## On the Changed Position of the **Earth**, or the **Heavens**: formerly **upright**, today **oblique**: and the **Phenomena** that followed therefrom: the **Testimonies** of other ancients.

<margin>Chapter 10.</margin>
The remaining witnesses of the truth, who follow in succession, can be divided into their own classes; since they are many and of different orders. The philosophers deservedly lead the procession: those who have warned us again and again about the changed position of the **Earth** <note>Latin: *Telluris*</note>, or the declination of the pole <note>Burnet argues that the Earth's axis was originally perpendicular to the sun, creating a perpetual spring, and that it tilted during the Deluge.</note>. We have brought forward their testimonies, which are quite clear, in the second book of the *Theory* <note>Referring to Burnet's own work, *The Sacred Theory of the Earth*.</note>. It is not necessary for us to repeat these for a reader who remembers; but for one who has forgotten, we refer them back there. Only this one thing must be advised in this place: In citing these witnesses, the inquiry concerns only the **Fact**, not the **causes of the fact**; nor do we seek the reasons for the changed position of the Earth from these philosophers, which they were almost entirely ignorant of; but rather that they might attest to us those things which they received from other learned men, by a certain literary tradition, concerning the changed position of the Earth or the pole. However, we neither demand nor linger much over their own conjectures as to what the causes of such a great mutation might have been.

<header>Ancient Doctrine of the Origins of Things.</header>

<note>original Greek: "Δια δὲ τῆ̄ ἀρετὴ̄ τῆ̄ νήσου..."</note> Due to the excellence of the island and the temperate nature of the air, more than enough food is produced spontaneously. — — — — The people there are exceedingly long-lived, reaching as many as one hundred and fifty years, and for the most part, they remain free from disease.

*The best temperature of the sky exists there (for they live under the equinox). They are troubled neither by heat nor by cold. The fruits of the trees are considered ripe there throughout the entire year. There, the day always equals the night: nor do shadows fall at noon, because the Sun is directly overhead. Such is the virtue of the island and the kindness of the air, that more than enough food grows of its own accord. The inhabitants are of a very great age, as those who prolong their lives to one hundred and fifty years, mostly without any disease.*

These descriptions do not fit any climate or any region of the modern <term>Earth</term><note>Latin: *Telluris*</note>. Those who now enjoy an equinox throughout the whole year are only those who live in the middle of the <term>Torrid Zone</term><note>Latin: *Torridâ*; the equatorial region once thought too hot for habitation.</note> and directly under the equinoctial line. That place is indeed habitable, but it is neither without heat nor without rains; furthermore, it is subject to violent storms. Additionally, people do not live longer under the Torrid Zone than in other places, nor are the inhabitants immune to diseases or poverty.

<margin>On Paradise, chapter 13.</margin>
Therefore, these conditions do not apply except to a universal equinox, or to the Earth in an upright position. The ancients adapted these conditions first to their <term>Elysian Fields</term><note>Latin: *Elysiis*; the mythological paradise for the heroic and virtuous.</note>, and then to other regions that were to be adorned in the manner of the Elysian Fields. Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325 AD), an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent defenses of the faith using classical philosophy.</note> pursued this argument at greater length; and when he had objected to the Philosophers that humans could not have been born from the Earth because of the force of cold in winter or heat in summer, he responds, according to the mind of the ancients: *“In the beginning of the world,” they say, “there was no winter and summer; but a perpetual temperature and a stable spring.”* <note>original Latin: "non erant, inquiunt, in principio mundi, hyems & æstas; sed perpetua temperies & ver æquabile."</note> This was indeed the opinion of the ancients. For the **Christian Fathers** <note>The early influential theologians of the Christian Church, such as Gregory of Nazianzus or Augustine.</note> repeat and emphasize this quite often; and in this matter, as in many others, they accuse foreign authors of a certain plagiarism <margin>In the Life of Basil the Great.</margin>. I omit further examples: this is the sum of the matter—just as some truth is usually hidden beneath ancient fables as a foundation, so the **Original Earth** [Tellus Primigenia] <note>Burnet’s term for the Earth before the Flood, which he believed was perfectly smooth and without seasons.</note> seems to me to have provided the occasion for many fabulous narrations. It was a real thing, of which ancient men retained some shadow or dim light; and out of whatever memory they had of that most longed-for state, they fashioned new Lands, or regions of the earth, after the model and image of this *Original Earth*. And they usually placed these in inaccessible locations—beyond the Ocean, in the air, or among the inhabitants of the Underworld—lest they be caught in error by <margin>On the Face in the Orb of the Moon; Photius, Bibliotheca, Codex 166.</margin> eyewitnesses. 

Such was the island of **Ogygia** in **Plutarch**; or the pleasant island situated on high above **Thule**, according to **Antonius Diogenes**. Archaeological Philosophy: or,

some call Paradise "Intelligible," <note>original: "Intelligibilem"; in a philosophical context, this refers to a spiritual or mental realm rather than a physical one.</note> bound to no specific place; others call it "Sensible," <note>original: "sensibilem"; meaning a place that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note> and here is where the first division of opinions occurs. Then, those who believe it to be sensible and corporeal place it either on this Earth, or outside of this Earth: namely in the air, or on the sphere of the Moon. <margin>Theory [of the Earth] book 2, chapter 6.</margin>
We have explained these differences of opinion more fully elsewhere; especially that view which transfers Paradise beyond the Equator, the Torrid Zone, the Ocean, and our Northern world. It is not that this opinion pleases me above the others, but rather that it is supported by the calculations of the ancients, and it clearly teaches us that the idea of Paradise being fixed in Mesopotamia is a fiction of the Moderns. <note>original: "Neotericorum"; Burnet frequently critiques "modern" scholars of his time who tried to find a literal, local Eden in the Middle East.</note> Meanwhile, as far as the **Theory of the Earth** <term>Burnet's "Theory of the Earth" was a famous 17th-century attempt to explain the planet's history—including the Flood—through physics and reason.</term> is concerned, it does not dwell on a "Topical Paradise" <note>A "topical" paradise refers to a specific, localized geographic spot.</note> in any particular part of the world, since it considers the entire habitable globe in that **New World** <note>The "New World" here refers to the Earth as it existed in its first, uncorrupted state before the Great Flood.</note> to have been like a Paradise. Consequently, and in agreement with the Mosaic hypothesis—which teaches that the entire human race, however great it may be, sprang from one man and one woman—you may call their birthplace and first homeland "Paradise" if you like: a place most delightful with waters and trees. This is acceptable provided you likewise grant to the other regions of that same Earth a *Perpetual Spring* <note>original: "Ver perpetuum"; a hallmark of the Golden Age in classical literature.</note> and what follows from it: spontaneous fertility and the longevity of its inhabitants. For we have proven, from the nature of the matter and the faith of the ancients, that these conditions prevailed everywhere in that new world.

...turning in every direction, they guarded the way that led to the tree of life.

Regarding Paradise and the fate of the first humans, this is the summary of the Mosaic narration: which, while preserving its meaning, I have explained in other words, so that we might judge the matter more freely, as if it were written by a new author. Almost everyone acknowledges that there are certain parabolic elements in this narrative, which are not to be strictly measured by the letter. Some even wish the whole discourse to be a skillful <term>hypotyposis <note>original Greek: ὑποτύπωσιν; a vivid, life-like description or rhetorical sketch used to represent a subject to the imagination</note></term> for explaining true things: namely, the novelty and the degeneration of the human race; then, the Paradisiacal state of primeval nature, and its subsequent degeneration. For although, at the beginning of the discourse, this Paradisiacal state seems to be restricted to a single region, which is called *Gan-Eden* <note>original Hebrew: the Garden of Eden</note>, nevertheless later, when the curse of sterility is brought forth, the whole Earth comes into the reckoning. The Earth shall no longer bring forth spontaneous yields, nor fruits without farming and cultivation:

> but in the sweat of your brow, says God, you shall for the future procure for yourself the necessities for life and sustenance.

Therefore, before this change, or curse, the Earth brought forth spontaneous crops and fruits, without sowing and without labor: otherwise this curse would have effected nothing new, and would have changed nothing in the nature of things. Furthermore, it is evident from other sources that it was not merely some small region, or a few acres of land—such as a garden is—that uniquely possessed this fertility and the other privileges of both soil and sky: but rather the entire habitable world, in the first state of things. For what if Adam had remained innocent? What place would there have been for his descendants within the walls of a single garden? Or if you shut them all in there, like featherless chicks in a nest, what would become of the other vast tracts of the great Earth? Would they have stood empty, deserted, and without inhabitants? Great is the force of habit and preconceived opinion upon human minds. ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things
<page-num>285</page-num>

...whether he used a popular or a philosophical style. A popular one, I say—not a fabulous one, although that name might be used if we were dealing with a foreign <note>original: *exotico*</note> author. Of fables, some are pure fictions, through and through; others, however, are based on a foundation of truth but are decorated with additions and external ornament. Furthermore, there are certain narrations in which truth lies beneath—not in every tiny detail <note>original: *apicibus*, literally "the points of letters"</note>, but regarding the substance of the matter and the intent of the author. This is seen in the parable of **Christ** regarding **Lazarus and the Rich Man**, and in many things told about the **Day of Judgment**, as far as the outer shell <note>original: *corticem*</note> and exterior form are concerned.

I believe narrations of this kind should be called not fables, but sometimes parables, and sometimes **popular hypotheses** <note>original Greek: *ὑποθέσεις δημώδεις* (hypotheseis demodeis)</note>. If you place the narrative currently at hand in this class, I will not be offended, as the name and honor of the author remain safe. Let us, if you please, examine some points of this narrative.

Regarding the first point, I have always held the temporal origin of the human race as certain and beyond doubt; and that it occurred five millennia ago, or more, according to the faith of **Sacred Chronology**. But from what material the first human was made, male or female, is not so easy to know, nor does it matter so much. If God willed to fashion <note>original: *extundere*, literally "to beat or hammer out"</note> woman from the rib of **Adam**, the material does indeed seem less suitable; but from any wood, or any stone, or any substance, God is able to shape a woman. 

Here the curious ask whether this rib was superfluous to **Adam**, and beyond the number required for a proper body? If not, then with it removed, **Adam** would have been maimed and deprived of a necessary part of himself. I say necessary, for we suppose there is nothing superfluous in the fabric of the human body; nor can any bone be snatched away without a defect of the whole, or some injury to its integrity. But if you say the other—namely, that it was a superfluous...

### Archaeologiæ Philosophicæ: or,
<page-num>286</page-num>

...indeed, and that this rib was useless to Adam: and that on one side he had thirteen ribs, while on the other only twelve. This, they say, is like a monster: as if the first man had been made with three feet or three hands, or had more eyes or other limbs than the use or integrity of the human body requires. *But all things were made by number, weight, and measure from the beginning.* <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20, a common philosophical principle in the 17th century suggesting that God’s creation is mathematically perfect.</note>

I do not settle this dispute: what makes me more anxious is, how from a single rib the entire mass of a female body could be constructed? For a rib does not equal a hundredth, or even a thousandth, part of the whole body. And if you say the rest of the matter was taken from elsewhere, it would be truer to say that Eve was formed from that other matter—whatever it was—than from Adam’s rib.

<margin>Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *mor. Nev.*</note>, part 2, chapter 30. Genesis 1:27.</margin>
I know that the **Rabbinic Teachers** explain the whole matter differently. Specifically, they say the first human was two-bodied, male and female; clinging to one another at the sides, or, as others prefer, by their backs. But they say God cut these apart, and gave the Eve so torn away to Adam as a bride. **Plato** has a very similar fable in the *Symposium* concerning the first **Androgynous** human, who was then split into male and female halves. Finally, others conjecture—which is not improbable—that **Moses** explained the origin of the female in this way so that he might instill mutual love between the male and female, as if they were parts of the same Whole; and by that reasoning, he might more effectively recommend the institution of marriage (by which they are united again), as if it were rooted in nature itself. But I, leaving these things behind, hasten to others.

The second article deals with the *Garden of God in Eden*: irrigated by four rivers, which arise from one source. Some want this **Garden of God** in Moses to be the same as the <margin>*Symposium*</margin> *Garden of Jove* <note>original Greek: *Διὸς κῆπον* (Dios kepon)</note> in **Plato**; and that there is the same history or allegory <note>original: *allegoriam*</note> in both places...

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things
<page-num>287</page-num>

...allegory <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "allegoriam" from the previous page's catchword.</note> **according to certain secret discourses of Moses**, or *Following the secret meanings of Moses*: <note>original: "κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους λόγους Μωσέως" and "Secundum arcanos sensus Mosis"</note> says **Eusebius**. <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 12, chapter 11.</margin> And I embrace this secret meaning concerning the **Garden of Eden** all the more willingly because there is no place on earth where all the signs and characteristics of that Garden truly fit; for, to say nothing of the perpetually clear sky and the spontaneous fertility of the place, there is a most wearying and as yet unfinished controversy among theologians and geographers, both ancient and modern, regarding the rivers alone. These rivers are called by **Moses** *Pishon, Gishon, Hiddekel,* and *Perath*: which ancient authors interpret as the *Ganges, Nile, Tigris,* and *Euphrates*. And that, in my opinion, is correct. For it seems Moses intended nothing else than to bring down to water this Garden four of the most celebrated and fertile rivers on Earth.

But, you will say, these four rivers do not arise from the same place, or from the same head; correctly so, nor do any other four named by the various Interpreters. This objection will therefore hold weight everywhere, against both modern writers and the Ancients alike. Indeed, even if you restrict these rivers to just two—as some do, namely to the *Euphrates and Tigris*—neither of those two rivers comes from the same source or from the same spring. But in truth, it is an evasion, not an explanation, to reduce many rivers to few, contrary to the history of **Moses**, merely so they may more conveniently be traced back to the same origin. These are the words of Moses: <margin>Genesis 2:10</margin> *“Now a river went out of Eden to water the Garden; and from there it divided and became four heads. The name of the first is Pishon, etc.”* From this it is clearly evident that, either at the entrance or the exit of the garden, there were four rivers: and those four rivers broke forth from the same source in **Eden**. And please do not say that only two arose from that **Edenic** source, and the remaining two arise from the **Tigris** and **Euphrates** at the point where they branch out near the sea and are split into two paths, as it were. This in no way matches the words of **Moses**. Furthermore, **Moses** mentions the **Pishon** and **Gishon** in the first place, and then the **Tigris** and **Euphrates**, as if they were lesser rivers. You, on the contrary, would want the former to be derived from the latter, as if they were secondary rivers. This is a manifest distortion of the historical narrative.

But to cut through these difficulties, or controversies, regarding the origins and beds of the rivers of **Paradise**, you will perhaps say finally that the heads and courses of the rivers were changed by the **Flood** <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>; and that it can no longer be established where they once emerged, or what lands they traversed. So be it; I feel the same way as you—provided you admit that a breaking and disruption of the **Earth**, such as we suppose, occurred during the **Flood**. But from a simple inundation, or an overflow of waters, a change of this kind could not have arisen. Furthermore, according to which **Geography**, or **Hydrography** <note>The science of mapping bodies of water.</note>, would you have **Moses** describe these rivers: the pre-flood or the post-flood? If you take the latter, no significant change of the lands has happened since the time of **Moses** or the **Flood**. If you take the former, you make the **Mosaic** description superfluous and useless for investigating the location of **Paradise**. 

Finally, it can hardly be conceived that any rivers at all—these or others—existed from the very origin of the **Earth**, whether you look at their waters or their beds. Riverbeds are usually formed gradually and by long-term attrition <note>Erosion caused by the flow of water over time.</note>. But if they had been made by digging out and piling up the earth—like ditches and furrows—there would have been great mounds and heaps of earth everywhere on both banks of the river, or at least on one. This, however, seems clearly for- <note>The text ends mid-word, likely "fortuitum" (fortuitous or accidental).</note>

...let us grant; for they often run through plains, and the banks of rivers are equal to, or as high as, the adjacent fields. Moreover, where would the water for these channels come from at the first foundation of the **Earth**? If you say that when the bed of the **Ocean** was made on the third day, the channels of the rivers were also made—and just as the greatest part of the waters of the **Abyss** <note>The "Abyss" refers to the vast subterranean reservoir of water that many early modern theorists believed lay beneath the Earth's crust.</note> fell into the depths of the sea, so the remaining parts flowed into these river channels and formed the first rivers. So be it. But besides the fact that such water would be salty, just like sea water, there would be no perennial springs to feed these rivers. Therefore, once the first river or stream had flowed away, since there would be no more water following from behind, these rivers—or these water-gatherings—would have immediately dried up. I say there were no perennial springs because whether springs arise from rain or from the sea, they could not have formed in such a short time. Not from rain, for it had not yet rained; nor could the waters of the **Abyss** run down from the most inland places to the sea, then return through the bowels of the earth, seeking out new paths, and rise up filtered to the sources of the rivers, all in the space of a single day. But enough regarding the rivers; let us proceed to the rest.

But what are we to believe **Eve** knew of it? If she had considered it a mute animal, the very act of it speaking would have terrified the woman and driven her away from any conversation. But if the serpent was naturally talkative and a speaker from the beginning, and lost its speech because of this crime—because it had corrupted the piety and faith of **Eve** with its flatteries—**Moses** <note>The traditional biblical author of Genesis.</note> would by no means have remained silent about this kind of punishment. ...licking the dust, had substituted it in its place. Furthermore, would you have it that only the genus of serpents, or all the beasts of the field, were vocal in Paradise, just as the trees were once said to be in the grove of Dodona? <note>original: "nemore Dodonæo"; a reference to the ancient Greek oracle of Zeus at Dodona, where the rustling of oak leaves was interpreted as the speech of the gods.</note> If all were vocal, what did the others commit that they should lose the use of their tongues? If only the genus of serpents enjoyed this privilege, how could such a foul animal, and one so utterly alien to the human form, deserve the grace and benefit of speech above all others? Finally, since all conversation implies the use of reason, whatever animal you grant speech to, you thereby constitute that animal as a rational being.

But I easily believe that the defenders of the literal sense will solve this knot differently. They say, of course, that the Devil, or an evil demon, was hidden within this Serpent, and that he, using the mouth and organs of this animal, addressed the woman with a voice that seemed human. But on what witness, on what author's authority, is this said? The literal word of Moses—of which they are so tenacious—does not claim this. What else does the text seem to imply but to attribute the deception of Eve entirely to the natural cunning of this animal? For thus Moses prefaces it: *Now the serpent was more cunning than any beast of the field which the Lord God had made.* Then he adds: *He said to the woman, has God really said, etc.* Furthermore, if Eve had heard an animal naturally mute speak by the power of some <term>evil spirit</term> <note>original: "Cacodæmonis"; from the Greek "kakos" (bad) and "daimon" (spirit).</note>, she would have fled from the monster in terror. She, on the other hand, receives him familiarly: they carry on conversations, they chat, they argue, as if nothing strange or new had happened. If you say that all this proceeded from the ignorance and weakness of the woman, it surely would have been just for good Angels to have come to the aid of the ignorant and weak woman from the other side. Just spectators of human affairs would hardly have tolerated such an unequal contest. For what if, by the trickery of an evil Demon—who is all-knowing and most well-versed in managing affairs—she was conquered...

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...was she a defenseless woman, who had not yet seen the sun rising or setting; newly brought into the light, and inexperienced in all things? Surely such a beloved person <note>original: "charum caput"; literally "dear head," a Latin idiom for a person held in high esteem</note>, who held the salvation of the entire human race bound to her own, deserved—I say, deserved—Angelic protection.

But you will say the woman should have been careful not to violate the law sanctioned by the penalty of death. *On the day you eat of it, you shall die: You and yours:* <note>original: "Quo die comedetis, moriemini: Vos & vestri"</note> so the Law stood. To die! What sort of thing is this? says the ignorant maiden, who had never seen anything dead—not even a flower. She had not yet perceived even the image of death, such as Sleep, or the darkness of night, either with her eyes or in her mind. Furthermore, what you add regarding her descendants and their punishment is not expressed in the Law. No laws should be twisted or distorted, least of all those involving punishment.

Regarding the punishment of the Serpent, there is also no small question. If the Devil did the whole thing under the appearance of a serpent—or if he compelled the serpent to act or suffer those things—why does the serpent pay the penalty for a crime committed by the Devil? Then, as to the mode and form of the punishment inflicted on the serpent—namely, that henceforth it should *go prone upon its belly*—what this might mean is not easy to explain. One would hardly say that the serpent had previously been upright, or that it walked in the manner of four-legged animals. But if indeed it was carried prone on its belly from the beginning, like modern snakes, it might seem absurd that what it always had by nature should be imposed or attributed to this animal as a punishment and for the penalty of a specific act. But enough regarding the Woman and the Serpent; let us move on to the Trees.

I understand there to be two trees here, in the middle of the Garden: the *Tree of Life*, and the *Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil*. The Tree of *Life* is so called, as they say, because it was intended to give a very long life to humans. One thing remains to be considered: in how very little time all these things are narrated to have been performed—in the space of a single day, or perhaps half a day. Theologians <term>Theologians: Burnet refers to the "Literalists" of his day who insisted the Earth was created in six literal 24-hour days</term> suppose that Adam consummated his marriage with Eve on the first night. They then say that if Eve, while still innocent, had conceived her firstborn, she would have likewise given birth to an innocent child, free from all stain of original sin. From this, she would have also preserved her offspring—as far as the Father is concerned—untouched by the same evil. But there is no such offspring, immaculate or even semi-pure; we are all infected by the same stain and suffer from the same disease <note>original: "morbo"; referring to the theological concept of Original Sin</note>. Therefore, we must conclude that all these things were carried out on the sixth day of creation, before they went to sleep or shared the embraces of the marriage bed <note>original: "genialis lecti amplexus"</note>.

Yet how many, and how great, are the things that must be crowded into this one day! Let us repeat these briefly, if you please. On that day, God created all cattle, all wild beasts, and all creeping things; finally, He created Adam. And when He had created all these, He brought every kind of animal before Adam so that, according to the nature of each, he might impose names upon them. Within the space of a single day, we read that all these things were accomplished: great and many-sided affairs. But I burn with grief when I see everything overturned and thrown into disorder in such a tiny amount of time; and the whole nature of things, scarcely yet composed and adorned, rushing to ruin and being deformed before the setting of the first Sun. In the morning of that day, God said, ***All things were good***; by evening, all things are accursed. How fleeting is the glory of created things! A work labored over for six days, and that by an almighty hand, an infamous Beast destroyed in as many hours.

This is the account of things and times in the history of the first man and of Paradise. I am, however, angry with Celsus, who calls this narrative an "old wives' tale," or <term>a certain myth told as if to old women</term> <note>original Greek: μῦθόν τινα ὡς γραυσὶ διηγούμενον; Celsus was a 2nd-century critic of Christianity who mocked the literal interpretation of Genesis</note>. From this you see that in the first centuries of the Christian Church, in which Celsus lived—and even among the Jews before the birth of Christ—the more reasonable interpreters retreated from the literal letter of the Mosaic narrative.

That which certainly seems most serious and harsh in this narrative is that God is said to have punished, or rather destroyed, the human race on account of a trivial matter, perpetrated through the flightiness of a woman’s disposition. For this reason, some feel—and I do not disagree with them—that Moses assigned such a great punishment to a seemingly slight sin so that he might secure force and authority for his Laws, which often decree heavy penalties for matters that are frequently minute and neither good nor bad by their own nature. For who would not fear to violate even the smallest command that comes in the name of God, if the eating of a single forbidden fruit brought such ruin upon the human race? But concerning these and other points of the Mosaic narrative, let each person enjoy their own opinion, provided they do not undermine the foundation. By "foundation" here I mean: the Doctrine of the temporal origin of the human race and of this Earth; the degeneration of both; and that humanity is to be redeemed by the seed of the woman. This Mosaic **Cosmogony** <note>A theory or story regarding the origin of the universe.</note>, therefore, which is held to be more ancient than all the others we mentioned before, we must weigh more diligently, and settle or dissolve these disputes through a friendly interpretation, so that in the meantime truth—which is of equal concern to both sides—may be preserved safe and sound.

Indeed, the *Hexaëmeron* <note>original: "Hexaëmeron"; referring to the "six days" of creation described in Genesis.</note> and the *Theory* <note>Referring to Burnet's own work, "The Sacred Theory of the Earth."</note> agree in the first threads of things, so to speak: because both suppose *Chaos* as the underlying matter of the world. They also agree in the general order, in that they establish the inanimate world first, then the animate. It must therefore be observed first, what form of the world and what limits the *Hexaëmeron* proposed for itself. It is well known that two systems of the world are debated among the learned and the common people: one of which has the Sun for its center, and the other, the Earth. It is asked, therefore, which system the *Mosaic Hexaëmeron* relies upon, this one or that. It is certain that Moses began his work from the Earth, as if it were the base or foundation of the entire machine; and that he did not bring forth the Sun until the fourth day, as he says, with the *Earth* and *sea* already constructed and finished. Thus, the Sun was not the center of the whole work, since it did not exist until after the work was half-finished. Furthermore, both the Sun and the remaining stars are presented by Moses as being created for the use of the Earth, like servant bodies, so that they might measure for us the days, and years, and other seasons. According to the other hypothesis <note>The Copernican or Heliocentric system.</note>, however, the Sun and the **Fixed Stars** <note>original: "Fixæ"; stars that appear not to move relative to one another.</note> are not only the largest bodies, but also the most noble: the primary parts of the entire universe, and the foundations of a massive structure.

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.

It is clear, therefore, for both reasons, that *Moses* followed the common system: that which pleases the people, which flatters the senses, and which is believed and understood—or seems to be understood—by the majority. In this matter, he rightly consulted the public welfare, and neglecting philosophy, he adhered to more serious counsels and reasons of greater importance. <note>Burnet suggests that Moses prioritized religious and social stability over scientific accuracy in his writing.</note>

Secondly, since it is evident that the Earth was the center of this *Mosaic Chaos*, we must next ask how far upward this blind and confused mass extended. Indeed, the *Hexaëmeron* <note>original: "Hexaëmeron"; referring to the "six days" of creation described in Genesis.</note> seems to suppose that this *Chaos* filled and occupied the entire Universe, however large it may be: all the heavens and the ethereal regions spread out in every direction. Furthermore, it suggests that the brightest stars were composed of this chaotic matter, and that none existed before the rise and birth of our Earth. This is what the literal sense of the *Hexaëmeron* seems to present; but it is resisted by the nature of things and by philosophical <note>scientific</note> reasons.

It is well established that the Fixed Stars <term>Fixed Stars: The celestial bodies that appear not to move relative to each other, as opposed to planets; here recognized as distant suns.</term> are fiery bodies; nor do they all reside upon the same surface, but some are more remote from the Earth than others, and are more deeply immersed in the heavens. Therefore, there is no common navel <note>original: "umbilicum"; a central point or hub.</note> for them all. At the very least, it is contrary to the nature of things and to all reason that our Earth—a blind and sordid particle of the universe, smaller than any of the Fixed Stars in both mass and dignity—should be, I say, the heart of this immense body, its most noble and vital part. I say again with indignation, that it can hardly be said or thought, without reproach or insult to both the work and the Workmaster <note>The Creator.</note>, that this Earth—the dregs and refuse of nature—is the head of all things and as it were the first-born of every creature. Furthermore, if that terrestrial Chaos had been extended through the immense totality of things, and the Earth were the sole center toward which all the thicker parts flowed together: that Earth...

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

it happens that both the **Angelic world** and the **super-firmamentary world** <note>original: "super-firmamentarius"; the regions of the universe located above the visible sky or firmament</note> are said to be established before the **Mosaic world** <note>original: "mundum Mosaicum"; the world as described in the creation account of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses</note>; in these words: *Although He also established Angels in the higher parts—that is, even above the firmament itself—arranged spiritual powers, placed Thrones and Powers in charge, and founded many other immense spaces of the heavens, etc.* This makes it appear that this world of ours is more likely God’s **most recent** work, rather than His only or unique one. Regarding this passage, Pamelius <note>Jacobus Pamelius (1536–1587), a Flemish theologian and editor of early Christian texts</note> remarks: *This was the opinion not only of Novatian, but also of the Blessed Jerome, and indeed of all the Greeks: That the Angels were established first (that is, before every creature of our world).* Finally, Cassian notes that this was the common opinion of Catholics in his time, namely at the beginning of the fifth century. Concerning this, he says, *none of the faithful doubt.* <margin>Book 8. Conference chapter 7.</margin> And when he had explained this dogma more fully, he adds, *There is no doubt that God created all those heavenly powers before that temporal beginning in Genesis.*

And to ensure there is even less doubt regarding this **pre-existence of the Angels**, we have the words of the Lord to Job, chapter 38, verse 4, etc.: *Where were you when I laid the foundations of the Earth: when the morning stars praised me and all the Sons of God shouted for joy?* To which Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century deacon of Alexandria and biblical commentator</note> adds, <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τούτου δῆλον, ὅτι πρῶτοι οἱ Ἄγγελοι τοῦ κόσμου γεγένηνται"</note> *It is manifest from this place that the Angels were established first in the creation of the world.* It is evident, of course, from these words that before the foundations of the Earth were cast, the Angels existed and sang praises to God during the first construction of our world. Furthermore, if you take the **morning stars** literally, it is clear from here that the Stars and the heavens preceded the foundation of our Earth. Moreover, Jerome extracts the **pre-worldly existence** of intellectual beings from those places in the sacred scriptures where something is said to happen "before eternal times" <note>original Greek: "πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων"</note>, as in *Titus 1:2* and *2 Timothy 1:9*, or "before the ages" <note>original Greek: "πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων"</note>, as in 1 Corinthians 2:7.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

...that **Angelic matter**, or the **vehicles of the Angels** <note>original: "Angelorum vehicula"; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the "chariot" or subtle body that carries the soul</note>, preceded the origin of the **Earth** <note>original: "Telluris"</note>, as the **Greek Fathers** philosophized: all matter, in some way, preceded [the Earth]. Indeed, the arrangement and ordering of that matter, according to its various parts, regions, and forms, took place in different ways and at different times, according to the prescription of **Providence**.

Thus far we have dealt with the pre-existence of Angels, and of matter itself insofar as it is connected with the Angels, based on the authority of the Fathers. Let us now return to the nature of things and the visible world; for there is no lack of further arguments in the corporeal world which confirm this same antiquity of Matter. These arguments sufficiently testify that the **Mosaic Epoch** <note>The biblical timeline of creation beginning in Genesis</note>—which spans roughly six thousand years—does not encompass the origin of the entire universe, but only the ages of our Earth and the time of its formation from its own **Chaos**. If we survey the phenomena of the heavens again, and the dances of the Stars—both the **Wandering** <note>original: "Errantium"; the planets</note> and the **Fixed** <note>original: "Inerrantium"; the distant stars</note>—we will easily believe that such a numerous progeny, worthy of a better parent, is not the offspring of a single Earthly Chaos. Nor could they suffer their ages and histories to be enclosed within the narrow barriers of so short a time.

Let us consider, if you please, what is now established for everyone: that the Earth is a **Planet**; and that there are many Planets besides the Earth, of the same nature and similar matter and form. It is probable that all of these had the same mode and principle of origin: namely, that each one rose out of its own **Chaos**. Since the Earth was made, however, we have seen the birth of no new Planet; and therefore, either all are older than the Earth, or they are of the same age. If the former, the matter is settled; but if you make them of the same age, it will be necessary to suppose as many Chaoses as there are primary Planets. For it is established that **Jupiter**, for example, which rotates its own **satellites** <note>A reference to the Moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo earlier in the 17th century</note>, is a center for itself, and does not

...depend in any way on our Earth; just as neither do the others, except for the Moon.

Furthermore, the **Fixed Stars** <term>Stellæ Fixæ; stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets</term> seem to be older than the **Planets**, and each one is the center of its own orb or **vortex** <note>original: "vorticis"; a reference to Cartesian physics, which proposed that celestial bodies are carried by vast, swirling whirlpools of subtle matter</note>. Thus, as many systems are to be established in the heavens as there are Fixed Stars. Since these are the greatest in number and mass, they swallow up this tiny point of **Earth** <note>original: "Telluris"</note> as if it were less than nothing. Friends of the heavens, or any fair judges of God's works, will easily grant that the origins of the stars are not to be sought from Earth, nor are they indebted to it.

Finally, it is probable that the **Planets** were once **Fixed Stars**, and the Earth itself should be counted in that same rank and order. You will not easily explain the origins of the planets by any other hypothesis—at least if they have fire at their **Center**, which is highly probable. Furthermore, we have seen the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"</note> with its face sometimes covered by dense spots; and we read that for several days it has appeared pale, dark, and as if struggling in the very grip of death. Now, he who falls ill can die: and what happens to one can happen to others of the same kind (and all Fixed Stars are of the same kind). Therefore, the Fixed Stars are **extinguishable** <note>original: "extinguibiles"; capable of being put out like a flame</note>. A Fixed Star is extinguished when, covered by a thick crust of spots which it cannot break through, it degenerates into a dark and opaque body—which is exactly what a Planet is.

Lastly, the **new stars** <note>Referring to "Novae" or "Supernovae," such as those observed by Tycho Brahe in 1572 and Johannes Kepler in 1604, which proved the heavens were not unchanging</note> which have appeared in the heavens in recent years had no connection or kinship with the Earth regarding their origins. Nor do **Comets** have any such link; although for some they are of doubtful and difficult explanation, they seem to me to be nothing other than the **corpses of Fixed Stars**, so to speak—not yet buried, not yet laid to rest. They wander through various regions of the sky like **Shadows** <note>original: "Umbrarum"; often used to refer to ghosts or spirits of the dead</note>, until they find suitable seats; Which [found,]

These and similar celestial phenomena can hardly be reconciled with a **six-thousand-year epoch** <note>original: "Epocham sexmillennem"; the traditional chronological age of the Earth based on a literal reading of the Bible</note> while keeping the laws of nature intact. Rather, it must be admitted that the origin of our **Earth** <note>original: "Telluris"</note> and of the entire **Universe**—whether **Intellectual** or **Corporeal**—was not the same, nor did they begin at the same time. Nor should it seem strange that **Moses** did not make this distinction, or that he did not treat the origin of the Universe separately from that of our **sublunary world** <term>Sublunary world; literally "below the moon," a term used in ancient and early modern science to describe the Earthly realm of change and decay, as opposed to the "unchanging" heavens</term>. For the common people do not make these distinctions, nor do they value them separately. The greatest part of men considers the rest of nature and the Universe to be a kind of appendix to our World or Earth—something that has no value in itself, but is stitched on for the use of the human race and to serve our needs. Therefore, the most wise **Lawgiver** <note>original: "Legislator"; referring to Moses as the author of the first five books of the Bible</note> rightly left that task to the philosophers, so that when the human intellect had matured through age, experience, and observation, they might arrange the works of God in a different order, one adapted to divine perfections and the nature of things. But enough on this chapter; let us proceed to other matters.

Thirdly, Moses mentions in his **Six Days of Creation** <term>Hexaëmero; from the Greek for "six days," referring to the creation narrative in Genesis</term> a famous phenomenon that appears nowhere else in nature. God is said to have spent an entire day creating these waters or arranging them in their places—no less time, indeed, than he spent creating the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and the whole host of the heavens! These magnificent bodies deservedly claim twenty-four hours of labor, but we begrudge that so much work was devoted to something so obscure and unknown. Come then, let us ask—

# The Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

We seek these invisible waters: in what place do they reside, or did they once reside? **Moses** says they were placed above the **Firmament** <note>original: "Firmamentum"; in ancient cosmology, this was the solid "expanse" or vault of the sky that separated the Earthly realm from the heavens</note>; yet the Sun and the rest of the stars are also said to be in the Firmament. By that reasoning, he places those waters above all the **Stars**, or the starry heaven; nevertheless, he establishes the **Earth** as the center of all these things. Since waters are heavier than celestial matter, and even heavier than the air itself, how can they remain in that highest place, supported by no intermediate bodies of a thicker substance? 

**Saint Augustine**—who, in treating this very argument, advises us with such gravity and purpose—forbids us from simply resorting to divine omnipotence in this matter.

<margin>Book 2 of The Literal Meaning of Genesis</margin>
*And let no one say that, according to the omnipotence of God, for whom all things are possible, we ought to believe that waters as heavy as those we know and feel are spread over the celestial body in which the stars are located. For now, it is proper for us to seek how God established the natures of things according to His scriptures, and not what He might wish to work within them, or from them, as a miracle of His omnipotence.* <note>original: "non autem quod ipse in iis, aut ex iis, ad miraculum omnipotentiæ suæ velit operari"</note>

This harmonizes with what he taught us more generally elsewhere:

<margin>City of God, Book 7, Chapter 30</margin>
*God so administers all things which He created, that He allows them to exercise and perform their own proper motions.* Let the judgment be according to these rules.

Furthermore, if such waters (of whatever kind they might be) existed above the highest heavens, why would it matter for the common people to know this mystery? It is alien to the custom and purpose of **Moses** to record invisible and hidden things, or knowledge that is of no use, in his <term>Hexaëmeron</term> <note>The "Six Days of Creation"; from the Greek "hex" (six) and "hemera" (day)</note>. This work only follows the phenomena of the visible world, insofar as they strike the eyes of all people and lead them to desire the Creator. Those things which appear nowhere require no author and no explanation.

# Philosophical Archaeology: or,

Therefore, they establish a double firmament, an upper and a lower: the former, in which the stars reside; the latter, in which vapors, clouds, and meteors drift. Namely, the space that lies between the Earth and the middle region of the air, they call the **Firmament**. 

But according to this interpretation, what is it, I ask, that God created on the second day? A little bit of space? This interval that exists between us and the clouds? But that interval existed before; stretching out not only to the middle region of the air, but all the way to the highest heaven—whether you suppose the **primordial Light** or **Chaos** was placed in between. What then is the point, or what is the meaning, of "creating" an interval on the second day which already existed on the first? Nor is any solid barrier <note>original: "sepimentum"; literally a hedge or fence, here referring to a physical partition in the sky</note> now admitted within the fluid heavens.

But to further refute this interpretation, let us hear the words of **Moses**: *On the second day,* he says, *God said, "Let there be a Firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters."* <note>Genesis 1:6</note> Namely, the upper ones from the lower ones. Therefore, these waters existed—both the upper and the lower—before this "inter-aqueous" Firmament was made. For a boundary, or a separation, belongs to things already in existence. 

Tell me, therefore, what were these upper waters, or in what places were they located, before this separation was made? They seem to have been a continuous mass before, and were divided in two by this structural framing. But rain did not exist before, nor did clouds. Therefore, if you wish these to be considered the "upper waters," the interpretation does not match the Mosaic words. Finally, it would be absurd <note>original: "praeposterum"; literally "backwards" or "preposterous"</note> to establish clouds before the Earth; or to make so much of these coagulations of vapor—which are formed and perish every single day—that they should occupy a sixth part of the great God’s work.

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

The matter comes to this: the common people do not grasp the natural generation of rain through condensed vapors; instead, they believe rain is sent from heaven by divine power, or directly from God. So that **Moses** might favor this popular opinion, he established a common reservoir of Waters above the heavens: so that God, at his pleasure, might release or withhold the rain by opening or closing the floodgates <note>original: "Cataractis"</note>. This seems to me to be the mind and purpose of the sacred author regarding the supra-celestial waters. And in this way, the dignity of **Moses** is best preserved if, whenever there is a departure from physical truth, we suppose it is done "according to condescension" <note>original: "κατὰ συγκάταβασιν" (kata synkatabasin); a theological term meaning God or a prophet adjusts the truth to the limited capacity of the human audience</note>, by accommodating his **Cosmogony** <term>Cosmopœïam: the story of the world's creation</term> to the strengths and needs of the people.

But what kind of Light? Light without a source, without a fountain-head. Yet Light, if we are to philosophize, flows from some center where the heart and principle of its motion reside. Furthermore, in this **Cosmogony**, Light appears before any distinction of the heavens into spheres or vortices. Moreover, according to the literal word, God seems to have paused his work during the night, as men are accustomed to do: but I do not see how the other **Hemisphere** (celestial or terrestrial) could be completed if there were any interruption in the work, and if God did not act except where there was light. However, the common people do not care for these minutiae, nor do they dream of the **Antipodes** <term>Antipodas: people living on the opposite side of the globe</term> or the other hemisphere: rather, they conceive of the world like a Tent, whose roof is the heaven, and the flat surface of the Earth its foundation.

However, if you suppose they flowed down rapidly like rivers, from some Mediterranean <note>In this context, meaning "inland" or "middle of the land" rather than the specific sea</note> places to the sea, it would be a journey of several days.

## Archaeological Philosophy: or,
->The Ancient Doctrine concerning the Origins of Things<-

...were performed in these two days <note>Referring to the fifth and sixth days of creation, where animals and humans were brought forth</note>: produced from the waters and from the Earth. Today, the process of assembling the bodies of animals proceeds much more slowly; nor do I wonder at that, since they are of such great craftsmanship. But while the body of every animal and even the smallest creature is so accurately formed and composed, I will never be led to believe that the body of the Earth—the common Mother of all—was as deformed, gaping, and ruinous from the origin of the world as it is today. But this I mention only in passing.

Saint *Augustine* maintained that all these things, which are called the works of the six days, were created in a single moment; and that *Moses* divided them into classes and different times so that he might better assist the imagination of the people in conceiving the origins of things. It seems to me that God produced all substance—whether intellectual or corporeal—in a single moment and by an indivisible act, out of nothing. In that sense, *Augustine* did not miss the mark. But we are not dealing here (according to the truth of the matter) with universal substance, but only with the terrestrial world; nor with its creation, but its formation. Regarding the creation of all things from nothing, or from no pre-existing matter, there can be no doubt; nor can it be doubted that this was not from eternity. (For an eternal creature cannot be conceived by us). However, I have never dared to prescribe a limit of only six thousand years—a rather brief epoch—to the divine Creation. That, along with many other things, I more willingly leave among the **mysteries of God** <note>original: "arcana Dei"</note>.

These briefly noted observations on the **Genesis** of things proposed by **Moses** seem to argue that it was not the sacred author’s intention to explain the origin of the world according to **physical truth** <note>original: "veritatem physicam"</note>; for that would have been useless to a people unlearned in philosophy. Rather, his purpose was to propose the origins of things using a method that was easy to conceive, and which would instill piety in the minds of men and the worship of the true divinity.

Since each of the ancient nations—the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Chaldeans, and others—had their own <term>Cosmogonies<gloss>Stories or theories concerning the birth and origin of the universe</gloss></term>, usually placed at the beginning of their histories or their theology; Moses thought it appropriate to prefix or weave into the laws and institutions he was to write for the Israelites, not only the origin of his own nation, but also that of the entire world. And in order to uproot the foundations of idolatry, he did not present the heavens, the sun, the moon, and the stars—the greatest deities of other nations—as eternal, nor as created for their own sake: but as serving this <term>sublunary world<gloss>The region of the universe below the moon, specifically the Earth and its atmosphere</gloss></term> and human uses *.

...we are led, out of love for the truth and by the weight of arguments, to deliver a judgment not based on long-held opinion. However, I will explain the matter as briefly as I can, bringing forth arguments from both sides.

First, the adversaries of this interpretation say that **Creation** is one thing, and the **Formation** of things already created is another. They argue that Moses speaks of the Creation of things out of nothing <note>original Latin: "ex nihilo"</note>, the epoch of which he established a few millennia ago; whereas we interpret that whole process as the *Formation* of things, or the arrangement of "confused matter" <note>original: "materiâ confusâ" — referring to the primordial chaos</note> into a habitable world. We accept this framing of the question; but it cannot be proved from the words of Moses, nor from any other source, what is being claimed. The word *bara* <note>original Hebrew: ברא</note> among the Hebrews, *ktizein* <note>original Greek: κτίζειν</note> among the Greeks, and *creare* among the Latins, do not have that specific power <note>Burnet is arguing that these verbs for "create" can also mean "to build" or "to transform" pre-existing material</note>. Nor in any language, as far as I know, is the production of things out of nothing expressed by a single word. The force and usage of the said words in those three languages are well enough known: and specifically regarding the Hebrew, and its usage in the sacred scriptures, it is admitted by everyone that the word *bara* is applied to other actions or effects than the primary production of things. Therefore, nothing can be proven from that word. Nor, I say, can this objection be sustained from elsewhere, whether from the sacred scriptures or from reason.

<margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin>

The word *framed* <note>original Greek: "Κατηρτίσθαι" (katērtisthai) — also meaning "adapted," "joined together," or "constructed"</note> does not signify the production of a thing out of nothing. Therefore, the Apostle does not say the worlds were framed "not from things that *exist*" <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἐξ ὄντων" (mē ex ontōn)</note>, but "not from things which *appear*" <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἐκ φαινοµένων" (mē ek phainomenōn)</note>. "From things not appearing": either because they had already vanished, having been changed into another form; or because they were once dark and invisible <note>original Greek: "ἀόρατα" (aorata)</note>. ...you might say, or were they accommodated to the understanding of the common people? If in so many and such great matters the Holy Scripture does not shrink or fear to depart from the truth, why should **Moses** not have been allowed to use the same liberty in handing down the **Origins** of things? It was the custom not only among the Sacred Writers, but also among the philosophers of the Nations <note>original: "Gentium philosophos" — referring to non-Jewish/Gentile thinkers like the Greeks</note>, to instruct the people—"the many and common sort of man" <note>original Greek: τὸν πολὺν καὶ δημώδη ἄνθρωπον (*ton polun kai dēmōdē anthrōpon*)</note>, as they say—or even "neophyte" <note>original Greek: νεοφύτους (*neophytous*)</note> disciples, in a coarse or simplified manner. We have often noted this twofold method of teaching among the Philosophers in the preceding book, following that saying of **Parmenides** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his work on the nature of reality</note>: "philosophy is twofold, one according to truth, the other according to common opinion" <note>original Greek: διπλῆν εἶναι τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, τὴν μὲν κατ’ ἀλήθειαν, τὴν δὲ κατὰ δόξαν (*diplēn einai tēn philosophian, tēn men kat’ alētheian, tēn de kata doxan*)</note>. *That there is a twofold way of philosophizing: one according to the truth, the other according to common opinion.* But the Ancients did not hide the truth in only one way: sometimes through symbolic, parabolic, or otherwise figurative speech; sometimes through popular and common language; sometimes by explaining things "according to the divine" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸ θεῖον (*kata to theion*)</note> or "according to providence" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν πρόνοιαν (*kata tēn pronoian*)</note>, rather than according to the laws of nature. We have examples of all these methods in the sacred books; therefore, it is no wonder that **Moses** followed one or another of them in explaining the natural world and its origin.

We said above that in sacred matters, some things are more sacred than others; and as far as **truth** is concerned, we follow, conceal, or disguise it according to the weight of the reasons that depend upon it. To what honest or pious man is it ever a matter of religious scruple to mislead or deceive the sick, children, or those of unsound mind for their own benefit? ### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...and should the unteachable common people be treated in the same way? Certainly, when the situation demands it and for the sake of attaining a greater good. To use evil deceit to another's harm is a sin; but for the sake of the common good, and to help the weak, we deceive and are deceived without guilt. There is something more sacred and inviolable in the principle of the Good than in the principle of the Truth; when both cannot be reconciled, the latter yields to the former <note>Burnet is arguing that "The Good" (moral benefit) takes precedence over "The Truth" (scientific accuracy) in religious teaching.</note>.

To apply these things to our purpose and to our **Moses**: we willingly agree that one should not depart from the truth rashly or for a trivial reason. But truth that is brought forth without benefit is superfluous; that which is brought forth with grave harm is noxious. Now, our **Moses** was so situated with his people that he could not explain the refined origins of things to them either to their benefit or without causing harm. 

What if **Moses**, at the beginning of his creation-story <term>Cosmopoeia: From the Greek *kosmos* (world) and *poiein* (to make); refers to the narrative of the world's creation.</term>, had proposed the true system of the world? The Sun, meanwhile, who seems to us a most vigorous runner, completing the vast stadium of our sky in twelve hours, more or less, deceives us and plays tricks on our eyes. For he remains idle in his seat through day and night; and he entrusts that labor to the Earth, so that she might establish and measure out day and night and the different seasons of the year by her own motion. 

If **Moses** had begun his discourse in this way, would not the people have received him with laughter or disgust, as one telling absurdities and things foreign to common sense? And, not without grave harm to themselves, they would have regarded the holy man as if he were...

<header>*Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things.*</header>

I reply that it was not possible, nor safe, for **Moses** to completely omit the argument concerning the origin of the World or the creation of things. The neighboring Nations <note>original: *Gentes circumvicinæ*</note> had their own Cosmogonies, their own History, or "Physiology" <note>In the 17th century, "physiology" referred to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world and its laws.</note> regarding the world’s origin—most of which were flawed and hostile to true religion. The **Israelites** would have followed these or similar traditions and mythologies had they not been taught otherwise. If you do not give your daughter in marriage, she will find a husband for herself, perhaps from among the servants or the lowliest commoners. Likewise, unless you provide a people with their own faith, dogmas, and opinions, they will invent them for themselves, each according to his own intellect, his own passions, or his own vices.

Furthermore, what you might wish to object to in **Moses** can just as easily be objected to in **Christ** and the **Apostles**. The Future Life, whether in heaven or in hell, and the Final Judgment, cannot be correctly understood by the common people in their literal truth. Should these things, therefore, have been suppressed in silence or passed over with a "dry foot" <note>original: *sicco pede*, an idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without addressing the complexities.</note> by **Christ** and the **Apostles**? The Evangelical and Apostolic writings clearly testify to the contrary, as these things are frequently depicted there: not with scientific accuracy, to be sure, but through popular images that stick firmly in the memory and are suited to stirring the emotions. 

Thus, heaven is foreshadowed by the delights of Paradise and crowns of glory. Hell, however, is described by unquenchable fire, by extreme cold and darkness, and finally by worms gnawing at the skin and flesh. No less is the Day of Judgment described by the sound of the Trumpet, the opening of graves, the books of account laid open, and the raising of judgment seats. Thus it seemed good to the **Holy Spirit** to treat sacred matters in a human way, even in the full light of the **Gospel**. Those things which could not be grasped by us if proposed in their naked form and by exact reason, the Spirit did not think should be kept silent, but rather transformed into new shapes—into other shapes, I say, which

...so that they might be more vivid and conspicuous to everyone, driving people toward piety and firmly deterring them from evil. These arguments can easily be applied to the **defense of Moses** <note>original: *vindicias Mosis*</note>, who, led by the same purpose, did not omit the doctrine of the World’s origin—which is inexplicable to the common people in its pure form—but rather arranged and explained it using a method that would best serve religion, without overly burdening the intellect of the people.

Finally, an objection is raised: if it is permissible to depart from the literal wording of **Moses** in the first chapters of **Genesis**, why not in the rest as well? Where must we stop? By what limit or what law? Should we fear that, through a lightness of mind, the historical and literal sense might perish everywhere? I respond that there is a common and very well-known rule among interpreters: ***One must nowhere depart from the letter without necessity.*** With this as our guide, we will be safe; and if I have violated this law anywhere, I wish those things to be considered unsaid.

Furthermore, it should be noted that when the natural world is discussed in the Holy Scriptures, one may depart more freely from the literal sense in those passages than in others. Indeed, it is evident from a thousand examples that in this subject matter, the sacred authors spoke <term>anthropopathically <gloss>original: ἀνθρωποπαθῶς; speaking of divine or natural things in human terms or according to human emotions</gloss></term> or <term>laodogmatically <gloss>original: λαοδογματικῶς; speaking according to the common opinions or prejudices of the people</gloss></term>. The "natural light" <note>A common Enlightenment-era term for human reason.</note> is a gift from God, and it should not be hidden "under a bushel" or "in a shroud" <note>References to Matthew 5:15 and Luke 19:20; Burnet argues that reason is a talent that must be used, not buried.</note>. Rather, whenever there is a place for reason in the search for truth, we must use its help in unfolding the sacred oracles. It seems to me well-said that ***Philosophy is the interpreter of Scripture in natural matters***. However, by "philosophy," I do not mean something dry and shallow—a figment of an idle brain—but rather a philosophy that corresponds to the phenomena of nature, repeated experiments, and solid reasoning. Finally, in all things, whether we act as Theologians or Philosophers, we are bound to do so with a calm and moderate mind, and with the highest reverence and piety toward the Divine.

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things #

These seem to me the primary doubts, or main categories of objections, which might delay the reader, or perhaps deter them from embracing our view. Our *view*, specifically, is the one stating that *Moses*, having mostly bypassed physical truth, followed moral or—if I may put it this way—theological reasons in his narrative of the World's origin. Moses primarily established this: that God alone is the Author of the World, and that the origins, movements, and ends of all things are governed and established by His providence. And regarding the manner or order of the world’s beginning, although he turned away from the path of the sciences, he did not collapse into fables, trifles, or gross superstitions, as the cosmogonies <note>theories or stories about the origin of the universe</note> of the pagans are wont to do. If you compare them, you will easily recognize that the Mosaic account is much purer than all of them. You are familiar with the *Greek* account from *Hesiod* and others; the *Phoenician* from *Philo of Byblos*; and *Diodorus Siculus* relates the *Egyptian* version, as others do for other cultures. To these I now wish to add the *Arabian* and *Islamic* accounts, so that you may see and distinguish the character of each.

<margin>
Abraham Ecchellensis,
*History of the Arabs*,
chapter 9.
</margin>
The Arabs say that God, the Best and Greatest, when about to establish the universe, first of all created *a certain very large Tablet* and a *Pen*, so that He might record upon it every single thing that was to happen until the end of the world. *This having been done*, He brought forth a *white Pearl*; when He looked upon it with the eye of majesty, it was liquefied into waters, from which the *Abyss* emerged. This was followed by the production of the *air*, then of *Souls* and *Angels*. Moreover, as God worked upon the rest of the Creatures, He created a *white union* <note>original: *album unionem*; a "union" was a historical term for a large, high-quality pearl found alone</note>, which immediately liquefied at the divine gaze and began to boil, emitting smoke upward and foaming. Once this was done, God established *seven Earths* from its foam, as well as the waves and the mountains. From the smoke, however, He made an equal number of heavens. And in this way, Heaven and Earth were completed according to the Arabian traditions.

Far more absurd than these is the **Islamic Creation Story** <note>original: "Cosmopœia Mahometana"</note>: which occurs in the *Book of Subtleties on the Knowledge of Truths*, and proceeds in this manner. First of all, the **Light of Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahometi Lux," referring to the *Nur Muhammad*, a concept in Islamic cosmology where the prophet's light preceded creation</note> was created by God, bearing the appearance and form of a **Peacock**. God placed this in a brilliant white pearl, which He hung upon a most beautiful tree, where for about a thousand years it celebrated the Creator with the highest praises. However, when Muhammad beheld this light, he was completely drenched in sweat: Then, from the sweat of his head, God created the **Angels**: from the sweat of his face, the **Throne**, the **Tablet**, the **Pen**, the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the **Heaven**, the **Stars**, and whatever is in the heavens. Finally, to omit other most absurd things, from the sweat of his feet He created the entire **Earth**, and whatever is upon it.

Of such a kind are the creation stories <note>original: "Cosmogoniæ"</note> of foreign nations—futile and base. **Moses** has nothing related to or of the same character as these. If he departed from nature and from physical truth, he did so honorably and modestly, as a cultivator of piety and one devoted to the public welfare. We mentioned the saying of **Solon** <note>one of the Seven Sages of Greece, known for his legal reforms</note> above, who, when asked if he had established the best laws for the Athenians, replied: *The best, indeed, that they were willing to receive.* This is no less true regarding the doctrine and institutions of the **Hebrew Lawgiver** <note>Moses</note>. To anyone asking if Moses constructed the best Creation Story for the Israelites, it must likewise be answered: The best that they were able to bear or comprehend. That which is simply "the best" often cannot be attained in human affairs; but a wise and sensible man holds as his end and goal that which is the best among practical—or, if I may use the word, *practicable*—things. Neither do I find anything in the Mosaic writings or deeds that disagrees with or wanders from this rule. And therefore, in my judgment, he has always deserved and will deserve to be held as the greatest of the ancient sages and prophets.

Yet it does not escape our notice that the Mosaic account of origins <note>original: "Origines Mosaicas," referring to the account of creation in the Book of Genesis</note> has a poor reputation among foreign authors, and is held in mockery by some. **Celsus** <note>a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and early critic of Christianity</note> calls it an *old wives' tale*. **Simplicius** <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle</note>, somewhat more modestly, calls it a *mythical tradition* <note>original: "fabulosam traditionem"</note> taken from the **Egyptians**. 'If Philoponus points here to the Lawgiver of the Jews <note>Moses</note> speaking in this way: "In the beginning God made the Heaven and the Earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed; and darkness was over the deep; and the spirit of God moved over the water." But if he should think this to be the origin of the world, and that it was temporal <note>meaning it happened at a specific point in time rather than being eternal</note>, I would have him know that this is nothing other than a mythical tradition, extracted, for instance, from Egyptian myths.*

### Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

<note>original Greek: "ἐκ ἔστι δ' ἔνυδρον ζῶον ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλὰ χερσαῖον καὶ ἐναέριον..."</note>
Man is not a water-dwelling animal, but rather one belonging to the land and the air; and because he shares the light with many other creatures, God created many elevations and depressions in the earth. In this way, the water (either all or most of it) is gathered into the hollows, hiding the earth beneath it, while in other places the earth stands out, hiding the water beneath itself—except for that amount which is useful for the human race and for the animals and plants that live around it.

<margin>*Theory of the Earth, book 1, chapter 5*</margin>
Strabo calls this the work of **providence**, not of nature. He understands this as **extraordinary providence** <note>a direct, miraculous intervention by God that bypasses natural laws</note>; for **ordinary providence** is considered one and the same as the law and order of nature. This Author, as you can see, follows the very same path that **Moses** pioneered. There is nothing inherently wrong with this explanation, except that it violates that rule of the Philosophers: *Nature must not be abandoned without necessity.* For there is no physical necessity to manually elevate lands or to draw waters down into ditches and pits in order to build the first habitable world—as we have demonstrated elsewhere <note>referring to Burnet's own theory that the original earth was a smooth crust over the waters</note>. However, for other reasons which we have often pointed out, it was necessary for Moses to arrange the parts of his world and its entire structure according to the immediate command of the Deity and the will of Providence.

<margin>The word "Tyrrhenia" <note>Etruria, or ancient Tuscany</note></margin>
I have briefly touched upon these points from **Strabo** <note>a Greek geographer, c. 63 BC–24 AD</note> to show that the Mosaic **Cosmogony** <note>account of the world's creation</note> is not merely an "Egyptian fable," as **Simplicius** <note>a 6th-century philosopher who critiqued the Bible</note> argued, but was composed using a method unique to itself. Others later imitated this method, some briefly and others more fully. I believe that the account reported to us by **Suidas** <note>the author of a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> regarding the **Etruscan** Cosmogony was actually transcribed from our **Hexaemeron** <term>Hexaemeron: the theological study of the six days of creation described in Genesis</term>, with only a few changes. To be sure, the philosophy of the Etruscans was very ancient—older than all Greek philosophy, if I am not mistaken—but the doctrines of the ancients are not infrequently mixed and interpolated with more recent ideas. This occurs quite often in that "patchwork" collection by Suidas.

Finally, **Rabbi Moses Maimonides** <note>a major 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> often mentions his **Sabians** or **Zabiists** <note>a mysterious ancient sect often associated with star-worship</note>; he considers them even older than Abraham, let alone Moses. And in their books...

...even a tiny spark <note>original: *tillum*, likely the end of *scintillum*, meaning a small spark or trace.</note> remains among other authors, I have nothing further to say.

Finally, it is often debated whether Moses received these "Origins" of his through Tradition from someone else, or if he was the first to establish them. I do not see how this can be defined with certainty: but it seems much more likely to me that this **World-making** <note>original: *Cosmopœia*—the process or account of the creation of the universe.</note>, or elementary instruction in Natural science—just like his Law, or elementary instruction in Moral science—was first given to or conceived by Moses. It seems that nothing of this kind had been previously accepted by any nation, nor established by any philosopher or legislator. But enough has been said regarding doubts and objections.
