# The Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

...[vi]sible and earthly; others, finally, have established a **Paradise** of both kinds. <margin>*In the Exposition to Sabinus.*</margin> St. **Ambrose** <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and one of the four original Doctors of the Church.</note> reduced this to even narrower terms: for, when asked by Sabinus in a letter what he thought of Paradise, he replied that he had written an entire book on the subject. Having recounted the opinions of others, he says that they all agree on one point: that it is **Spiritual**. <margin>*Library of the Fathers, vol. 6, p. 663.*</margin> Finally, **Anastasius Sionita** <note>A 7th-century monk and theologian, also known as Anastasius of Sinai.</note> in his *Hexaëmeron* <term>Hexaëmeron: A traditional title for a theological treatise explaining the six days of creation</term>, lists a great many authors who, before his time, interpreted Paradise allegorically. But we shall not dwell on these. I only wish to note that these differences of opinion regarding Paradise did not provoke anger or enmity; for, as St. **Augustine** <margin>*On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius, ch. 23.*</margin> advised, this is done without harm to faith or good morals. Therefore, with our friendship intact, we may hold varying opinions about Paradise. But let us move on to others.

When **Celsus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and early critic of Christianity who argued that the Bible was poorly written and illogical.</note> objected to the Christians that their oracles were too obscure and uncertain, **Origen** <note>A foundational Christian scholar from Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) who famously argued that Scripture has three levels of meaning: the literal, the moral, and the spiritual.</note> rightly responded that in those matters regarding the correction of morals and common utility—and thus for all kinds of people—there is nothing doubtful in the Sacred Scriptures. However, those matters that require deeper study and are not for common use are mostly hidden from all but the wise under various "shadows" of speech.

*The prophets, therefore, spoke whatever was useful for the listeners to understand immediately, contributing to the correction of morals without any concealment, according to the will of God; but whatever was more mystical and visionary, involving contemplation beyond common hearing, they declared through enigmas and allegories, and what are called "dark sayings," and through so-called parables or proverbs.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ μὲν οὖν προφῆται ὅσα ἦν αὐτόθεν νοηθῆναι τοῖς ἀκούουσι χρήσιμα, καὶ συμβαλλόμενα τῇ τῶν ἦθων ἐπανορθώσει, χωρὶς πάσης ἐπικρύψεως, κατὰ τὸ βούλημα, τοῦ Θεοῦ, εἰρήκασιν· ὅσα δὲ μυστικώτερα ἦν, καὶ ἐποπτικώτερα, καὶ ἐχόμενα θεωρίας τῆς ὑπὲρ τὴν πάνδημον ἀκοὴν, ταῦτα δι' αἰνιγμάτων καὶ ἀλληγοριῶν, καὶ τῶν καλουμένων σκοτεινῶν λόγων, καὶ τῶν ὀνομαζομένων παραβολῶν ἢ παροιμιῶν, ἀπεφήναντο.</note>

# Philosophical Archaeologies; or,

This has been observed by others no less clearly. For instance, **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> says: *God, being in Himself unchangeable and immutable, adapts Himself to human weakness. God often speaks and establishes laws, not according to the fullness of His own power, but according to what we are capable of hearing.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ Θεὸς ὢν ἄτρεπτὸς κὶ ἀναλλοίωτος, ἁρμόζεται πρὸς τὴν ἀσθένειαν ἀνθρωπίνην. Λαλεῖ ὁ Θεὸς, κὶ νομοθετεῖ πολλάκις, οὐχ ὡς αὐτὸς δύναται, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἡμεῖς ἀκούειν δυνάμεθα." The author also provides a Latin translation of this Greek passage.</note> Truly, that which is useless should be kept silent, and that which is harmful should be concealed. The principle of what is Good, or Best, must always be the primary consideration.

Finally, to summarize several points at once: according to the doctrine of the **Church Fathers**, many things in the sacred scriptures were said or done <term>according to economy</term> <note>From the Greek *oikonomia*, meaning "stewardship" or "management." In theology, it refers to God's "management" of revelation—revealing truth gradually or in forms that humans can handle.</note> or "economically," as they like to say. Thus, they are often accustomed to explaining certain difficult passages—which seem far removed from the naked truth—as having been spoken *by way of dispensation*, or by way of <term>accommodation</term> <note>The idea that God "lisps" or speaks in simplified "baby talk" so that finite humans can understand infinite truths.</note> to some useful purpose, when the nature of the subject requires it. The Fathers apply this type of explanation to various cases; for example, when **Christ** says that He does not know the Day of Judgment, they say this was spoken "economically."

<margin>
*Treasury of the Holy Trinity*, Discourse 22, near the end.
</margin>
For Christ acts by "economy," says **Cyril of Alexandria**, in saying He does not know that hour, even though He is not truly ignorant of it. <note>original Greek: "Οἰκονομεῖ γὰρ Χριστὸς... μὴ εἰδέναι λέγων τὴν ὥραν ἐκείνην, κὶ μὴ ἀληθῶς ἀγνοεῖ."</note> **Photius** <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893 AD), a powerful Patriarch of Constantinople and a massive figure in Byzantine scholarship.</note> says much the same in his *Letter 228* concerning this same speech of Christ: *That He was unwilling to tell the disciples things which were not yet useful for them to learn—this method is not foreign to the benevolent providence of God toward men. He acted skillfully, presenting and feigning ignorance through "economy" for the sake of the divine plan.* <note>original Greek: "Τὸ μὴ βούλεσθαι τοῖς μαθηταῖς εἰπεῖν... μεθοδεύοιτο δ᾽ ἂν, ἐξ οἰκονομίας σχηματιζομένην τὴν ἄγνοιαν."</note>

# Philosophical Archaeologies: or,

...not to correspond to the reasons and calculations of philosophers. For it was not his entrusted business to teach those barbarians the theorems or the intricacies of philosophy, but rather religion, the worship of the true God, and His precepts. These things were no less suited to our Moses long ago than they are to a modern apostle to the Indians <note>The author refers to 17th-century missionaries; he argues that just as a missionary simplifies the Gospel for unreached tribes, Moses simplified the origin of the world for the ancient Israelites.</note>; indeed, much more so, if we compare the times and the peoples. But enough on this subject.

Fourthly and finally, those who cling stubbornly to the Mosaic letter and words in every instance must be warned: do not admit anything unworthy of God or our religion, lest you wound the majesty of the divine power with your own irreverence. We Christians, at any rate, worship the supreme power, God the Best and Greatest—or, as the common phrase goes, the *Infinitely Perfect Being*. Therefore, nothing should be attributed to God in our theology that is unbefitting an *Infinitely Perfect Being*. 

Do you really wish for us to say that the <margin>Genesis 3</margin> *Infinitely Perfect Being* descended from heaven, walked in the garden in the cool of the evening, and called out to Adam as he hid among the trees? That the *Infinitely Perfect Being* fashioned *coats of skins* and dressed the man and woman in them? Along with all the other things reported in that conversation between the *Infinitely Perfect Being* and Adam, the woman, and the serpent?

When we attribute things to God—not merely in words, but as actual facts—that are contrary to the divine nature, we sin against the dignity of the Deity. If this were done with a malicious spirit and regarding a grave matter, it would not only be an insult, but would take on the appearance of blasphemy. We must therefore be careful on both sides: we should not lightly or without just cause leap away from the literal words; nor, on the other hand, should we interpret things that were spoken <term>popularly</term> <note>original Greek: *ἰδιωτικῶς* (idiotikōs). In this context, it refers to "accommodation"—speaking in a simple, non-scientific way that the average person can understand.</note> with a superstitious weakness that damages the character of the Deity.

<margin>Miscellanies, Book 7, page 791.</margin> Clement of Alexandria rightly said: "The quality of what is worthy of God..."

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

A disposition is that which preserves what is fitting to God; only he who acts worthily of God is beloved of God. <note>original Greek: "ἕξις ἔστι τὸ πρέπον τῷ θεῷ σῴζουσα· θεοφιλὴς ὁ θεοπρεπὴς μόνος."</note> *The only friend of God is he who preserves for God what is worthy of His nature.*

No less must the dignity of our religion be preserved. The enemies of the Christian name used to seize the opportunity from the Mosaic writings—when they were explained too crudely—to insult or mock our Hebrew religion and our own as if it were ignorant or full of fables. <margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 6, p. 309.</margin> We gave examples previously in the writings of *Simplicius* <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who criticized Christian doctrines.</note> and in *Celsus*: who, among other things, calls the Mosaic account of the generation of the world "quite foolish." <note>original Greek: "μάλα εὐηθικὴν"; Latin: "admodum stolidam."</note> Now let us hear *Julian* <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism and wrote extensively against Christianity.</note>, who frequently harps on the same string. <margin>Cyril, *Against Julian*, book 3, objection 2.</margin> Speaking of the *Dialogue between Eve and the Serpent*, *Julian* asks, *How do such things differ from the myths invented by the Greeks?* <note>original Greek: "Τί διαφέρει τῶν παρὰ Ἕλλησι πεπλασμένων μύθων, τὰ τοιάδε;"</note> And concerning the *Garden of Eden*, <margin>Ibid. objection 1.</margin> and the *Woman* given to *Adam* as a helper—who nevertheless deceived him before evening—he says boldly and openly, *For these things are entirely mythical.* <note>original Greek: "ταῦτα γὰρ ἔστι μυθώδη παντελῶς"; Latin: "Hæc prorsus sunt fabulosa."</note> <margin>Ibid. objection 4.</margin> Finally, concerning the *ejection of Adam* from *Paradise* because he ate the apple—lest by tasting of the tree of life he should become a God—Julian has this to say: *Therefore, unless each of these things be a myth containing a secret theory (which is what I believe), those accounts are full of much blasphemy against God.* <note>original Greek: "τούτων τοίνυν ἕκαστον, εἰ μὴ μῦθος εἴη, ἔχων ἀπόρρητον θεωρίαν, ὅπερ ἐγὼ νενόμικα, πολλῆς γέμουσιν οἱ λόγοι περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ βλασφημίας."</note> You see how much offense has arisen among outsiders because they judged the things written by *Moses* in these narratives to be "unworthy of God" <note>original Greek: "ἀθεοπρεπῆ"</note> and utterly beneath a religion sent from heaven; that is, if we stick only to the "skin and bark" <note>A metaphor for the literal surface level of the text versus its deeper, "pithy" meaning.</note> of the words. Therefore, that interpretation seems praiseworthy to me which removes these scandals and this hatred from our religion.

# Philosophic Archaeologies: or,

Finally, Moses must be interpreted in such a way that he neither disagrees with himself, nor with other sacred authors, in his accounts of origins. For it must necessarily result in damage and disgrace to our religion if its oracles are at odds with one another. Thus, if Moses in his <term>Hexaëmeron</term> <note>From the Greek for "six days," referring to the biblical account of the creation of the world in Genesis 1.</note> presents us with the Modern Earth <note>original: "Terram Hodiernam"</note> in place of the Primeval Earth <note>original: "Primigeniæ"</note>; and afterwards introduces those phenomena which cannot be reconciled with the modern Earth—such as the longevity of those living before the flood, the breaking open of the Abyss during the Deluge, and the origin of the Rainbow only after the flood—then the *Hexaëmeron* must be explained in such a way that Moses does not depart from or disagree with himself. Furthermore, if the Royal Prophet <note>A traditional title for King David, the attributed author of the Psalms.</note> celebrates, among the wondrous works of God, the *Earth founded upon the waters* (Ps. 24:2) and the *Earth stretched out above the waters* (Ps. 136:6); and if Wisdom likewise records (Prov. 8:27) a *Circle drawn around the Abyss*; and finally if Saint Peter describes the Earth before the flood as being so constituted out of water and through water by the word of God, that it was thereby liable to a deluge of waters (2 Pet. 3:5, 6)—all these things, I say, must be so handled and composed that the common phrasing of the *Hexaëmeron* does not overwhelm both the author himself and many others of the same sacred rank. Especially since, by a suitable interpretation of one chapter—which is necessary for many other reasons—Moses can be reconciled both with himself and with the others.

However, I bring these matters forward as if arranged in a battle line, not because it is my pleasure to set the Sacred Writers against one another—the Prophets and the Apostles—so that in the dust stirred up between such great men, I might meanwhile slip away and escape. But when we are weighed down by the authority of a single passage or writer, it seems only fair to substitute another or several on the opposite scale; so that the case may return to an equilibrium at least, if it does not tip in our favor. But enough on these matters.

# Ancient Doctrine on the Origin of Things

To finally bring an end to this **Treatise**, a few things must be mentioned: though I am most convinced of the things we have discussed regarding the **Mosaic Origins** <note>The "Mosaic Origins" refers to the account of the creation of the world as described by Moses in the Book of Genesis.</note>, I would wish them to be regarded by others, however they see fit, only in the place of an *Attempt* <note>original: "Tentaminis"; the author is signaling that his work is a preliminary exploration or a "trial" of ideas rather than dogmatic certainty.</note>. We are often blind to our own errors, yet sharp-sighted in noticing the errors of others; therefore, I shall neither neglect nor despise second thoughts, nor the advice of others. 

Meanwhile, for what remains, let us close all things by pouring out prayers to God, that He might deign to forgive our errors, just as we forgive one another. May He be mindful of and take pity on the distress and darkness by which human souls are oppressed, in this flesh, in this prison; may He illuminate us more and more each day with His own light, and with Him leading the way, may He finally lead us to His celestial **Kingdom**, through **our Lord**, **Jesus Christ**.

# APPENDIX.

## *Regarding the modern Brahmins among the Indians, and their doctrines.*

<margin>Book 1, chapter 3.</margin>
Since we mentioned above the modern **Brahmins** <note>original: "Brachmanum." Historically, European writers used "Brahman" or "Brachman" to refer to the priestly and scholarly caste of India.</note> among the Indians—whom many signs and the similarities of their affairs and studies give us reason to believe are descended from an ancient stock—I think it will be neither unpleasant nor foreign to our purpose to weave in here, by way of an Appendix, some things regarding their doctrines about the **Origins and revolutions** of the world. These doctrines are usually neglected by most people because they are handed down through mythology and obscure the truth with the thick shadows of fables.

Under the name of "Indians," we here include, besides the **Chinese Empire**, the **Kingdom of Indostan** (or that of the **Great Mughal**), the Kingdoms of **Siam**, **Malabar**, **Cochinchina** <note>original: "Chinquachina." This refers to the historical region of southern Vietnam.</note>, **Coromandel**, and any others known to us in the East that have somewhat cast off barbarism. In each of these, there is a certain class of Philosophers or Theologians; and in the kingdoms of Indostan, Siam, and other neighbors, they seem to be the offspring of the ancient Brahmins. They are separated and distinguished from the rest of the people by their customs, their way of life, their doctrine, and a language unique to themselves. They possess a certain **tradition** <note>original: "Cabalam." The author uses this term to mean a secret, orally transmitted body of knowledge, rather than the specific Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, or a doctrine passed down from one to another, which is unknown to the common people. This doctrine does not pursue individual points or the minute details of Philosophy, as is the custom of modern Philosophers:

philosophy : but, like the **Natural Theology** <note>Natural Theology refers to knowledge of God or spiritual matters obtained through reason and the observation of nature, rather than through supernatural revelation.</note> of the ancients, it treats of God, of the World, of the origin and end of things, and of the cycles of the World: of the primeval state of nature, and its repeated renewals. These doctrines are passed down more clearly by some, and more obscurely or through fables by others; but they clearly show that these ideas were originally scattered among these nations, where traces of them still remain. It is pleasing, by way of example, to note briefly certain chapters of this modern-barbaric Theology or Philosophy from recent travel accounts.

It matters little from which Kingdom or Region we begin. Very great is that of the Mughal, called **Indostan**, which many Europeans have visited—witnesses who are suitable and worthy of belief. In this kingdom, besides the Muslims, there are Gentiles or Pagans. And among these Gentiles there is a certain tribe or order of men who bear the title of Wise Men, Priests, or Philosophers, and perform those duties. They have a language peculiar to themselves, which they call **Sanskrit** <note>original: "Hanscrit." The author is referring to Sanskrit, the sacred liturgical language of Hinduism.</note>, or the "Pure Language." In this language, they keep certain very ancient Books which they call **Sacred**, and they say these were given by God to the great Prophet **Brahma** <note>original: "Brahme."</note>, just as the Law was once given to Moses for the Israelites.

<margin>*China Illustrated, part 3, chapter 7.*</margin>
You can find the alphabet of this Brahmanic Language in the works of **Athanasius Kircher** <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar and polymath who published "China Illustrata" in 1667.</note>, as described by the hand of Father **Heinrich Roth**, who for many years devoted himself to the study of Brahmanic literature among the Indians. In this language, they write down and conceal not only their Theology but all kinds of Philosophical systems.

Beyond the **transmigration of souls** <note>original: "μετεμψύχωσιν" (metempsychōsin). The belief that the soul moves into a new body after death.</note> and the **abstinence from living creatures** <note>original: "ἐποχὴν ἐμψύχων" (epochēn empsychōn). Referring to the practice of vegetarianism or non-violence toward animals.</note>, which are very ancient doctrines, they philosophize in the manner of the ancients regarding the creation of the universe and its end or destruction. They explain these things through a "coming forth" or an "outflowing"...

### Appendix.

...the flow of all things from God, and the return or retraction into the same. They express this in a **Kabbalistic** <note>In the 17th century, "Kabbalistic" was often used broadly to mean a mystical or symbolic interpretation of the divine, rather than referring strictly to Jewish tradition.</note> or **Mythological** manner. For they imagine that a certain immense **Spider** <note>This metaphor of the universe as a spider’s web is a Western attempt to describe the Vedantic concept of "emanational" creation, where the world is made from the substance of the Creator rather than created out of nothing.</note> is the First Cause of things: which, having drawn out matter from its own bowels, wove the web of this universe and arranged it with wonderful skill. Meanwhile, She sits in the citadel of her work, and feels, rules, and moderates the movement of every part. At last, when she has played enough in decorating and contemplating her web, she retracts the threads she had unrolled, and thus reabsorbs everything into herself, and the entire nature of created things vanishes into nothingness. In this way, the modern **Brahmins** represent the world's origin, order, and destruction. Nor do these things differ much from the opinions of the ancients mentioned above (*Book 1, chapter 7, pages 63, 64, etc.*) if, once the mythical husk is removed, we see the kernel <note>The author is suggesting that beneath "pagan" fables lies a "kernel" of ancient, universal truth (Prisca Theologia) that aligns with his own philosophical views.</note>. More about the Gentiles of **Hindustan** <note>original: "Indostanis." A geographical term for northern India.</note>, if time permits, can be read in the works of **Henry Lord**, **François Bernier**, and other travelers who have investigated their literature more diligently.

In the Kingdom of **Siam** <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note>, or the Siamese Kingdom, bordering the **Mughal Empire**, there is the same lineage of Brahmins. **Guy Tachard**, of the Society of **Jesuits**, who accompanied the French Ambassador to the King of Siam, reported these things to us concerning their Philosophy or Theology.
<margin>Voyage to Siam, p. 39.</margin>
They say that the first humans were larger than those of today, longer-lived, and lived for many centuries, immune to diseases. They say the current Earth, dried up by long heat and burning, will be consumed by fire, once the Ocean is dried up, the mountains melted, and the entire surface of the Earth leveled. These things I find in the aforementioned author. However, there is more in others, which a recent poet has compiled and explained playfully in these verses:

The Siamese Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes Siamenses." The author uses "Brahmin" as a general term for Eastern priests, here specifically those in Thailand.</note> teach not only that the present Earth is destined to perish, and that by Fire, but also that a new Earth will be born from its very ashes. This will be an Earth *without a sea*, just as the Prophet John saw; and without the annual changes of the seasons, *blessed by a perennial spring*, exactly as we described in the fourth book of our *Theory* <note>The author is referring to his own work, *Telluris Theoria Sacra* (The Sacred Theory of the Earth), where he argued the primitive and future Earth lacks a tilted axis and thus has no seasons.</note>. One may indeed marvel that a semi-barbarous nation has retained these doctrines all the way from the time of Noah; for from nowhere else than tradition could the knowledge of these things have reached them. Nor could this tradition have flowed or taken its beginnings from anywhere else but Noah and the antediluvian Sages <note>Wise men who lived before the Great Flood.</note>. But from which author or Siamese itinerary <note>A travel journal or geographical account.</note> the **Poet** took these verses, is not yet known to me.

Furthermore, the Kingdom of *Coromandel* <note>The Coromandel Coast is the southeastern coastal region of the Indian subcontinent.</note>, on the southern coast of India, has its own Brahmins <note>original: *Brachmanes*. The priestly and scholarly caste in Indian society.</note>: whose customs and doctrine were explored with no little diligence by Abraham Roger <note>Abraham Rogerius (d. 1649), a Dutch chaplain whose work was one of the first European accounts of Hinduism.</note>, who wrote *The Open Door to the Secrets of Heathenism* <note>original: *Januam apertam ad arcana Gentilismi*, published posthumously in 1651.</note>, having stayed there for many years. Moreover, they assert that there are several worlds existing simultaneously in different regions of the universe, and even several successive worlds; namely, that the same World is destroyed and renewed according to certain cycles of time. They hold that our terrestrial World began from a certain golden age and is destined to perish by fire. Finally, they retain the doctrine of the *World Egg* <note>original: *Ovo mundano*. An ancient cosmological motif where the universe or a creator deity is born from an egg.</note>, comparing the World to an egg, as the ancients—both Greek and Barbarian <note>In this classical context, "Barbarian" refers to non-Greek cultures, such as the Egyptians or Persians.</note>—were accustomed to do.

Robertus Nobilius* (1577–1656), an Italian Jesuit missionary famous for adopting the dress and customs of a Brahmin to convert the local nobility.</note>, the founder of the so-called Madurai mission, spent a non-negligible part of his life; he was learned in both the common Indian language and the Brahmin language <note>The author likely refers to Sanskrit, the liturgical language of the Brahmins.</note>. # Appendix.

...secret alphabet <note>original: *alphabetum arcanum*. Likely referring to the sacred scripts used by the Brahmins or Buddhist monks mentioned on the previous page.</note> so highly that, as if it were something sacred and most ancient, they are accustomed to inscribe it upon their idols.

Finally, I pass over the Muslims <note>original: *Mahometanos*</note>, who are spread widely throughout the East under various rulers, as they are a recent and unphilosophical <note>original: *ἀφιλοσόφους* (aphilosophous). The author reflects the common 17th-century European view that contemporary Islamic culture had moved away from its earlier "Golden Age" of philosophy.</note> people. What the Egyptian Priest once said to Solon <note>Solon (c. 630–560 BCE) was a famous Athenian statesman; the dialogue mentioned is found in Plato’s *Timaeus*.</note>, *“You Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek,”* applies much more here, with the names changed. Nor did the Egyptian explain the reason for his saying poorly: *“You are all young in your souls; for you have in them no ancient tradition, no old renown, nor any learning gray with time.”* <note>original Greek: "Νέοι ἐστὲ τὰς ψυχὰς πάντες· οὐδεμίαν γὰρ ἐν αὐταῖς ἔχετε, δι᾿ ἀρχαίαν ἀκοήν, παλαιὰν δόξαν, οὐδὲ μάθημα χρόνῳ πολιὸν οὐδέν."</note> These words fit perfectly with the Muslims, wherever they are scattered. They retain nothing of ancient wisdom, and their desire for dominion has stripped from them all love or study of good literature.

In Persia itself, where the mystical philosophy of the great Zoroaster <note>The ancient Iranian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism.</note> and the Magi once flourished, nothing remains today worthy of mention. Henry Lord <note>Henry Lord (b. 1563) was an English chaplain whose 1630 book provided early European accounts of the Parsi and Hindu religions.</note>, whom we named above, relates that when the Saracens flooded into Persia and defeated and killed King Jezdegird <note>Yazdegerd III (d. 651 AD), the last monarch of the Sasanian Empire.</note> around the year of Christ 628 <note>Historical records typically place the fall of the Sasanian Empire and the death of Yazdegerd slightly later, in the 640s and 651 AD.</note>, some of the Persians who could not bear the yoke of new servitude and a new religion took to ships and transported themselves and their belongings to India. Having sworn loyalty to the Indian Kings, they practiced their own religion and ancient worship with impunity. The same author reports several dogmas of these Indo-Persians <note>Known today as the Parsis.</note> concerning the origin, ages, and end of the world; but they are filled with so many fables that they seem hardly worth repeating.

And it should be noted in general regarding modern pagans <note>original: *Gentilibus*</note> that there sometimes survives among them...

<header>Appendix.</header>

...mention, except for some traces of the most ancient dogmas handed down from the fathers <note>original Greek: *πατροπαραδότων* (patroparadotōn)</note> concerning the natural world <term>natural world <gloss>original: Mundum naturalem; referring to the study of physics and the cosmos</gloss></term>. Yet these traces are covered over by neglect, filth, and grime; they are also for the most part burdened with fictional additions, even to the point of nausea, so that they are of no account or weight when the matter is dealt with through vigorous reasoning. Indeed, I pity the Eastern lands <note>original: *Terrarum Orientalium*</note>, once the first seat of the wise and formerly the most flourishing marketplace of good literature, which for many centuries now have been turned into a foul barbarism.

->Is there such great anger in heavenly minds?<-
<note>original Latin: *Tantæne Animis cœlestibus iræ?* This is a famous quotation from Virgil's *Aeneid* (1.11), often used to question why divine providence allows such suffering or decline.</note>

May God grant that we do not undergo these same changes, nor that He, in His anger, withdraw that light in which we rejoice in the West; but rather may He spread it more and more into all parts, until *the knowledge of God shall fill the earth, as the waters cover the sea.* <note>A reference to the biblical prophecy in Isaiah 11:9.</note>
